events.title: 140 Years of Everyday Moments
events.summary: As DFI Retail Group marks its 140th anniversary, Group Chief Executive Scott Price says the company’s future will depend on fulfilling the needs of our customers, investing in innovation and continuing to earn trust in the everyday moments that define modern retail. A morning stop for breakfast before work. A coffee picked up between meetings. A grocery stop on the way home. A stop for health and beauty products. A weekend trip to choose furniture for a growing family. A rewards offer that helps make the weekly shop go further. These are ordinary moments in Hong Kong life. Yet for DFI Retail Group, they represent the foundation of a business that has grown with the city for 140 years. Founded in Hong Kong in 1886, DFI has evolved from a local enterprise into one of Asia’s leading retail groups, serving millions of customers every week through brands spanning food, convenience, health and beauty, home furnishings and loyalty rewards. For Scott Price, Group Chief Executive of DFI Retail Group, the anniversary is not only a milestone in the company’s history. It is also a reminder of the role retailers play in daily life, often in ways that consumers rarely stop to consider. “Retail is woven into people’s lives in ways that often go unnoticed,” Price says. “It is there in the everyday decisions people make for themselves and their families. When retailers do their job well, they make life a little easier, a little healthier and a little more convenient.” DFI is marking its 140th anniversary under the theme “140 Years of Everyday Moments”, a phrase Price says reflects both the Group’s history and its continuing purpose. While anniversaries are often viewed as opportunities to look back, DFI is using the milestone to recognise the customers, team members and communities that have shaped the business, and to focus on how retail must continue adapting to changing expectations. Price explains that few industries are as closely connected to the routines of everyday life as retail. Across DFI’s portfolio, customers encounter its brands at different moments and for different needs. From supermarkets such as Market Place to Mannings and Guardian for health, wellness and self-care products, to 7-11 for a snack or collectible, and to IKEA for homewares, Price says its brands are connected by a common purpose: Serving Asia sustainably for generations with everyday moments. That role has become more important as lifestyles have changed. Consumers today are busier, more digitally connected and more discerning. They expect retailers to provide not only the right products, but also convenience, value, reliability and a seamless experience across physical and digital channels. In a city such as Hong Kong, where time, space and household budgets are constant considerations, retail is expected to work harder for customers. “Customers consistently value businesses that understand their needs and earn their trust,” Price says. “That has remained true even as the way people shop has changed dramatically.” Adapting Through Generations of Change Reflecting on DFI’s 140-year history, it has unfolded alongside Hong Kong’s transformation from a trading port into a global financial and commercial centre. During that period, the retail industry has been reshaped by urbanisation, rising living standards, changing family structures, technological innovation and the emergence of digital commerce. Shopping habits have shifted from traditional high-street transactions to omnichannel experiences, loyalty ecosystems and data-driven personalisation. For retailers, the challenge is no longer simply to operate stores. It is to understand customers across multiple touchpoints and respond quickly to changing needs. “Over more than four decades in Asia, I’ve seen enormous change in how people shop and interact with brands,” Price says. “But customers consistently value businesses that understand their needs and earn their trust.” Price explains that maintaining that trust requires continuous investment. As such, the Group is strengthening its capabilities in technology, talent, supply chain and customer engagement, while remaining focused on the fundamentals of quality, service and value. The company is also operating in a market where expectations of retailers are broadening. Customers increasingly want businesses to act responsibly, support healthier lifestyles and contribute positively to the communities in which they operate. For Price, these demands are not separate from the future of retail. They are central to it. Retailers that succeed over the long term, he believes, will be those able to combine operational excellence with a deeper understanding of people’s lives – how they shop, what they value, how they make choices and what kind of support they expect from trusted brands. In such a competitive and fast-changing sector, trust has become one of retail’s most important assets, Price says.

events.title: Residents fear there is no stopping $32b hyperscale data centre
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Western Downs residents fear being steamrolled as council assesses $32b data centre Ross Thornton says he is "mildly opposed" to the hyperscale data centre outside Dalby. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) A proposal to build a massive data centre near the Western Downs town of Dalby has locals wondering about the details of the plan. Anthropic has already signed a deal to use a portion of the site despite no approvals being issued. Some residents are petitioning against the plan, while others would like to meet and learn more. Dalby antiques dealer Ross Thornton is surrounded by history but worried about the future now that a $32 billion data centre is proposed just out of town. "People don't know enough about it," he said. Dalby is a country Queensland town 200 kilometres from Brisbane. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) The 70-year-old is calling for a public meeting amid fears residents will be steamrolled in the push to embrace the artificial intelligence boom. Anthropic has signed a deal in Australia to use the first of four buildings at the proposed hyperscale facility, well before it has received any approvals. The Queensland government confirmed it will be taking over from local governments as the "responsible assessor and coordinator" of data centre applications in a yet to be released planning framework. About 50 per cent of the Western Downs is cropping land. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) Mr Thornton has lived through the rapid industrialisation of the country town before, when the coal seam gas industry swept through more than a decade ago. "It caused a boom-bust cycle and no-one wants that," he said. "[We want to know] what's the impact going to be … and any of the pros and cons relating to it." Dalby antiques dealer Ross Thornton wants a public town hall for more information on the proposed data centre. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) A petition to parliament opposing the Western Downs Digital Park has gained more than 21,000 signatures — more than any petition currently open in Queensland. "We know that when big business comes in, the locals don't have a say," Angela Prenzler, who has been promoting the petition, said. Angela Prenzler has lived in Dalby all her life and is concerned about the proposed data centre. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) The Dalby resident said she was sceptical of the developer's plans to predominantly use rain and recycled water for its operations. "We are always in drought," Ms Penzler said. She said the online petition was gaining traction, including in other country areas. "They know it could happen in their regional town too," Ms Prenzler said. Dalby businessman Doug Machin, who owns a machinery business, a café and a grocery shop in town, feels conflicted about the project. Doug Machin and his daughter at the Dalby Machinery Centre. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) "You never knock back development," he said, then added it would be challenging to source the suggested 1,500 jobs required to build the data centre. "If you went to most businesses and farmers, we just don't seem to be able to get the [workers]." Unlike New South Wales and Victoria, Queensland has no dedicated data centre planning pathway. The Crisafulli government said it was in the process of developing a framework that would "mirror its reforms to renewable energy development". "This will ensure a consistent and transparent framework across the state, as many councils don't include data centres in their planning schemes, which creates confusion and inconsistency," the government said in a statement. "Any deals done must be with the backing of councils and communities." The Western Downs region is known as the "energy capital" of Queensland but has historically been an agricultural area. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) Western Downs Mayor Andrew Smith said he had been assured the project in his region would remain under his council's purview — but it may be out of the council's hands. Singapore-based developer Zerra DC has applied for "prescribed project" status, which means Queensland's coordinator-general could step in and fast-track approvals to prevent "unnecessary delays". "We've had good conversations with the state. We're confident in our ability to assess large scale development," he said. Chinchilla resident Shay Dougall earned her doctorate researching the impacts of the coal seam gas industrialisation of the Western Downs and says history should guide decision-making. Shay Dougall says residents deserve to have a say about what happens in their area.

events.title: Short-stay operators have mixed reactions to SA's register proposal
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Short-stay accommodation providers have mixed response to SA register plan Jenny Bickley says renting out her property on a short-term basis is more profitable than a traditional rental. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) South Australia is set to join New South Wales and Western Australia with a registry for short-stay accommodation. The scheme is still being shaped but the initial feedback from operators has been mixed, with some raising concerns about security and the impact on local government decisions. Public consultation closes on October 30. Accountant Jenny Bickley makes about $45,000 in profit each year from guests hiring her dual-abode property in Mount Gambier. "The Airbnb model is way better than renting," she said. While Ms Bickley is one of many South Australians who run a short-stay accommodation business, it is not exactly clear how many there actually are. Jenny Bickley says most of her guests are tourists. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) Last year, the state government wrapped up its inquiry into the sector amid nationwide concerns about the model affecting housing and rental affordability. Among the takeaways: SA lacked the data. The committee floated a registration scheme, a concept already seen in Western Australia and New South Wales. Jenny Bickley is concerned about "severe security risks" from a short-stay accommodation register. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) The Short Term Accommodation Association Australia (STAAA) backed a statewide register but wanted the approach reconsidered and warned of "unnecessary duplication". The details have not been locked in, but a discussion paper indicated councils could apply their own land-use codes and decide rates, something the STAAA was not keen on. "We need one state, one register and one consistent registration system," executive director Keiran Craig-Jones said. Ms Bickley, who fought council rate hikes in Mount Gambier, believed registration could help shake any "cowboys" operating unlawfully but echoed the STAAA's concerns. Ms Bickley said most of her booking were people visiting the town for events. Fourth generation farmer David Galpin entered the world of short-stays last year when he pitched his purpose-built paddock-view property in Penola as a luxury escape. Mr Galpin welcomed the register and believed it could inform the family's future business moves and even lead to more short-stay rentals. David Galpin says despite his research he does not have a "full picture" of the supply of short-stay accommodation. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) Ms Bickley said she understood the benefit for government decision-making, but was concerned about potential security issues. "Nobody actually knows the location [of my property] until they complete the booking," she said. Keiran Craig-Jones says legislation should be clear about exactly what information is collected and for what purpose. ( Supplied ) Mr Galpin was less concerned by the risks of a public register given his farm was "different to having a flat or something in a city or town". Ms Craig-Jones said while security was a "legitimate issue to consider", she was not aware of any increased burglary, squatting or similar offending following registers in other jurisdictions. Short-stay accommodation challenges National Shelter chief executive Jackson Hills said there were hundreds of local government areas nationwide, but about 40 or 50 faced "a much bigger challenge" around short-stay accommodation. In certain hotspots, such as Noosa in Queensland , he said policymakers may have "got the balance wrong" given shortages in the local workforce. Jackson Hills says knowing the real number of short-stay accommodation places would better inform decisions. ( Supplied ) Mr Hills said Australia would be better off understanding what the actual levels were before moving to "arbitrary policy responses". "There are local governments focusing on their local economies and that's exactly where the conversation should be," he said. Public consultation for South Australia's registry closes on October 30 at 5pm.

events.title: Meet David Robinson, the OpenAI safety leader who quit and warned that the company isn’t careful enough
events.summary: David Robinson led safety transparency at OpenAI. Now he's speaking out against the company. Reuters David Robinson, formerly OpenAI's safety lead, has long been interested in rules around technology. Robinson quit OpenAI this week and said the AI giant is moving too fast without regard for safety. Robinson said he would now work from outside the company to strengthen safety incentives. David Robinson, a leader on OpenAI's Safety Systems team who quit the company this week, once had ambitions to bring philosophy to journalism. A Rhodes Scholar, Robinson graduated from Princeton in 2004 with a degree in philosophy. At Princeton, he led the school newspaper's opinion section. In a 2003 interview with the Daily Princetonian, Robinson said he wanted to be the kind of reporter who "tells you what the facts are and then gets to the philosophical differences that explain the situation." Now, Robinson's name is in the headlines — and a notable byline. He left OpenAI, the same week three other safety researchers were fired , and issued a blistering essay for The Atlantic about what he said is OpenAI's inadequate approach to safety. "I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren't being nearly careful enough," Robinson wrote in the essay. Neither Robinson nor the  PR firm he said he hired  responded to Business Insider's requests for comment. A review of his published essays, interviews, and books dating back to his days as an undergraduate paints a picture of a man deeply concerned with the impact of technology on humanity. "All through my life, I've been fascinated by the rules that surround technology and how we decide when and how we're going to use it," he said in a 2022 interview on the Princeton Alumni Weekly podcast. From journalism to tech policy Robinson grew up in Potomac, M.D., an affluent suburb of Washington, D.C. As a child in the 1990s with a mild case of cerebral palsy, Robinson said his teachers created a new rule that allowed him to use a word processor in lieu of pen and paper. "Ever since then, I've been interested in the social impacts of new digital technologies," he said in a UC Berkeley interview in 2021. During summers as an undergrad at Princeton, he interned at Time Magazine and The Wall Street Journal, according to his LinkedIn page. He told the Daily Princetonian in 2003 that after gaining experience as a reporter, he hoped to write for a literary magazine like The New Yorker or Harper's. After Princeton, Robinson got a degree in philosophy, politics, and economics at Oxford before returning to Princeton to start a research center about the relation between technology and public policy . "Part of the idea was that, if you're navigating the policy and the values choices that come up around new technologies, it's a big help to have some real depth of technical expertise," he said in the Berkeley interview. In 2011, Robinson and a colleague from Princeton founded Upturn, an organization that aimed to use algorithmic technologies to make government data more accessible. He joined OpenAI after lecturing tech execs about ethics After research and teaching roles at several universities and a one-year tenure as a faculty director at Apple University , where Robinson gave seminars for Apple executives on the ethical questions prompted by new technologies, Robinson joined OpenAI in 2023. Originally the head of policy planning at the ChatGPT's maker, Robinson wrote in a LinkedIn post announcing his new position that "I look forward to helping shape OpenAI's engagement in the broader AI policy debate, at this critical moment." In a 2023 appearance at the AI Governance Summit hosted by the World Economic Forum, Robinson said OpenAI performs robust safety checks before releasing models and that the company wasn't solely motivated by profit. "We believe in deploying gradually and then learning as we go," he said. Recently, however, Robinson has posted concerns on X about OpenAI's ability to balance safety with increasingly advanced models. "Things @openai are indeed changing significantly by the day, but I do not know whether we are changing fast enough," he said last month. "I think it is still true, as @hilbertspaess puts it, that many of us 'have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes.'" Then, on Friday, Business Insider exclusively reported that Robinson was out at the company. The next day, he published a lengthy essay in the Atlantic explaining why he left. What's next for Robinson? Robinson's departure follows that of Jacob Coxon , a former Anthropic engineer who quit last month and warned that AI could cause mass extinction. In his Atlantic essay, Robinson addressed the argument that he could do more to improve safety by staying at OpenAI than by leaving. Robinson wrote that, by working on the outside, he "can help more people understand the risks I saw, and strengthen the incentives OpenAI and other firms have to be safer." He said he chose to leave because "as the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed." In response to Robinson's essay, an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement that the company is working to ensure that AI models don't outpace the safety measures it has implemented. "As our models become more capable, we continue to strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today while building safety cases to anticipate the risks of future advances," the spokesperson said. "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down." events.title: Are Coles and Woolworths centralising their supply chains? Some experts think so
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Coles, Woolworths supply chain tactic driving small farms out, producer says When middlemen or wholesalers are involved in trade agreements with major supermarkets, small producers have "no power", says one grower. ( ABC News: Hamed Akrami ) A small-scale banana farmer who has had his agreement with Coles ended due to the supermarket simplifying its supply chain says the move signals the end of small-scale farms across the country. Industry experts have claimed Coles and Woolworths are centralising their supply chains in a bid to cut costs. Some experts worry producers will become more vulnerable if supermarkets continue to do so. After 30 years of selling bananas to Coles, New South Wales farmer Amrit Singh believes the supermarket's decision to stop buying his produce is signalling a possible end for small, family-run farms like his. In the past two months, Coles and Woolworths confirmed they would pull various local products from their shelves, with suppliers told the decisions were due to changes to the supply chain. Amrit Singh says small-scale growers are "price takers", not price makers. ( ABC News: Samuel O'Brien ) Industry experts have claimed major Australian supermarkets were centralising their supply chains in a bid to cut costs, warning some producers could now be at greater risk of having their products removed from supermarket shelves. Woolworths said its supply chain network had expanded, while Coles rejected the experts' claims. An inquiry by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) into supermarkets last year found Coles and Woolworths had overwhelming power in their trade relationships with suppliers. Amrit Singh labelled Coles' decision to pull local bananas from its shelves as "anti-competitive" and said supermarkets should be encouraging diversity in growing regions. ( ABC News: Giulio Saggin ) In August, Coles confirmed it would stop selling Coffs Coast bananas, pumpkins and cucumbers, in an effort to simplify its supply chain. While Tasmanians can shop at 17 Coles and 32 Woolworth supermarkets, there are no Aldi stores — and that won't be changing anytime soon, according to the company CEO. Mr Singh sold his bananas indirectly to Coles through a wholesaler, an agreement he said was worth hundreds of thousands of dollars a year. The produce is now expected to come from north Queensland, but Mr Singh believes his business is too small to compete with north Queensland's banana industry. "Freight costs [involved in] getting access to those [new] markets are going to be extremely high," he said. Mr Singh said farmers who did not sell directly to supermarkets had "no power" to negotiate trade agreements and were forced to reduce prices to support promotions and specials. Coles says keeping its supply chain efficient helps it absorb costs and reduce the impact on grocery prices. ( ABC News ) Rise in 'middlemen' leaves farmers vulnerable NSW Farmers' principal economist Samuel Miller said supermarket giants had long been centralising their supply chains. He explained one way they were doing this was through buying produce from packhouses or "middlemen" — selling on behalf of a group of growers — instead of directly from them. "When those supermarkets make a decision like consolidating their suppliers or rejecting some produce … it affects not just that supplier in the middle, but it can affect dozens, 40 or 50 other farmers down the line." Samuel Miller says supermarkets have a large share of the market, so they hold negotiating power. ( Supplied: Samuel Miller ) In a statement to the ABC, Coles said it continued to source directly from a range of Australian producers. "In fresh produce, aggregators are not new and have long played an important role in Australia," a spokesperson said. In August, Woolworths confirmed it would stop selling Tasmanian beef in stores around the country from early next year. ( ABC News: Laurissa Smith ) Queensland University of Technology retail marketing professor Gary Mortimer said meat was one of the main supply chains where processing had been centralised, citing Woolworths' decision to stop selling Tasmanian beef from early next year. Gary Mortimer says supermarkets centralising their processing can give shoppers greater product consistency. ( Supplied: Gary Mortimer ) Some suppliers said they were told this was due to rising production and shipping costs. "Over the last 10 to 15 years, what we've seen is that reduction of in-store processing back to centralised processing," Dr Mortimer said. "Less trade butchers in stores and more of that processing taking place centrally.

events.title: In Connecticut, my husband and I mostly talked logistics. In Spain, we started dating each other again.
events.summary: The author and her family moved from the US to Spain. Courtesy of the author We sold our house in Connecticut and got rid of most of our belongings before moving abroad. Starting over in Spain brought plenty of stress and uncertainty. Depending on each other through it has ultimately strengthened our relationship. One year ago, my husband left his 18-year teaching career behind, we sold our house, got rid of 95% of our belongings, and moved our family from Connecticut to Madrid. These days, we live in a small flat with our 7 and 10-year-old boys. We don't own a car. We're learning Spanish one day at a time. On paper, that much upheaval could've broken us. Instead, it's brought us closer than ever. We were coexisting, not connecting Back in the US, my husband Jeff and I were coexisting more than connecting. Most conversations revolved around logistics : who was taking which kid to which activity, what meeting we needed to attend, and what to make for dinner. By the time the boys were in bed, we were too spent to connect meaningfully. We'd sit beside one another, exhausted, on our phones or trying to watch a movie we never finished because one of us always fell asleep. The author says in the US, she and her spouse weren't connecting. Courtesy of the author I never imagined that would be our marriage. Yet, there we were. Moving to Spain made us reevaluate things Here in Spain, we're still busy. Arguably busier. We spend about three hours a day getting the kids to and from school via train and bus. But we're also spending far more time together than before — and it's given us more opportunities to connect beyond logistics. Part of what's driven this connection, too, is watching the locals go about their day around us. "Busy" doesn't mean the same thing here as it does in the US. It's not a reason to delay the connection. People stop for each other mid-errand, midday, without apologizing. They make the time. We started doing the same. Stopping for an unplanned coffee or a caña. Exploring a new neighborhood hand-in-hand just because. Taking a few extra minutes for us instead of rushing on to the to-do. It's made more of a difference than I expected. You don't have to move abroad to do this, of course. You just have to decide that the list can wait. Going through the unknown together It's just the four of us now. We need each other in a way we didn't before (and that's not automatically a good thing). Being each other's only support can bring out the best in a marriage , or the worst. This past year tested us more than once. Jeff spent months in a 600-hour language course, while simultaneously trying to find work and switch off his student visa before it expired. Between the exhaustion of full-time language study and the pressure of a ticking clock, it would have been easy for that stress to become tension between us. And some days, it did. Navigating new rules, a new language, and a hundred small unknowns daily—it's hard. I won't pretend it's not. But we kept showing up for each other anyway, and we came out stronger. A weekly ritual that's helped One thing that's anchored us through this new chapter is a practice we started years ago in the US. After our second son was born, I created a marriage meeting journal. We'd answer 10 questions together and document the answers. Questions like: What's something your partner did last week that made your life easier? What support do you need this week? Are there any goals or commitments you could use your partner's help with? Is there something in our relationship or home that needs attention? How will we connect as a couple this week? It's nothing fancy, but it's an hour that keeps us sailing in the same direction — even more important now that we're living abroad. We still do it most Sunday mornings. And while it was technically my idea, Jeff loves it as much as I do. If we let it slide, he points it out. You don't need to do it weekly or answer all 10. You could start tonight, with one question. After the move, we also started something new: short day-dates. After Jeff's last class of the week, we'd meet up for a drink, lunch, and a rose garden stroll. Nothing grand, and sometimes, it costs nothing. It was another block of intentional time to connect. I don't know what that will look like this year now that he's secured a teaching position, but I know we'll find some version of it — because it matters. The part we didn't see coming If you'd asked me before we moved what I thought would change, I'd have said: the language, the culture, the community we'd build, the places we'd explore. I never would have guessed how much closer we've become. And it didn't stop with our marriage. Evening strolls through the plaza with just a ball or hacky sack to pass among the four of us. Morning hikes and long talks with my oldest. Word searches and laughing with my 7-year-old on the ride home from school. We didn't plan for any of that. It might be the best part of the whole move. events.title: Australia's fossil fuel expansion 'slap in the face' to Pacific nations
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Pacific leaders challenge Australia's fossil fuel expansion ahead of pre-COP31 talks in Fiji Marica and Sami have been living in a tent for five years, waiting for their village to be rebuilt. ( ABC News: Lice Monovo ) As she sits crossed legged on the floor inside a large tent, 66-year-old Marica Malumuca describes the place she's called home for the past five years. "When it rains heavily it feels like we're living in a balloon because we can see the parts of the tent bulging where it's filling up," she said. Ms Malumuca's village, Nabavatu, was declared unsafe in 2021 after two cyclones cracked the ground beneath it, and she was moved to a temporary settlement in Savadrua. There are 37 tents at the temporary site. Some can fit three people and others accommodate up to seven. Ms Malumuca's son, Sami Veloko, moved home from the city to look after her as they wait for Nabavatu to be rebuilt. Pacific communities are already feeling the impacts of climate change. ( ABC News: Lice Monovo ) "Those people who stay in these tents, they used to stay in a good house; a cement house, a wooden house of a high quality," he said. "You cannot believe — even they themselves cannot believe — that they stay in this kind of tent." Small island states are already being disproportionately affected by displacement as climate change drives more extreme weather. The United Nations warned the impacts of tropical cyclones have become more severe due to rising sea levels and an increase in heavy precipitation. More than half of Pacific Island countries' infrastructure is located in coastal areas at risk from rising seas, which happens as higher temperatures melt glaciers and ice sheets. Nabavatu is yet to be rebuilt, five years after it was damaged by cyclones. ( ABC News: Lice Monovo ) As world leaders prepare to descend on Mr Veloko's home country for high-level climate talks, he has a message for them. "We are getting the effect of climate change and we are the vulnerable people, the Pacific people," he said. "Because of what they have contributed to carbon dioxide, the industrialisation that they have developed in their countries, we are getting the worst of it." Climate diplomacy at heart of security strategy Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will join global leaders at the pre-COP event, which will feature preparatory talks ahead of next month's United Nations COP31 climate summit. Australia has led the charge for the lead-up talks to be held in the Pacific and is spending millions of dollars on the event as part of its broader regional security strategy to become the "partner of choice" for the Pacific islands. Anthony Albanese attended the 2026 Pacific Island Forum in early September. ( ABC News: Mark Moore ) The Albanese government has vigorously pursued a series of bilateral security deals with Pacific nations since coming to office including Vanuatu, Fiji, Tuvalu, Nauru and Papua New Guinea, with almost all of them including commitments to act on climate change. According to the Lowy Institute, Australia remains the Pacific's largest bilateral donor and biggest development partner , having spent almost $19 billion of a committed $20.6 billion. Wes Morgan, a research associate with the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at UNSW who lived and worked in the Pacific for more than a decade, said the federal government understood that to become the Pacific's partner of choice it must act on the region's key security threat. "That is why there has been the inclusion of commitments on climate change in these bilateral security arrangements, but more broadly why Australia is working with Pacific island countries to drive global action on climate change," he said. "That's why Australia had its hand up to host the UN climate talks with the Pacific." For Pacific islands like Ebeye, rising oceans caused by the continued burning of fossil fuels is a real and acute problem. ( Supplied: Hall Contracting ) But Dr Morgan said Australia remaining one of the world's largest fossil fuel exporters "flies in the face of the narrative Australia's pursuing with Pacific Island countries". "Australia's biggest contribution to the climate crisis is the export of coal and gas, so the emissions associated with Australia's exports of coal and gas more than doubled the emissions from Australia's entire domestic economy," he said. Can Australia be both a gas giant and a climate leader? Seven years after it was first mooted, the extension of Australia's biggest gas project could not have landed at a more critical juncture for the nation's climate credentials.

events.title: Lina Khan says AI companies are following the same playbook that got Big Tech into trouble
events.summary: Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan said the AI industry shouldn't self-regulate. Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images Former FTC chair Lina Khan doesn't believe AI companies can effectively self-regulate. She referenced Big Tech's attempt with social media, calling it "a proven failure." The Trump administration isn't keen on implementing federal-level guardrails. Lina Khan has some advice for AI companies attempting to self-regulate the advancing tech. The former Federal Trade Commission chair said doing so would be a fool's errand during an interview on ABC's "This Week." "We've seen that self-regulation efforts by Big Tech have been a proven failure," Khan said on Sunday. "We need to remember what happened a decade ago." She referenced Big Tech companies that tried to self-regulate in the early days of social media. "We've seen just innumerable harms come from the unchecked nomination of these Big Tech companies, and so now, as we face new horizons with these advanced AI systems, it would be an enormous mistake to repeat that playbook," Khan said. Since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in 2022, major players in the tech industry have become caught in a global race to develop their own systems. Companies like Microsoft, Google, and Meta have invested heavily in their products in hopes of dominating the global market. However, the speed of AI advancement has prompted calls from politicians, advocates, and even some tech leaders for guardrails. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on his industry peers to pace the development of frontier AI systems last month. In a blog post, he said the "most effective" method would involve regulation that targets US frontier AI companies. His essay drew support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon Musk. The Trump administration has avoided implementing regulations on the AI industry. Last week, President Donald Trump said tech leaders had signed an AI safety agreement to regulate themselves. Although overarching regulation is still up in the air, Khan said there are already laws in place to address issues in the AI industry. "I think one thing that's especially odd about this moment is that you're hearing from these executives that they are effectively developing malfunctioning products, AI systems that are engaging in repeated hacks of the servers of other companies, of the servers of other governments, and yet that they are somehow helpless as to do anything serious about it," she said. A spattering of cybersecurity incidents has cast a harsh glare on AI companies. OpenAI agents hacked another AI company, Hugging Face, in July. In September, an AI startup's research team used Claude to hack into OpenAI's codebase, and The Wall Street Journal reported that Google's Gemini had hacked three companies in the spring. Recently, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent hacked into a government website this summer. In a blog post, OpenAI said it should have shared the preliminary findings with Australia's government sooner and kept agencies abreast of developments. During her interview, Khan told "This Week" that the idea that adopting new technologies exempts companies from current laws is "totally laughable." "I think when you have a pattern of these agents engaging in this type of dangerous behavior, and you still have these companies developing in the same way, not putting the full guardrails in place, I think that starts to raise very serious questions," Khan said. events.title: My favorite place in California is a tiny mountain town that's worth visiting in every season — also, its mayor is a dog
events.summary: I try to see Mayor Max whenever visiting the mountain town of Idyllwild. Mar Yvette One of my favorite escapes from Los Angeles is the rustic, uncrowded mountain town of Idyllwild. The tiny community is isolated but offers plenty to see and do year-round. It offers a laid-back getaway where you can be immersed in nature and meet a local dog celebrity. One of the best things about living in Santa Monica is having the ocean on one side and the mountains on the other. Although there are plenty of mountainous spots nearby to choose from for a getaway, my husband and I keep going back to the small town of Idyllwild. We've been there at least 20 times over the past decade, and it remains one of our favorite places to visit. Idyllwild is about a two-hour drive east of Los Angeles, and the winding road up into the mountains feels like part of the adventure as the urban sprawl below shrinks in the distance. Before you know it, you're surrounded by towering pines and crisp alpine air in a town that feels much farther from LA than it is. With a population of around 4,000 people and an elevation of about 5,300 feet (just over a mile high), Idyllwild feels like a real escape from the big city while still being close enough for a quick overnight or an extended stay. The town feels wonderfully old-school Cute mom-and-pop shops line the streets of Idyllwild. Mar Yvette Downtown Idyllwild is small enough to explore on foot, with woodsy architecture, independent shops and restaurants, and easy parking all around. At night, the town cab get very quiet except for the sounds of wildlife that add to the feeling of being close to nature. Over the years, we've stayed in little local lodges, inns, B&Bs, family-owned cabins, and whole-home rentals. Most of them have been within walking distance of downtown. It's easy to find parking downtown, and many lodgings are within walking distance. Mar Yvette Even though some spots have come and gone, it still feels like the same charming village , especially since you won't find major chain businesses, fast-food joints, or strip malls. The town's local grocery stores are also independent, so if you need a big-box store, you'll have to drive back down the mountain. There's enough to do without feeling like you need an itinerary We've caught live performances from musicians like Keith McCabe at Taryn's Place. Mar Yvette Idyllwild is isolated, but it isn't boring. I've enjoyed arts and crafts, gardening lectures, wine tastings , holiday festivals, and outdoor concerts. Naturally, there are lots of good hiking trails , but my husband and I tend to stay in town, taking easy strolls, browsing the shops, eating at restaurants, and relaxing among the pines. It's fun chatting with locals, from store owners and lodge managers to bikers who pass through town. It's hard to beat the scenic views here. Mar Yvette There's also a historic movie theater, the Idyllwild Nature Center with its museum and community events, and the renowned Idyllwild Arts Academy boarding school, all of which contribute to the town's cultural and creative character. Since there's always something happening, we usually arrive without any set plans. That said, we've often taken the two-hour drive just to hear our friend Keith McCabe — who we met 10 years ago in Idyllwild — play acoustic guitar at one of the local restaurants or bars. I must also mention that the town's mayor is a dog Having a happy moment with Mayor Max the Third. Mar Yvette Yes, it's true. Idyllwild is an unincorporated community with no official local government, but in 2012, residents elected a canine as their mayor . Mayor Max is an adorable golden retriever (the current Mayor Max is actually the third generation to hold the title), and I've had the supreme pleasure of meeting all three over the years. Mayor Max's duties include attending meet-and-greets, taking photos, spreading joy and goodwill, and promoting the town. You can catch him on certain days of the week in the back of his caretaker's pickup truck in the middle of town (or get in touch with his people via email to arrange a visit). Every season offers a fresh way to enjoy the town Christmas is a lovely time to visit when the trees are lit up in the center of town. Mar Yvette Over the years, we've experienced snow, holiday festivals, warm-weather trips, and plenty of dry seasons. Being that this is Southern California , Idyllwild has had more than its fair share of droughts, fires, and occasional deluges. Strawberry Creek, which runs through the town, isn't always flowing and can look dramatically different depending on rain and snowmelt. It's refreshing to be surrounded by mountains and tall trees. Mar Yvette But no matter what time of year we go, there's something invigorating about being up there so close to nature, surrounded by those mountain peaks and soaking in the nostalgic simplicity of it all. It's a great place to make memories with the people you love Some of our happiest moments have been spent with my grandparents in Idyllwild. Mar Yvette I've made so many great memories in this small mountain town with friends and family, including my grandparents, who recently passed. My husband and I even have friends who decided to get married there after we introduced them to Idyllwild — and he officiated the wedding! After all these years, Idyllwild remains one of our go-to places when we want an easy escape from the hustle and bustle of city life. It harks back to a simpler time, allowing us to be surrounded by nature and enjoy a slower pace for a few days. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The Guardian view on trapped leaseholders: Labour must keep its promise to set them free | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on trapped leaseholders: Labour must keep its promise to set them free The government pledged to end an unfair system. Ministers must give homeowners power over costs, rather than another place to complain “T o the millions of leaseholders across the country, you have my word. The days of you being squeezed for every penny are coming to an end,” Andy Burnham told the Labour party conference . Only a few hours earlier, his housing secretary, Angela Rayner, had announced that the government would legislate for a new independent regulator and launch a consultation to cap “rip off” administrative fees. While these are undoubtedly steps in the right direction, they are miles away from Labour’s manifesto promise to “finally bring the feudal leasehold system to an end”. In its modern form , leasehold in England and Wales turns homes into income streams for freeholders. It should be abolished. There are powerful vested interests – billionaires , aristocrats and big businesses – that would oppose this move. But the system of service charges is crippling the housing market because its exorbitant cost puts off prospective buyers. The average annual service charge for a flat in England and Wales is now £2,405 , up 32.6% since 2020 and 55.6% over a decade. Owners of flats in high-rise blocks in London are paying service charges of more than £7,000 a year. Little wonder that first-time buyers are increasingly bypassing flats . The current system sees homeowners enter into long-term leases in which they must pay sums annually to freeholders. These can rise quickly to very high levels. The government proposes a £250 annual cap on ground rents for existing residential leases and limits on fees for requests such as keeping a pet. Ministers are consulting over whether residents could pay less to buy out freeholds . But there is no sign of action on annual service charges for maintenance costs determined by distant firms. Last year, 37% of flats across England and Wales had a service charge that exceeded 1% of their value – making them hard to mortgage and sell. Surely homeowners should not have to buy their freedom at an outrageous price while being charged for years by a management system they cannot realistically change? The issue of leasehold has become a campaign flashpoint in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Six out of seven homes sold in the constituency last year were sold as leasehold. The Green leader, Zack Polanski, who is standing to be the MP, has made the issue a concrete test of Labour’s credibility . The Greens have paired leasehold abolition with rent controls and affordable housing as part of their claim to end “rip-off Britain”, accusing Labour of favouring developers. Labour denies this, but ministers know that housing is a political powder keg that has already exploded in Berlin and across Spain . It is remarkable that while legislation banning new leasehold properties is expected before the next election, it is unlikely to come into force until after it. Ministers are said to be afraid of being taken to court by freeholders. But government has already won against them in the courts when defending Michael Gove’s housing bill. The question for the government is whether the proposed reforms give the owners of the existing 5m leasehold homes a credible route out of their dependency – or just regulate their continued subservience. Ministers must show how a leaseholder trapped today will in the future take back control – by obtaining the right to manage property, being able to buy the freehold or converting to commonhold. If ministers offer just another complaints mechanism, they will have broken their promise to end an injustice.

events.title: LIM Advisors founder George Long: ‘We’ve been here 30 years. We’re going to be around’
events.summary: Thirty years of Asian alternatives, from the 1997 crash to Japan activism, a smaller firm on purpose, and a caution that no asset class is perfectly safe [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] George Long does not talk like a man selling vision. The founder, chairman and chief investment officer of LIM Advisors is understated and unshowy. After three decades running an independent firm in Hong Kong, what comes through is a temperament suited to difficult Asian markets: calm, pragmatic and focused on protecting capital when conditions turn. Long left Barclays’ Asia Pacific asset management business in late 1995 to set up LIM Advisors, one of the longest continually running alternative investment firms in Asia. The Hang Seng had fallen 31 per cent in 1994, and clients wanted a less volatile way to manage money. “A lot of my investors said, can you create a more stable way, a more diversified way, not so much dependent on the stock market.” Convertible bonds were his answer. LIM rolled out its first fund in January 1996 focused mainly on Asian convertibles. A year later the Asian financial crisis hit. Long recalls the Hang Seng falling about 25 per cent over two years, yet “we were up about 12 per cent.” “It was really tough because no one wanted to invest in Asia at that time even though the market was extremely cheap.” The SARS pandemic in 2003 arrived before the region had fully recovered. The Hong Kong market fell nearly 18 per cent and travel almost stopped. LIM later lived through the Japanese banking crisis around 1999, the 2008 global financial crisis, Covid and the latest Iran war shock. His father did not invest at the start but after about 15 years he did. “When I set up my business, my father didn’t give me money. After 15 years he said, okay, I’ll now give you money, because you’ve proved you can survive.” “Now we’re 30 years old. We proved we can survive.” Japan is an important part of the firm’s focus. Long has covered the country for four decades. LIM has maintained a research team in Tokyo since 2002. He says it “may be the second oldest hedge fund office in Japan”. Foreign interest was thin for years and has only revived over the past three years. Precious metals and mining stocks are a major bet. Long thinks they gain from persistent inflation and a weaker dollar reserve role. The portfolio also holds copper miners. He sat on Australian mining boards in the early 2000s. He also thinks Hong Kong can become a serious gold trading centre, given storage, no capital controls and the old bullion market. The latest Policy Address sets out a gold clearing system, tax concessions for commodity trading and a larger official role for bullion. China is another large bet. “The Chinese stock market is relatively inexpensive compared to, say, the US stock market. China went through a major correction and has only partially recovered. They’re still relatively good value.” Chinese convertibles remain “an interesting niche opportunity.” He also holds Hong Kong property and financial names. The first fund has evolved over three decades. Convertible-bond and other Asian arbitrage, then high-yield, largely dried up. As those trades thinned out, the portfolio was steered towards corporate events, metals and China. The fund has since been renamed the LIM Global Opportunities Fund. “It’s a broader fund now and can invest in any liquid asset anywhere based on my 40 years of experience.” Fifteen years ago capital came more from Western institutional investors. International investors, especially Americans, lost some interest in Asia. More of the money now comes from Asian family offices, foundations and funds of funds. He will not give up Hong Kong. The city, he says, is still a major international financial centre, with a good legal system, infrastructure and talent. “But sometimes the government can take a while to change things such as the taxation of funds, but they generally move in the right direction.” Tokyo is the only other Asian office. There is a small New York office. Looking out five or ten years, he sees a rougher climate. “Interest rates are going up; inflation is in the system.” He started at a major New York bank in 1982, when US rates were high. “Most people who are even in their 50s have never seen high inflation and interest rates. I’ve seen that. I also saw a lot of commodity inflation early in my career.” No asset class, he says, is perfectly safe. The dollar is no longer as dominant as it was. Gold should hold its value, even if it fluctuates, as it did recently. Japan will still matter, and so will China. “We’ve been here for 30 years,” he says. “We’re going to be around.”

events.title: I left my dream life in London to move back in with my dads at 41. I have no regrets.
events.summary: The author moved home to Colorado after living abroad for many years. Courtesy of Jen Kaarlo. I left my home in Colorado more than two decades ago and eventually built a life in London. When I turned 40, I started to think more and more about the distance between me and my dads. Soon after, I moved home and a year later, I'm still happy with that decision. When I think back to how my life looked this time last year, I can't help but laugh out loud. Last August, I was sipping cocktails by the pool at White City House with London illuminated in the background, wondering if I was ready to let this life go. I was chatting to a friend-of-a-friend, a woman around my age, who was aghast at the idea that I was abandoning my life in the British capital to move halfway across the world to live with my two dads in Denver. So much so that her perfectly manicured hand almost dropped her spicy margarita when I told her the news. She wasn't alone. Most people were flummoxed as to why I would swap a charming flat in the heart of Marylebone and a thriving social calendar to live in our family house smack dab in the middle of America. The author (left) pictured with her dad and step-dad after returning home to Colorado to be closer to them. Courtesy of Jen Kaarlo, By many definitions, you could say I had made it I left the Mile High City over two decades ago and called Miami, NYC, and London home for varying lengths of time. I had a stacked résumé and traveled to over 50 countries, many of them solo. Though none of that seemed to matter as much after I turned 40. What mattered most to me was that I didn't want to take time with my family for granted. As an expat , I always find myself coming back to a cost-to-closeness ratio. Many moons ago, I was having dinner with a new friend I'd been introduced to through mutual friends in Paris. Over escargots and red wine, he told me all about the glamorous adventures he had embarked upon, seemingly plucked right from the scenes of "The Devil Wears Prada." What stuck out to me all these years later is not how he knew every designer under the sun, but how he spoke about the calculations behind his trips back to the States. He suggested that we were both in our 30s and that, if we were lucky, we could manage two trips back home a year, but some years it might be just one. If we were even luckier, we would have our parents with us for at least another 25 years. His grand takeaway was: if the experiences you're living while you're abroad no longer make your heart sing, then was living so far away worth it? Time with family became perilously finite So, one Sunday afternoon after a deliberate bout of hemming and hawing, not to mention a few pints at my local, I called my dad and said I was coming home. Unlike many of my peers, I didn't look at the move as a step back . Instead, I chose to look at the adventure as my "Glitter Gap Year," as I called it. Besides, if all else failed, I had my UK citizenship and could always move back. The author said moving back to the US has been a better experience than she expected. Courtesy of Jen Kaarlo. It's been nearly a year since I hopped on that plane back to my beloved cow town, and it's been a robust adjustment, but oddly, an even better experience than I could have ever dreamt up. Sure, there are times when I miss my independence and wish I could catch a last-minute showing in the West End as I often did, but there is a beautiful luxury to seeing my two dads at the start and end of every day that few things can compare to. What I've learned to appreciate are the small moments. Getting to chat about the state of the garden, shaking my head at ridiculous dad jokes, and relishing in every single hug. events.title: Nigel Farage questioned by standards commissioner over £5m gift
events.summary: Reform UK leader was interviewed for half an hour last month over money from crypto billionaire Nigel Farage has been interviewed by the standards commissioner for an investigation into whether he should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne . The Reform UK leader spent about half an hour being questioned over the money, the Sunday Times reported. Farage maintains the gift was for his personal security. The interview conducted last month is a sign the process is nearing a conclusion, although Reform UK is not believed to have been informed that the report is finished. An MP under investigation is usually notified before the conclusion of the process. If the commissioner finds that there has been a serious breach of the rules, the matter is passed to the standards committee of MPs and lay members, which can ask for further evidence. The committee can recommend a sanction or override the report. If it suggests more than a 10-day suspension from the Commons – and parliament agrees – the Reform UK leader could find himself facing a recall petition and second byelection in his Clacton constituency. Farage has been under investigation over the gift since shortly after the Guardian revealed in May that Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024. The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter , not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament. After a slide in the polls over the summer, Reform is about to embark on a major reorganisation at its headquarters to try to revive its fortunes. Insiders said it would involve a big shake-up of staffing, in addition to the suspensions of James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, Farage’s close aide. The pair are facing an internal investigation into whether they encouraged illegal foreign donations during an undercover investigation by reporters from Verbatim. The inquiry is being carried out by lawyers who are expected to reach their conclusions soon. The matter is also the subject of a police inquiry. The party is working out how to spend £72m in donations from Harborne and another crypto billionaire, Ben Delo. The huge sums have prompted calls from political rivals for a donation cap. Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning A possible use of the money is the relaunch of a TV channel that produces Reform-related video coverage and a show fronted by Farage. Farage told the Sunday Times he thought the reaction to the donations would be “far worse” but had produced “some grudging respect – the fact that I managed to pull off a coup of that magnitude, I think people were quite impressed”. It is not clear whether the donations fall within the rules because the government is putting forward legislation to ban overseas donors from giving more than £100,000 in a calendar year – backdated to March this year. Harborne joined the UK electoral register only this summer and Delo has been largely based in Hong Kong, although on the register for some years. If the donations are ruled impermissible, Reform could have to hand them back, a prospect that is likely to lead to court action.

events.title: Yemeni and Saudi forces launch counteroffensive against the Houthis
events.summary: Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis on Sunday in an effort to win back territory from the rebel group, the head of Yemen's presidential council said in a speech. "We have exhausted all opportunities for deescalation with the Houthi militias," Rashad al-Alimi said . Why it matters: One of the key objectives of the operation is to regain control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports. When the Houthis took over territory on the Red Sea coast close to the strait, it gave them — and Iran, which backs them — powerful leverage over the U.S., its Gulf allies and the world economy. Despite pleas from Saudi Arabia, the U.S. is not getting involved in direct combat against the Houthis for now. It is providing intelligence and targeting support, U.S. officials say. Driving the news: The counteroffensive has been planned for many weeks by Yemen's internationally recognized government and Saudi Arabia. Tens of thousands of ground troops loyal to the Yemeni government are participating. The Saudi military is mainly providing air cover for Yemeni forces and conducting airstrikes against Houthi targets. The goal is to retake the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control for several years. The Houthis continued launching missiles at Saudi targets over the weekend, including at facilities of state-owned oil giant Aramco. The intrigue: President Trump is caught between wanting to help Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, his friend and ally, and avoiding getting entangled in a new front in the Middle East. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also had serious reservations about launching strikes in Yemen, viewing it as a distraction from its focus on Iran, a U.S. official said. On Thursday, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to brief him on the planned operation and ask again for U.S. airstrikes against Houthi targets, the official said. A second U.S. official said that the U.S. "is not going to take kinetic action for now," but stressed that could change if the operation runs into problems. What to watch: On Friday, Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the conflict in Yemen, Axios first reported. It's unclear whether the meeting ended with new policy recommendations for the president regarding Yemen.

events.title: Retailers are making returns harder. A carpet seller taught me why that’s a mistake | Gene Marks
events.summary: Retailers are making returns harder. A carpet seller taught me why that’s a mistake A standard business practice offsets future costs by funding a reserve for returns – but many small businesses don’t do it I n my 30-plus years of being an accountant I have learned many business lessons from people who were much smarter than me. Jerry Crawford was one of those people. Jerry taught me about product returns. Jerry – who sadly passed away a decade ago – sold carpets wholesale from a nondescript little building in south Jersey. He employed about 50 people and counted many local and national carpet retailers as his customers. When I reviewed Jerry’s books, I noticed a large reserve for “returns”. “They’re a part of every business,” he told me. A “reserve” is something businesses create for potential future costs. Some reserve for bad debts. Others reserve for inventory that grows old and will need to be disposed of. And plenty of businesses – like Jerry’s – reserve for the potential costs that will be incurred if a customer returns their product. Returns are just a normal part of business. Plenty of small business owners like Jerry go to great lengths to make the process as easy as possible. Some big companies, such as Amazon, do the same. “There’s a cost to do this,” Jerry said. “So I make sure to build a reserve for that cost.” Makes sense. And yet, it seems that many businesses still haven’t learned this lesson. According to the Wall Street Journal , many Americans are complaining that it’s getting harder to return things. They’re seeing “surprise fees, shorter return windows and more questions about their reasons for sending products back”. Some, according to the report, are “getting warnings that they won’t get a refund on their next return”. Jerry would be shaking his head at this. To him, it wouldn’t make sense. And it doesn’t make sense to me either. Yes, there are a few bad actors that will take advantage of the practice. And yes, accepting returns adds costs for a business. But, like credit card fees, health insurance and overtime, this is a cost that can easily be recouped. All you need to do is capture those costs over a year or so, build a history, estimate what the next year’s cost will be and then factor those costs into your overhead. Your overhead is then factored into your pricing. In Jerry’s case, he reserved one half of 1% on each of his sales as a returns allowance based on his history of returns. He built up this reserve throughout the year, then charged returned products against it. A .5% reserve meant that instead of charging $1,000 for a roll of carpet, he charged $1,005. His customers didn’t notice the $5 difference. Would you? The difference is negligible. But for a business, those costs add up and, by doing this, those costs are covered. You’d think that, after thousands of years of business practice and the knowledge of some of the finest institutions, pundits, academics and experts, our business leaders today would understand this concept. So why don’t retailers realize this? It’s a mystery to me. They must see that creating obstacles and charging their customers for returns only creates animosity, ruins their loyalty and results in unfavorable press coverage. It’s shocking to me how businesses continue to make the same mistakes over and over again, despite the lessons of history. You can keep your customers happy, build loyalty and grow your business by not nickel-and-diming them. Jerry Crawford, a small business owner with a high school education who profitably sold carpets for decades, understood this.

events.title: I'm a matchmaker for people over 50. The couples who end up in the happiest relationships don't look for chemistry first.
events.summary: Brigitte Weil is a matchmaker who works with older clients. Photo Credit: Andrew French Brigitte Weil is a matchmaker based in Manhattan, working with the 50+ crowd. She says superficial details like looks and finances become less important with age. Widowed clients focus on what they want, while divorced clients focus on what they don't want. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Brigitte Weil . It has been edited for length and clarity . My parents have been married for 62 years, and my grandparents were married for 76. I've always been surrounded by longevity in relationships , and it's something that captivates me. Becoming a matchmaker who works with older adults was a natural fit. Dating in your 70s or older is radically different from dating in your 30s or even 50s. Younger people are looking for someone to build a life with, but older people are seeking someone who can share a life that's already been created. Lifestyle compatibility becomes critical with age When I match older clients, I need to know that their lifestyles will mesh well. We're talking less about chemistry, or someone who checks all the boxes, and more about how their lifestyles can be shared. Older clients care less about a man's height or a woman's appearance in a bikini. Even finances play a smaller role. Instead, geography becomes a big issue: many people don't want to move and give up their community and family connections. To find long-term love , clients must share values on topics such as grandchildren and travel. People know their nonnegotiables Finding lifestyle compatibility can be a challenge. People become wiser with age, and they know themselves. They know what they're willing to compromise on, and what they're not. Take my client Sol , who at 96 is by far the oldest person I've worked with. Sol wants a woman to wake up next to every morning. He's not alone — most of my clients want cohabitation, even as marriage becomes less important to many of them. Sol's been on some great dates, but many of the women his age aren't interested in moving house. They already have their routines. She says her older clients know what they want in a partner. Photo Credit: Andrew French My clients are building on their experience with love Rarely do I work with someone who's never been married before; Most of my clients are divorced or widowed. Widowed clients usually start by telling me exactly what they want in a relationship. They've experienced a loving partner, and know what qualities and traits matter most to them. Divorced people , on the other hand, tend to tell me what they don't want. They're looking to make different choices this time around and create a healthier, happier relationship than the one they left behind. Both types of clients often need a little encouragement. They need to know it's possible for them to fall in love again. I teach them they're not starting over; they're building on all the experiences they've had. A date gone wrong led to love One of my favorite success stories is of a couple who were both right around 70 when they met. For both of them, going on this date was a big deal. I was excited for them, but the day of the date, the man called to say the lady didn't show. That was unlike her. A moment later, my phone rang. My client was frantic — she'd gotten a flat tire on the New Jersey Turnpike, and was waiting for AAA to come replace it. When I told her date, he insisted on going to wait with her. She was frazzled, her hairstyle and makeup drooping, but she appreciated the gesture. He waited with her until the fire was fixed, then they headed home. A week or so later, he asked her out on a proper date. Now, they travel the world together , sending me pictures from all these beautiful locations. I'm getting married this fall Lots of people want to know about the matchmaker's love life . I'm divorced, and was single for about 10 years. I did a fair amount of dating, but dating as a matchmaker was hard. I was constantly exposed to so many wonderful single people. Yet, that reminded me that there's not just one great person out there. I met my now-fiancé, Michael, through my matchmaking network about five years ago. We were absolutely meant to meet when we did. I really admire Michael for the choices he's made in raising his own family. That admiration just melted me. We're getting married in November. events.title: Brazil presidential vote pits Trump ally against Lula, who is seeking fourth nonconsecutive term
events.summary: Brazilians are heading to the polls for a high-stakes presidential election SAO PAULO -- Brazilians began voting Sunday in a high-stakes presidential election pitting incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, ideological opposites who are each seen as having a shot at an outright victory. If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, the top two vote-getters will head to a runoff on Oct. 25 in Latin America's economic powerhouse. Ten other candidates are expected to garner much smaller numbers of votes on Sunday. Bolsonaro, 45, is the son of far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro and an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump. Lula, who at 80 is one of the world’s oldest heads of state , is running in his seventh presidential election and has strengthened Brazil's ties with Beijing. Trump allies have found support in recent years in some Latin American countries, including Argentina, Colombia and Peru. Almost 159 million Brazilians are eligible to vote in this tense political showdown. Where Bolsonaro has leaned into his ideological alliance with Trump, Lula has criticized Washington. The incumbent president has often spoken about risks of U.S. intervention in the Brazilian elections after the Trump administration imposed high tariffs against Brazilian exports , revoked the visa of the country’s ambassador in Washington and sanctioned a Supreme Court justice who chaired the investigation that ended up resulting in the sentencing of Jair Bolsonaro , Lula's predecessor. Lula told journalists after voting Sunday that he needs “to do double of what we have done” if reelected and expressed confidence he would win in the first round. Flávio Bolsonaro has touted his proximity to the White House , although he denies his campaign received help from the U.S. government. He has insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including the rare minerals economy . Brazil estimates that its deposits hold up to 21 million tons, second only to China. Bolsonaro also has campaigned on releasing his father from his 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup and bringing him back to politics. “Brazil needs change. Brazil can’t stand so much suffering,” he told reporters at the Rio de Janeiro voting center, where he cast his vote Sunday. Brazilians will also elect 27 state governors, members of state legislatures, all 513 federal members of the lower house of congress and 54 of the country’s 81 senators in Sunday's vote. Thomas Traumann, a political consultant based in Rio de Janeiro, says last-minute mistakes by either candidate or by their allies could make all the difference for undecided voters. Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' “ Polarization in Brazil created a trap . There’s no third candidate. You only have two options, and they fight each other in an atmosphere that becomes worse and worse,” Traumann said. “It is much more a competition of accusations than a competition of proposals.” Four years ago, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by 2.1 million votes — a margin of just under 2 percentage points. At the time, Brazilians were upset with the then president’s handling of the coronavirus pandemic, his repeated threats against democracy, his attacks on the electronic voting system, and the poor shape of the nation’s economy as inflation was on the rise. Now, the incumbent faces a tough battle because of an affordability crisis and a corruption scandal that ensnared the same justice who led the investigation into Bolsonaro . Carlos Melo, a political science professor at Insper University in Sao Paulo, says some voters have grown weary of Lula, who is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term as president. He is one of the oldest presidents on the continent, along with Trump and Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega, both of whom also are 80. “Many in the Lula campaign were not expecting such a difficult election a few weeks ago, and it is clear to them that the present election is a tough battle and the next ones, without Lula, could be even more so,” Melo said. Bolsonaro has seen his political career tainted by several corruption accusations, the latest of them involving a disgraced banker paying him millions of dollars , allegedly to produce a movie on his father's life. More recently, he has been under fire from Roman Catholics who fear he might make too many concessions to his evangelical base. Associated Press writer Eléonore Hughes in Rio de Janeiro contributed to this report.
