events.title: I ranked the signature burgers from McDonald's, Wendy's, and Burger King. My favorite surprised me.
events.summary: I tried the signature burgers from three fast-food chains: McDonald's, Wendy's, and Burger King. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I tried the signature burgers from three fast-food chains: McDonald's, Wendy's, and Burger King. I thought McDonald's Big Mac was underwhelming and needed more sauce. I liked the smoky flavor of Burger King's Whopper and the chain's  recent upgrades . As a food reporter, I've tried and tested many burgers over the years. But for my latest taste test, I decided to go back to basics. While I've compared the biggest burgers at fast-food chains and practically every fast-food double cheeseburger , I wanted to see if the signature burgers from three of America's most beloved chains really are classics. I tried the McDonald's Big Mac, the Wendy's Dave's Single, and the Burger King Whopper to determine which is best in terms of taste and value. Even though they're menu mainstays, not all the burgers have remained unchanged: Burger King recently updated its signature  Whopper , and it's already helping boost the brand. Inspired by customer complaints that the burger was often squished during transit — it used to be simply wrapped in paper — the fast-food chain updated the Whopper in February with new box packaging, a new bun, and new, "creamier" mayonnaise. In August, the chain reported that US same-store sales jumped 8.5% in the second quarter, a surge that company president Tom Curtis attributed to the updated burger and new family-focused promotions, such as Burger King's Mandalorian meal collab, showing the power a signature burger can have. Here's how the three burgers compared and how I ranked them, from least to most favorite. My least favorite of the signature burgers I tried was McDonald's Big Mac. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Arguably the most iconic fast-food burger, the Big Mac is a staple on McDonald's menu. Created by owner-operator Jim Delligatti of Pittsburgh in 1967, the first "Big Mac" featured a triple-decker burger and sold for 45 cents, according to McDonald's. The burger rolled out across the US in 1968 and quickly became the chain's signature burger. Today, an estimated 900 million Big Macs are sold each year around the world. A Big Mac comes with two 1.6-ounce beef patties, pickles, shredded lettuce, chopped onions, a slice of American cheese, and layers of Big Mac sauce on a sesame-seed bun. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The Big Mac cost me $8.39, excluding tax, at my local McDonald's in Brooklyn, New York. Right away, I wasn't obsessed with the flavors or texture of this burger. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The burger I received was mostly lettuce, which covered up the flavors of the cheese, meat, and sauce. I wanted more of a tangy flavor from ketchup, mustard, or simply more Big Mac sauce. I thought it could have used an extra layer of sauce or cheese on top of the burger. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The burger tasted dry to me — I think a lot of that could be remedied if the burger wasn't so bottom-heavy with its toppings. The cheese and layers of Big Mac sauce were all toward the bottom of the burger, rather than the top, which meant the dry bun and burger were hitting the roof of my mouth with little to no flavor or moisture happening. While I understand that this is the most iconic burger on the McDonald's menu — and that preparation can vary slightly by location — it is by no means my favorite. Next time, I'll order a Quarter Pounder . My second-favorite burger was the Dave's Single from Wendy's. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Named after Wendy's founder, Dave Thomas, Dave's Single is Wendy's signature burger. It is available in multiple sizes, from a single to a triple-stacked burger . It features one of Wendy's signature square patties and is the chain's take on a classic cheeseburger.  The Dave's Single burger comes with a quarter-pound beef patty, a slice of American cheese, lettuce, tomato, pickles, ketchup, mayo, mustard, and onions on a potato bun. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The burger cost me $8.74, excluding tax, at my local Wendy's in Brooklyn. The burger was noticeably saucier than both the Whopper and the Big Mac. Erin McDowell/Business Insider It was practically dripping with sauces, which I didn't necessarily mind. Some of the flavors were slightly masked by the two condiments, but I thought the cheese was tangy and the onions cut through the burger's sweeter elements. There was also a generous serving of pickles and a large slice of tomato. Overall, I thought this was a good, classic cheeseburger. Erin McDowell/Business Insider If I had to change one thing, I might remove or ask for a half-serving of mayonnaise. But I thought it was an overall solid choice for a late-night snack. My favorite burger was the Whopper with cheese from Burger King. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Burger King's signature burger has been around for decades. Released in 1957, just four years after the chain opened, the Whopper was 37 cents compared to Burger King's original burger, which cost 18 cents. Whoppers — and all Burger King burgers, for that matter — are flame-grilled, giving their burgers a distinct smoky flavor. You can order a Whopper with or without cheese. Erin McDowell/Business Insider For the sake of this experiment, I decided to order a Whopper with cheese to ensure a fair comparison with the other signature burgers.  The Whopper cost me $9.18, excluding tax, at my local Burger King in Brooklyn. A Whopper comes with a quarter-pound beef patty, pickles, onions, lettuce, tomato, ketchup, and mayonnaise on a sesame-seed bun. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Burger King updated the Whopper to include a new premium mayonnaise and a new bun, and now serves it in a clamshell box instead of wrapping it in paper. The thicker, fluffier bun gave the burger more heft, which held in the generous amount of toppings. The flavorful burger was my favorite for both taste and texture. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The lettuce, tomatoes, and onions all tasted very fresh, adding a delicious crunch to the burger. The patties had a smoky, savory flavor that made the burger taste freshly grilled. Their wider, flatter shape also made the sandwich easier to eat than some of the thicker burgers I tried. The new, creamier mayonnaise had more flavor, without making the burger a soggy mess. Overall, I thought the burger was worth its higher price tag, which surprised me. Comparing the three signature burgers made me feel like a fast-food Goldilocks: One was too dry, one was too juicy, and this one was just right. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? | Emma Beddington
events.summary: Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? Their careers are peaking, they’re rich in money and time – and young people think they’re cool. But maybe it’s not as simple as that ‘S top sleeping on gen X.” I heard this on TikTok recently. I misinterpreted it, with a guilty start, as: “Stop sleeping, gen X,” because I am 51 (peak X), so always tired; while not sleeping at the time, I may have been resting my eyes. In fact, Joel Marlinarson, a marketing guru , was suggesting my generation have become a powerful, if underrated, force online. Aged between 46 and 61, gen Xers with proper jobs are peaking, career-wise (although it’s a different story for those out of work, as a report last month on the struggles of over-50s jobseekers made plain). We’re more likely to own homes than the following generations ; we’re emerging from the trenches of childrearing and, the argument goes, ready to indulge in some me-time. “If gen X were a country, it would be the world’s second-largest consumer market,” the World Economic Forum reported last year , with gen X women in particular influencing 70% to 80% of all consumer spending. That makes us great customers – witness the tidal wave of menopause-washed wellness guff (Which? reported last month that many pricey supplements were no better than a cheap multivitamin ) and beauty brands for people suddenly horrified by their necks . But does it give us content-creating clout? We’re supposed to be (or at least meme lore presents us as ) the forgotten generation, low-key, countercultural slackers on the sidelines in the grudge match between millennials and boomers; aspiration and self-promotion aren’t really part of our brand. Sure, kids are scrambling for Oasis tickets and rediscovering zines ; US Vogue called us “the cool ones” and the New York Times went further with “the greatest generation”. I get the argument that it’s our time to shine. But real gen Xers have a lot on their plate and it doesn’t necessarily lend itself to fun, aspirational content. Being peak career means peak responsibility: our parents are faltering (I’m writing this as my mother-in-law is moving into sheltered accommodation) and our kids are facing awful geopolitical and economic prospects that undermine their mental health and chances of independence. We’re falling apart physically: for women, the sorting hat of perimenopause doles out a set of grim symptoms, while men are wondering what will fell them next – heart, stomach, back or knees? Who wants to hear about that? And who can be arsed to make perky TikToks? I’ll tell you who: Kathryn Turner . I was introduced to Turner, M&S Food’s director of product development, by Marlinarson, for whom she is evidence that over-50s employees are “ the next biggest influencers ”. Turner, a cheery woman in smart trousers who exudes quiet competence, has worked for M&S since 1995. She launched her account in May, but her TikToks already garner up to 2m views and her nearly 250,000 fans are devoted: “Would follow that woman into war,” commented one . “Why did we give Andy Burnham the job over her,” asked another . “ I love you Kathryn turner [sic],” wrote an account claiming to be the Heartstopper actor Joe Locke . I love her, too: Turner’s calm sunniness, as she talks viewers through innovations in the picky bits space, is a balm in a fractious world. Turner isn’t Kate Moss, Miranda July or any of the other impossibly glamorous gen X figureheads – she seems like a normal, middle-aged woman who knows her stuff and does it well. I love that she’s popping up on TikTok and I get it – I’m projecting, but I bet Turner’s great in a crisis, her desk drawer and handbag well stocked with protein-rich treats, blister plasters and ibuprofen. Maybe this is our online USP. Could watching grownups quietly bossing their busy, complex lives be the next ASMR? Because, mostly, gen X aren’t the “cool ones”: they’re the knackered ones, dealing with life, death, work and frozen shoulders. I don’t know any Mosses or Chloë Sevignys, but I know lots of Turners and I, too, would follow them into war, or at least get a dopamine hit from watching them be extremely competent in short-form videos. No one would want to watch me staring at a screen then breaking to fold some pants, obviously, but I’d love to see more of my capable peers ditch the self-deprecation (very gen X) and shine online. Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behind
events.summary: Women hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruption T here’s a common fear among people who work in Silicon Valley: snag one of the fast-growing, high-paying jobs in artificial intelligence, or get trapped in the “permanent underclass”, a phrase describing the fate of those who won’t have upward mobility in the age of AI. The phrase usually describes a future in which AI automates human jobs. But for women in tech, it’s starting to look like the present. “A lot of people say: ‘Oh, AI is lowering barriers, it’s equalizing the playing field for women,’” said Urvashi Batra, co-founder and CEO of Prioriwise, an AI platform for IT service providers. “I actually think it’s the opposite.” Batra said people take her less seriously as the founder of an AI company than her male co-founder. When pitching investors, she and her co-founder have learned that they are more likely to get an investment if he does the pitching. Women made up only about a quarter of new hires in AI roles in the last year, compared to 50% of new hires in non-AI roles, according to a recent report from LinkedIn. In executive roles, that number drops to just 13%. At the same time, LinkedIn’s research shows that women are more likely to work in roles with high exposure to AI disruption, like customer service, meaning they are also at higher risk for job loss due to AI. AI jobs, whose postings have doubled since 2023, come with a salary premium, on average paying more than twice as much as roles that don’t involve working with AI, according to LinkedIn’s research. But women who do have jobs in AI are disproportionately concentrated in low-paying roles, like data annotators, said Sarah Steinberg, the head of global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn. Across all AI occupations, men have $45,000 higher median pay than women, partly due to the types of jobs they are likelier to have. “AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying and most consequential jobs in the global economy,” said Steinberg. “Women are just strikingly underrepresented.” The ongoing trend could produce the greatest gender pay gap in generations and leave women out of building a technology that shaped the economy, advocates for women in tech said. “What we’re witnessing is a sort of backsliding,” said Brenda Darden Wilkerson, president of AnitaB.org, a non-profit devoted to advancing women in tech jobs. Initiatives to promote women in the tech industry have been ongoing for years, with mixed results. Women now hold about one-third of tech jobs in the US. But research has found that women leave the tech industry at a much higher rate than their male counterparts, citing factors like non-inclusive cultures and barriers to advancement. ‘I’ve seen so many women fall through the cracks’ Women working in AI may face even greater challenges. “AI moves extremely fast, and the pressure to keep up is immense,” said Jayeeta Putatunda, an AI engineering lead at investment firm Turing. “I have seen throughout my career so many amazing women I know kind of fall through the cracks.” Putatunda said it’s not uncommon to be the only female engineer on a team, and that when women are outnumbered, they have to speak up louder to make their ideas known. Mentorship in the AI field, especially by other women, can be hard to come by. And the breakneck pace of AI advancements means anyone working in the field should expect to put in long hours in order to keep up. “If you have very ambitious career goals in this field, there will be seasons when you work beyond normal hours,” she said, noting that a culture of working 12-hour days to keep up was not uncommon. “I don’t think there is always a neat shortcut around that than to put in the hours.” Those kinds of work expectations can make it impossible for everyone to stay in the field. “I went on maternity leave for four months , and by the time I came back, there were completely different frameworks and levels of models,” Putatunda said. Getting caught back up was overwhelming. She said it was only possible with the help of supportive co-workers and a husband who equitably split childcare. “That is one way women get pushed out of AI,” she said. “They don’t lack the interest or ability to keep up. They may lack the infrastructure that makes keeping up possible.” The AI industry is so new and fast-moving that it should in theory be more meritocratic. No one has a decade of experience working with a model developed one year ago, which should mean everyone has a level playing field. But instead the field has indexed more on personal networks and other loose signals, according to some women who work in AI. “Companies are hiring at a breakneck speed, but they’re finding people through the same networks, the same referrals, the same filters that they’ve always used,” Wilkerson said. “Generally, that’s not given women the same sort of exposure they should have.

events.title: New York has a socialist mayor. Los Angeles may be next
events.summary: LOS ANGELES — Voters could make history next month by giving the two largest U.S. cities something in common: South Asian immigrant democratic socialist mayors. Why it matters: Such a pairing would capture two forces reshaping urban America — its growing diversity and the Democratic Party's shifting ideological boundaries. New York, the nation's largest city, is already led by democratic socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani . The challenger in Los Angeles is Nithya Raman, an Indian-born urban planner and two-term City Council member who is trying to unseat Democratic Mayor Karen Bass on Nov. 3. Bass, elected in 2022, is the first woman to serve as mayor of Los Angeles. State of play: Raman became the first Asian American woman and first South Asian elected to the L.A. City Council in 2020. A Harvard and MIT graduate, she entered politics after working on homelessness and neighborhood organizing. A September Berkeley IGS/L.A. Times poll found Raman at 39% among likely voters, Bass at 28% and 33% undecided. The intrigue: The Berkeley poll had Raman ahead 66%-4% among likely voters under 30, while 56% rated Bass' response to the Palisades Fire poor or very poor. It also found an even wider gap among likely Latino voters : Raman led Bass 45%-21%, with 34% undecided. What they're saying: "I'm getting a little emotional thinking about it," Raman told Axios and Noticias Telemundo on Wednesday at Visionarios when asked what it would mean if she and Mamdani led the country's two largest cities. Raman, who immigrated to the U.S. as a child, said her family came to America seeking opportunities they didn't have in India. She contrasted the welcome her family received with what she sees as a harsher moment for immigrants today under the Trump administration. "The idea of this city welcoming an immigrant as its mayor ... is just so deeply moving to me at this moment." The other side: Bass strategist Julie Chavez Rodriguez told Axios and Noticias Telemundo that voters are talking about rent, affordable housing, public safety and whether they can afford to raise families in Los Angeles. Rodriguez credited Bass with accelerating nearly 47,000 affordable housing units, a figure also cited by the mayor's office for units in the city's pipeline. She also defended Bass' response to federal immigration raids, pointing to lawsuits and restrictions on using city property to assist immigration enforcement. Zoom in: Raman's version of democratic socialism sounds less revolutionary than municipal. She told Axios that Americans are pushing back against an establishment they believe favors wealthy and politically connected interests. Her alternative: make City Hall deliver basic services and prove government can work for ordinary people. Raman called it "sewer socialism" or "pothole politics," adding: "I just want government to work for the people." Zoom out: Mamdani has made a similar ideological bet in New York, declaring at his inauguration that he was elected as a democratic socialist and would govern as one. Yes, but: Raman isn't simply the West Coast version of Mamdani. She calls herself an independent leader and has repeatedly split with Democratic Socialists of America-LA — accepting a pro-Israel group's endorsement that earned her a DSA censure . She also backed Jim McDonnell for LAPD chief over the group's objections and sought changes to L.A.'s voter-approved mansion tax that housing activists opposed.

events.title: Scoop: A powerful new model from startup Reflection is set to shake up the AI race
events.summary: A closely watched Nvidia-backed startup called Reflection is preparing to shake up the AI race with a powerful open-weight system that could threaten Chinese upstarts and U.S. AI giants alike. Why it matters : The marriage of an American open-weight model and Nvidia GPUs would give individuals and companies a new, cheaper alternative to Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. Open models, designed to compete with Chinese rivals, can be harder to monitor and regulate than the Big Three so-called frontier models. Supporters of such ecosystems say their widespread availability and transparency also bring security advantages. Reflection's first model is set to be joined by other open-weight models from other Western players this month, sources tell Axios. That will bring a new competitive dimension to the AI boom. State of play : Reflection's model, set to be released soon, is expected to initially lag behind the most cutting-edge U.S. models and be competitive with top Chinese open-weight models. Sources tell Axios it will still boast powerful intelligence — capable enough to help companies build their own proprietary, low-cost AI systems. Combining a lower-tier open model with high-quality company data can yield results that rival the most expensive frontier AI systems in certain situations. A Reflection spokesperson declined to comment. The big picture : Open-weight models, the most powerful of which are almost uniformly made in China, have taken Silicon Valley by storm. As opposed to closed models like Claude and ChatGPT, open-weight models like Reflection's are generally available to be downloaded freely and can be used and customized by anyone. On platforms that serve many models, their combined market share at times has surged to take up a majority of usage. However, in the far higher-spending arena of enterprise use, which is typically handled through API and corporate billing, open-weight models account for a small proportion of usage, AI execs and analysts say. Zoom in : Reflection's ultimate goal is to pioneer the "AI factory" — a product allowing institutions to spin up their own localized AI ecosystems. A company, for example, would take its own proprietary data, use Reflection's models and secure its own computing firepower to build a highly customized, cheap AI system. Some institutions, particularly hedge funds and trading firms, are already eager to build proprietary AI systems using their own highly guarded data. The startup has already begun testing this concept, announcing a sovereign AI factory partnership with Shinsegae Group in South Korea. Behind the scenes : In preparation for the launch, Reflection has held discussions with interested parties in Washington and elsewhere in recent weeks to detail its model release and explain how the AI factory will work, sources told Axios. It is also aggressively locking up the compute capacity required to scale. In recent weeks, the startup signed massive deals with Nebius and SpaceX to rent Nvidia AI servers. What they're saying : Reflection CEO Misha Laskin has indicated it will take time for its models to reach the most advanced capabilities. "They're kind of like rocket ships," Laskin, a Russian–Israeli researcher who previously worked at Google, told CNBC . "To build a big rocket ship, it takes time." The Nvidia factor : The AI factory has been a core vision of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for years. He has described a scenario combining computing hardware with open-source models, allowing enterprises to retain ownership of their data. Top AI users in Western business and government, such as banks or the Pentagon, balk at using highly capable Chinese models due to security risks. Reflection and other Western players are trying to fill that void. For years, Huang has sought to strengthen the open AI ecosystem and has been strongly supportive of Reflection's move toward building a top open system, according to stories in The Wall Street Journal and The Information . The bottom line : Reflection's release, and the startup's close ties to Nvidia, will bring a renewed focus on open-weight models, combining with other coming offerings to shake up the AI race.

events.title: My husband and I finally took a trip without our 5 kids. It didn't go at all how we expected.
events.summary: Our adults-only trip away from our kids didn't go the way I expected it to, but I'm still glad we gave it a try. Alexandra Frost My husband and I wanted to take a trip away from our five kids, so we planned a 4-day beach getaway . I didn't relax much, and it felt impossible to disconnect even though the kids had a trusted sitter. I missed my kids more than I expected, but I enjoyed being able to talk to my husband uninterrupted. My husband and I both work and parent our five kids, and some days the rat wheel of events and responsibilities feels endless. So, during a particularly tough season, we started scheming about whether it would actually be possible to "get away." First, we tried to plan a little weekend cabin retreat nearby, but I knew I'd just come right back if something went wrong, and it didn't feel like a real getaway without sand and water. How hard could it be, really, to hand off our day-to-day responsibilities to a fully qualified adult babysitter who is also a local teacher in our area? Once we planned to travel further, we started a spreadsheet to help us map out a few logistics. Four pages later, we were able to see the load we'd been carrying and how complex it would be to transfer it over. Yet, we did it. We headed to Florida from Ohio for a four-day beach getaway, hoping for the best. It didn't go as planned. Trying to relax was challenging even before all the messages began Let's just say toes in the water doesn't cure it all. Alexandra Frost I'm not someone who typically has a tough time being away from my kids. I don't struggle when we're separated at day-care drop-off , on date night, or during their occasional overnight stay at grandma's. However, as our plane landed several states away, anxiety started to build around how complicated it would be to get back in an emergency, and whether the sitter would really be able to handle five kids. It took a good 24 hours to calm down about it, which unfortunately was 25% of the vacation. I did notice that it was nice to be able to think about my own needs first for a bit. What did I want for dinner? What would be fun for us to do? These mini luxuries helped me start to understand why rediscovering yourself on getaways is necessary. But when you run your own seven-person three-ring circus, you can't really just turn off your phone, or it might all come crashing down. So I left it on, and couldn't really disconnect. The messages and notifications wouldn't stop. It started with a forgotten uniform. Soon after, it morphed into a disagreement with the babysitter about the rules. A grandparent wondered what time something was happening. A practice was canceled on the app that only I could see. A few beachside cocktails were a little bit helpful to get in the vacation spirit, but this didn't feel the same as a real vacation. I found this incredibly frustrating — we'd worked hard and paid a good amount of money to make it happen, and I couldn't calm down about my kids over 1,000 miles away? Everything's a little less cool when you can't show your kids — but uninterrupted time with my husband made the trip worth it It was nice for my husband and me to speak to each other without being interrupted by our kids. Alexandra Frost We found a nest of bunnies living next to the beach, which was the most shell-covered beach I'd ever seen. I wanted to show my kids, and I missed them. I'd head into the tourist shops to buy them shell necklaces, and feel nostalgic watching other families dig on the beach. I was sad they were missing this trip, and no amount of logic about how we really needed a break seemed to counteract the feeling. How ridiculous, I'd think to myself, that I spend time with them hoping to get a break away from them with my husband, and a break with my husband wishing they were there. I guess this is motherhood? Despite the crises with my kids — which kept getting more severe and distracting, from behavior issues to logistics problems — one bright spot in the vacation was some uninterrupted conversation. I learned that my husband and I actually have a great time together when we can finish a dang sentence. That made me excited for future trips where the kids are a little more self-sufficient and a couple's only getaway can feel a little more like that — a getaway. Until then, I'm already planning to head back to the beach with the kids, where I'll probably spend a lot of moments wishing I were able to get out of my head and enjoy an adults-only trip . events.title: The demands of Welsh devolution are simple: just give us what Scotland has | Will Hayward
events.summary: The demands of Welsh devolution are simple: just give us what Scotland has Andy Burnham is a Westminster leader whom Welsh nationalists could finally work with - but only if he stands up to the devo-sceptics in UK Labour A s I sat in the first Plaid Cymru conference since the party won the Welsh election and started leading the Welsh government, I heard things I had never heard before. I have been to a lot of Plaid conferences and not once have I heard people being really positive about a UK Labour leader. But there was no mistaking it: the Welsh nationalist party feels that Andy Burnham is a man it can work with. When I interviewed Welsh first minister Rhun ap Iorwerth , he indicated he was hopeful – in a way he never was under Keir Starmer – that there was a prime minister who had a genuine desire to give Wales meaningful concessions when it comes to additional powers. In his speech in Llandudno, the first minister said that the prime minister had “looked me in the eyes and promised he would not [bypass the Senedd]”. He said he had written to Burnham with a “formal ask” for “a new deal for Wales”. There were five demands from the Welsh government to Westminster: powers over policing and justice, powers over rail infrastructure, control over the crown estate , “fiscal fairness” and control of welfare. Seems like a pretty long shopping list, right? Well, it can actually be summarised in just five words: “Give us what Scotland has.” The Scots have control of the crown estate, a better funding settlement, with more money through the Barnett formula , heavy rail is devolved , and the Scottish government controls policing and justice, as well as having partial control of welfare spending . When you look at it from that perspective, it’s not as if the Welsh government is asking for something unprecedented. The UK government only has to look north to see the precedent. You don’t have to be a Welsh nationalist to think it’s unfair that Wales’s government is equipped with fewer tools than its Scottish counterparts to meaningfully tackle Wales’s challenges. Wales has less borrowing capacity than a local council and, as mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham had more power over policing in his area than the first minister of Wales does. The stars are aligning for Wales to get more parity with Scotland. If Burnham follows his own devolution logic – that decisions should be taken closer to the people they impact –then how could he defend a region of England getting more autonomy than a nation? Though figures within Plaid clearly believe that Burnham is genuinely open to giving Wales more powers, they have real concerns that the more devo-sceptic figures within both the UK Labour party and the civil service will hinder their attempts. These fears are not unfounded. A leaked memo from Starmer revealed that he warned his cabinet against being “overly deferential” to devolved governments. In December 2025, 11 Labour Senedd members wrote to the then PM accusing him of “rolling back” devolution. This fear led to one of the better lines in ap Iorwerth’s speech, where he said that if Burnham fails to give Cymru concessions: “Wales will know again that our best interests will never be served by Westminster, and that it matters little whether who lives in No 10 Downing Street is an Evertonian or an Old Etonian.” With all the talk of “the Burnham bounce”, one thing that I think is being missed in the wider media is the total collapse of Labour’s status in Wales. Before the Senedd election in May, Welsh Labour was the most successful democratic party in history, having been the largest party in Wales at every general and Senedd election since 1922 . Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more When Labour was struggling in England and Scotland against the Tories, led by both David Cameron and Boris Johnson, Welsh Labour was winning election after election. But now Labour’s dominance in Wales is over. In a 96-seat Welsh parliament, Labour now has just nine seats . At Labour conference in Liverpool, speaking to people on both the Welsh and UK sides of the party, it was clear to me that they were facing very different trajectories. UK Labour members were full of hope, optimism and excitement for what is to come: the conference was like an engagement party, to celebrate a union with their new partner. Meanwhile, Welsh Labour members had just broken up with their partner of 27 years and were totally cut up about the divorce. They were at the engagement party, trying to keep a stiff upper lip while nursing a can of strong lager and wondering how they were going to afford to furnish their new one-bed flat. But this is a very bad time for Welsh Labour to have an identity crisis. All of the demands made by Plaid to Burnham are longstanding Welsh Labour policies . For so long, Welsh Labour and devolution were synonymous with each other, but now the mood music is very different.

events.title: I replaced Spotify with CDs for my 8-year-old. It's one parenting decision I haven't regretted.
events.summary: The author introduced the kids to CDs. Courtesy of the author I wanted my 8-year-old to have the freedom to discover music on her own. Spotify exposed her to distracting videos, AI songs, and inappropriate images. I switched her to CDs, where she can choose freely from music I've approved. Lately, I have been filling our home with piles and piles of CDs. I'm not alone: physical media (primarily vinyl, but also CDs) have been on an upward sales trend for the past five years. But unlike vinyl collectors or tastemakers looking for rare albums, I am listening to CDs as a parenting move because of my 8-year-old daughter. I didn't want her to listen to AI slop As she grew out of the " Baby Shark " music of her toddlerhood and into appreciating rock, pop, hip-hop, and folk, I wanted her to have the opportunity to explore on her own and the freedom to choose what she liked. But when I put Spotify in my daughter's hands, she would scroll, listen for a few seconds, then scroll again. She would become mesmerized by the short videos that play with the music. She would try searching for "narwhal" or "axolotl" and find AI slop songs . The final straw came when dozens of playlists popped up in the search results with NC-17-looking playlist cover art. I looked down at my phone screen filled with anime seductresses, and I was done forever with trying to let my child navigate Spotify on her own. I gave my child a pile of CDs An experiment ensued: a CD player and a pile of CDs. My CD player in 2026 is handsome, wooden, and Bluetooth-enabled. She can pick anything. If streaming were a sprawling trash pile filled with needles, CDs are a playground with a beautiful fence. If streaming were an art museum with AI-generated animations suddenly flashing in front of the Mona Lisa, CDs are a quiet gallery with perfect light. The author didn't want her 8-year-old listening to AI slop. Courtesy of the author Streaming wasn't just harmful for my kid; it was harmful for me. I had grown increasingly dissatisfied as my personalized playlists served me more and more familiar tracks, sending me into the same well-worn rivulets of songs that are inoffensive and foolproof for me. When I put on a CD, it is easier for me to surrender to letting it play from front to back. When I want to look up a lyric, I pull out the liner notes. There is no risk of my seeing a notification. The cover art might be faded and stiff, but it is not going to pivot to video. CDs are part of my war for presence, a small but crucial reclaiming of what it means to be still in a space and listen to a song. We've been buying new CDs I have been delightfully surprised to find that CDs are still readily available out there in the world, at thrift stores, estate sales, and even Target and Walmart. CDs have traits that children crave: they're tactile objects made of glass and plastic that require careful handling. They come with their own context — the cover art, liner notes, track listing. Importantly, they come with very little censorship overhead for parents. In amassing a small CD collection for our family, I've replaced the constant "no"s and negotiations my daughter and I had over Spotify with music that is a hearty yes for me. Yes to Bonnie Raitt, yes to the Cranberries, yes to Soul and R&B Today. The author has been buying new CDs. Courtesy of the author Vinyl records have a similar physicality, but CDs have a few key advantages over records, in my humble opinion. They're smaller and cheaper. If you really want to, you can still burn almost any CD. And the audio quality of a CD is unbeaten, though lots of people have woo-woo beliefs to the contrary. The seduction of a needle dropping into a physical groove is real, but I'll take the less romantic, plucky CD any day. I've discovered new artists Our joint adventure into CDs has blasted me out of the algorithmic doldrums and into a space of discovery and receptiveness. I've been listening to new-to-me artists like Lucinda Williams and Bill Evans. I dug up my old CD books and found mixes my friends made for long road trips. I remembered how central music was to life and friendship back when I was a teenager, and CDs reigned. The author discovered new authors. Courtesy of the author I want my daughter to have that kind of deep relationship with music someday. She's a typical 8-year-old who puts on Taylor Swift 90% of the time; every now and then, we rock out to Queen, Avril Lavigne, or The Donnas. When we look for something to listen to together, we just scan our plastic cases and pick something. We get to the fun part faster. She digs the new Muna record, which has an apropos track, "Big Stick," in which lead singer Katie Gavin becomes the voice of the algorithms that rule our lives, chanting, "I can make you want what I want you to." We dance, we holler, and I enjoy the satisfaction of knowing that no one is making us want anything we haven't chosen for ourselves. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: A cargo ship, 20 crew, and a huge stash of cocaine: the seafarer imprisoned for smuggling – on no evidence
events.summary: After Turkish police found drugs on board the Phoenician M, the ship’s chief mate, Ali Albokhari, was sentenced to 30 years in prison. His wife is still fighting to free him I n the early hours of 6 October 2023, Elena Albokhari was woken by a text message from her husband. Ali Albokhari, 42, a Finnish-Syrian with dark hair and cherubic features, was chief mate on a cargo ship named the Phoenician M and had been at sea since June. The 180-metre bulk carrier had docked at Ereğli in the Turkish Black Sea a few days earlier and Ali was due to return home to Helsinki soon, but instead of feeling excitement, Elena was growing increasingly worried about his welfare. She’d had a similar feeling of unease a month earlier, when the ship had arrived at Barranquilla, Colombia . Ali had called in a panic to report that drugs had been found; Armada Nacional officers had marched onboard and uncovered holdalls stuffed with 137kg cocaine. Labels on the packages – the crest of Turkish football club Kayserispor – hinted at their destination: Turkey was the next port of call. “I never want to work as a seaman again,” Ali told Elena. “We are having big problems.” For two days, the ship was held at the port. Elena, 39, a tour guide from Russia, was so anxious, she could barely sleep. Then she received a photo from Ali of the crew happily drinking beer in a restaurant – the drugs had been removed and, after a meeting with the harbourmaster, the ship cleared to depart. “So will you go on working as a seaman?” Elena asked. “Yeah,” Ali said. “Sometimes it happens … so it’s OK.” Yet when the Phoenician M arrived at Ereğli on 2 October, loaded with coal, it was targeted by Turkish narcotics officers. The ship’s captain, Marko Bekavac, 63, a steely Croatian with three decades’ experience as a seafarer, had already informed the ship’s management company about the incident in Colombia, and when Turkish authorities boarded, he immediately declared that drugs had previously been found on the ship. Despite this, officers delivered a statement: should anything be found onboard, he would be accountable. The 20 crew members, including citizens of Russia, Ukraine, Poland and the Philippines, were ordered to remain in the ship’s mess room as the police continued to investigate. Nothing was found in an initial search but days later, as the coal was unloaded, suspicious bags were reportedly found buried in the cargo hold. They were packed with more cocaine. The captain and other crew were escorted from the ship. Ali, who was second in command, remained onboard as unloading continued. He had managed to keep hold of his phone and was sending Elena updates. These had done little to allay her fears. Now, in the middle of the night, a text message confirmed the worst: “They are going to arrest us.” U nless we are related to a seafarer, or live near a major port, most of us don’t encounter the people who work in shipping. Yet without them our lives would grind to a halt. Oceanic trade routes are the thread that weaves the world together. Merchant shipping – often described as the “lifeblood of the global economy” – is responsible for the movement of 90% of trade; every year, 11bn tonnes of goods, from coffee to fuel to fashion, are transported by ship. The scale of the maritime infrastructure is staggering, but the 2.57 million seafarers who operate within it remain largely invisible, as do many of the challenges they face. Elena never thought of Ali’s work as inherently risky, and the life of a merchant seaman can seem mundane. Cargo ships travel at around 15 knots (17mph). A boat like the Phoenician M can take more than two weeks to traverse the Atlantic. The routine involves inspections, maintenance checks, paperwork and long stretches at sea. But seafarers have become vulnerable to rapidly shifting conflicts – from the Russian invasion of Ukraine to the battle around the strait of Hormuz – as well as poor regulatory oversight, abandonment by shipowners and abuse by port authorities. Seafarers’ rights are frequently neglected and they are too easily scapegoated for events outside their control. When an incident occurs, it is often far easier for authorities to pursue crew members than the shipping companies that employ them, who have an incentive to let the blame fall on individuals, and the P&I (protection and indemnity) clubs that insure them are there to serve the company, not individual crew members. The very nature of the job means voyaging to far-flung destinations, so if things do go wrong, seafarers can be forced to navigate unfamiliar judicial systems, with discretionary legal support, and face long periods of detention in a foreign country. Data on the scale of the problem is limited, but one 2018 survey by Nautilus International, the maritime professionals’ union, found that 90% of seafarers feared criminalisation above anything else.

events.title: My 16-year-old still has a 9 p.m. bedtime. It's great for our whole family.
events.summary: The author said her teen goes to bed at 9 p.m. almost every night. DMP/Getty Images A 9 p.m. bedtime ensures my 16-year-old daughter gets enough sleep for school success. Our bedtime routine encourages open communication and connection with my daughter. Maintaining a consistent bedtime is crucial for my daughter's health and daily routine. As my daughter prepared to go back to school this year, there was the usual business of buying school supplies, wondering about her new Biology teacher, and thinking about her birthday, which falls a few weeks after school starts. One thing we didn't have to worry about was getting back into a good sleep routine , because she still has a bedtime. Even in the summer . Even on weekends. Which might not sound that unusual, except she's 16 years old, and I expect her to be in bed by 9. The author said her daughter thrives on routines, so sticking to a bedtime still makes sense for her family. Courtesy of Sarah E. White. We still talk at bedtime We didn't plan to keep bedtime going this long; it just happened that we kept telling her it was bedtime, and she kept listening. I know there are kids who would protest this, and family lifestyles that would not support it, but it works for us, and I'm grateful for that. With the start of 11 th grade, we've pushed bedtime to 9 p.m. Devices go away, we say goodnight, and I sit with her for a few minutes (sometimes more than a few) to give her time to talk about whatever she wants to talk about. Do you have a hot take on a common parenting belief? Email Jennifer Beck Goldblatt at jgoldblatt@insider.com to share your experience with Business Insider. Sometimes the bedtime chatter is about the video game she's playing or that video she watched about the history of Lunchables. But sometimes it's real talk , about homework or life worries. I know it makes me feel more connected to her, and I hope she feels the same way. We have a routine My daughter thrives on routine, not just at bedtime but throughout the day. When we've talked about potentially stopping the bedtime ritual, she says she could go to sleep without it, but she likes it for now. Bedtime itself isn't going anywhere. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, teens need 8 to 10 hours of sleep , and in a national sample, nearly 73 percent didn't get enough on school nights. High school is also the time when homework, extracurriculars, work, and other things might be keeping kids up later, even if they want to sleep more. But not getting enough sleep can put them at risk for all sorts of issues, from poor attention and behavior problems to an increased risk of obesity and Type 2 diabetes, to mental health woes and increased risk of accidents. I'd like to avoid those outcomes. It's not for everyone, but we love it I know a lot of teens and parents wouldn't want or be able to have this kind of nighttime routine . And there's probably something to be said for fostering independence in your teens by letting them decide when and how they go to bed. But I also know that sleep is so important, so, as long as my daughter is willing to go to bed at a time that allows her to get the sleep she needs, we're going to support that. The author (left) said she also enjoys spending time alone with her husband after their daughter has gone to bed. Courtesy of Sarah E. White. Sure, there are days she has to stay up late to finish homework, or wants to stay up late because something special is happening, but knowing that most of the time she'll be in bed by 9 is good for all of us. Sticking to this bedtime gives her time to shut her brain down without devices, and enough sleep to make the morning more bearable. It gives my husband and me time to be alone together in the evening, which is so important for parents (and couples of all sorts). And I hope it's fostering good sleep habits that she'll carry with her even when we're not there to gather up the devices and sit with her in the dark. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Amazon exec says finding FDE talent is very challenging: ‘These are unicorns’
events.summary: Amazon Web Services vice president for forward-deployed engineering, Asa Kalavade, said the company is looking for a specific skill set. Amazon Amazon Web Services has made a $1 billion bet on FDEs. Finding the right workers isn't easy, an Amazon exec told Business Insider. "These are unicorns," the exec said. Forward-deployed engineers are one of the hottest jobs in AI. Finding them isn't easy. "These are unicorns," Asa Kalavade, vice president of forward-deployed engineering at Amazon Web Services , told Business Insider. Like its rivals, Amazon has made a big bet on the future of FDEs. In June, AWS announced a $1 billion investment to create a dedicated AWS FDE organization. Popularized by Palantir, FDEs are often embedded with companies to integrate AI into their workflows and to build more customized solutions. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Microsoft have announced major initiatives in recent months to compete for the lucrative enterprise AI business. Forrester estimates that between May and July alone, the three companies and Amazon pledged roughly $9 billion to FDE-related ventures. "FDE hiring is sort of the rage in town these days," Kalavade said. "Everybody wants to be an FDE." Amazon is being selective as it builds the team, Kalavade said, initially focusing on engineers who can hit the ground running. "Our initial seed is what I call the insurgents, the frontier engineers who've been there, done this before," she said. Kalavade said it's "a really hard role," and that those best positioned to succeed have a startup mindset. She said Amazon is essentially looking for three things: a product customer mindset, deep software expertise, and agentic experience. "Different people will have different strengths, but at the end of the day, that's the package that we think makes the most successful FDEs," she said. Part of the issue, Kalavade said, is that colleges and universities are still developing FDE training programs. She said that recent groups of applicants have improved, especially in their familiarity with AI. "The batch that came out this summer was the first one that grew up with more AI native thinking," she said. Kalavade said AI models alone can get customers "halfway," but she said FDEs are needed to turn that into a customized solution. "Anyone can build an agent now, but how do you make sure the agent has the right guardrails?" she said. "How do you figure out, 'OK, what's the best underlying model that I can use from a cost-based perspective?' What do I need to do to update to the next model? How do I make sure that the right security policies are applied? So all of those things are areas that are needed around the model." Amazon wants to make AI integration easier, Kalavade said, while also making sure companies can become more self-sufficient. "We want them to look and co-build with us for one or two, or six months," she said, "but then the only way we can create long-lasting change is if they co-build and they adopt these methodologies to do more." events.title: ‘The violence is off the scale’: staff and passengers at risk as assaults on trains in Great Britain soar to record high
events.summary: Cases of abuse, spitting, head-butting and sexual harassment, have spiked as transport police numbers have dwindled When a train was halted outside Exeter St Davids station on Monday, rail staff leapt to one conclusion: there had been a violent incident on board. “Someone will have kicked off,” one staff member said. “It happens all the time. My boss got head-butted recently.” On this occasion, they were wrong – but their assumption told a tale. Figures released late last month showed the number of reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways had risen by a fifth, to a record high of almost 25,000 incidents in a year. Staff in particular have felt increasingly under threat. While the total numbers reported by the Office of Rail and Road in 2025-26 covered threats, verbal abuse, and contact that might not have resulted in any injury, they included nearly 2,500 physical assaults on workers – an average of about seven every day. Their unions said the numbers were horrendous, but unsurprising: the RMT and TSSA unions have campaigned for more staffed stations and policing, after the number of British Transport Police (BTP) officers fell by more than 10% between 2024 and 2026. Many rail staff wear body cams to record and log incidents of violence. “I think it’s so sad that we have those,” said Dave*, a rail worker in south-west England . However, after 20 years in the job, he said: “The threats, the abuse, the violence we see is off the scale.” Drink and drugs play a part, he added. “We’re also seeing a lot more people with mental health issues. If you’re out on the street you can steer clear, but if you’re on a train or a platform you can’t. Our workplaces are becoming more and more dangerous.” Steve, a guard based in the north of England, was punched in the head by a passenger: “It was my last train of the night. I’ve had to look away to see the door controls and the next thing I know, I’m waking up on the platform.” Every guard gets verbally abused on a daily basis, he said, with behaviour worsening since the pandemic: “Now it’s mostly bad days, and you’re searching for good days, where nothing’s said, or nothing happens. The amount of times we’re getting threatened now with physical attacks, even when you walk through the train and say, ‘Tickets, please.’” Even those working on the infrastructure can be on the receiving end. One rail contractor, Liam, based in Somerset, said: “We’re there working on the tracks and we sometimes get sworn at and even spat at. It’s just a minority, but somehow they think we’re responsible for slow journey times, cancelled trains. We’re in bright orange so we’re easy targets.” The railway is by no means unique: bus drivers have faced repeated abuse and threats, as the Unite union has highlighted. Transport for London staff working on roads are issued with “spit kits”, or forensic saliva collection tubes, so common is that form of assault. Violence against women and girls is of particular concern; at the Labour conference this week, the minister for buses and local transport, Simon Lightwood, described it as a “national emergency”. Speaking alongside him, the mayor for the north-east, Kim McGuinness, said that as well as measures such as more staffing, lighting and CCTV, a crucial point for women was “knowing that if you raise an alarm something is going to be done. It’s a choice to use public transport or not … if you’re accepting 50% of the population don’t feel safe, that’s not good.” The rail industry and police say some of the sharp rise in recorded assaults on passengers – up 36% last year – is due to greater reporting, including using discreet text messaging to the BTP. But while many more incidents are now reported, plenty are not. Emily, 24, was travelling home on a late-night train between Glasgow and Edinburgh last year when a stranger made a beeline for her. “He immediately tried to start a conversation and wouldn’t give up even when I showed no interest. He was asking what I’d been up to, whether I had a boyfriend, complimenting my outfit, and then it escalated really quickly.” The man began rubbing Emily’s upper thigh and asking her intrusive questions about her sex life. “I froze and didn’t know what to do. I looked around but everyone else was oblivious. I tried to move but I was on the inside seat and he just grabbed my leg harder and leaned in towards me,” she said. She managed to manoeuvre out of the seat and away from the man, who “shouted aggressively and called [her] a bitch”. Other passengers looked round but did not intervene. She moved to another carriage and arrived home shaken but decided not to report the incident. “I wanted to just move on,” Emily said. “But I never used to think twice about getting on a train by myself at night and now I’m much more nervous.

events.title: Americans’ love of oversized Halloween skeletons is still going strong
events.summary: The original Skelly has amassed a massive following since it launched in 2020. Jay L. Clendenin/Getty Images The original 12-foot Skelly from Home Depot first went viral in 2020. Six years later, the trend of jumbo Halloween yard decorations seems as strong as ever. Walmart-owned Sam's Club is tapping into the trend with an 11-foot reaper, but Skelly remains king. It wasn't all that long ago that towering Halloween skeletons weren't really a thing. That all changed seemingly overnight in 2020, when Home Depot introduced its  wildly popular 12-foot Skelly  decoration, driving record Halloween sales for the home improvement chain that year. The trend is still going strong, with more than a dozen online communities devoted to supersized skeletons, including a Facebook group with nearly 300,000 members. Walmart-owned warehouse chain Sam's Club told Business Insider that sales of their version, an 11-foot Reaper, have been running ahead of expectations since it was launched back in June. The Reaper quickly rose to become one of the chain's top ten selling Halloween items, and was sold out at some warehouse locations, as of Friday. "Halloween is now a season, just like Christmas," said Kara Deleon, Senior Director of Seasonal Merchandising at Sam's Club. "It is truly taking on a much bigger persona than it's ever had in the past." Americans appear to have embraced the Summerween creep, with online visits to Sam's Club's Halloween decor product listings up 67% in July compared to the year before, the company said. But few things embody that bigger persona than the jumbo skeletons (and their friends) that have been popping up in yards across the US. Some setups last for just a few weeks, while others stay up year-round — to the consternation of some homeowners' associations. Phil Michalski, an instructional assistant who lives near Philadelphia, told Business Insider he owns both the Home Depot Skelly and Sam's Club Reaper, plus a few others. "The majority are set up all year round, but the weather this year has beaten them down," he said. "My other skeletons will be up until the new year as I put Santa suits on some and a Ebenezer Scrooge hat on another." "I have the Deadwood up by my front door, and that's a local landmark," he said, referring to another 12-foot Halloween offering from Home Depot that looks like a menacing Groot from Marvel's Guardians of the Galaxy series. Nelson Bairos, an engineer who lives near Boston, told Business Insider he started a side hustle of 3D printing repair parts for the original Home Depot Skelly to help the decorations endure through years of heavy use. "When there's a storm somewhere in the US, I can pretty much guarantee that's where I'm getting orders from. It's a pretty easy correlation," he said. While Sam's Club and others — including rival home improvement chain Lowe's — have offered numerous variations on the jumbo spooky theme, Bairos said none have had quite the staying power of the original Skelly . He bases this observation on the volume of repair requests he receives, which would require him to purchase a specific model to design parts for. "I have two Skellies. One is complete," Bairos said. "The other one's sort of for parts — a little beat up." Deleon's colleague Bobbi Austin, a merchant for seasonal goods, said Sam's Club is trying to accomplish several things with this year's Reaper, which features a silver and black color scheme, as well as a sickle, robe, and spooky animatronics. Exclusivity is key, but durability is also a factor, she said, as each new jumbo decor design is only sold in clubs for one season, and club members can build up a collection over time. "They knew they were coming in for bread, but they didn't know they were going to walk out with an 11-foot reaper," Deleon said. Have a tip? events.title: I used AI to track my job rejections. It changed my search, and I got hired.
events.summary: In her job search, Margareth Felicia Gono created an AI workflow that helped her evaluate roles and analyze interview sentiment Courtesy of Margareth Felicia Gono Margareth Felicia Gono used AI to bring structure to her job search , landing a role at DoorDash. She built Claude tools to assess her résumé and analyze the sentiment of interviews. Gono said she didn't want AI to exaggerate her experience or make her sound like everyone else. Margareth Felicia Gono, 24, recently started as a senior associate at DoorDash after completing a master's degree in applied analytics in May. During her job search, she created an AI workflow that helped her evaluate roles and analyze interview sentiment. The following is based on conversations that have been edited for brevity and clarity. At the beginning of my job search, it was pretty scattershot. Because I was an international student and needed a visa, I felt I had to apply to anything that might relate to my experience, even if it wasn't the right fit. I grew up in Indonesia and didn't want to leave the US without getting corporate experience. My parents paid for my tuition at a private university, then an Ivy League master's on top of that. I started tracking my results. What roles got responses? What didn't? What patterns showed up? Anxiety is unprocessed data. I was tired of feeling bad about my search and figured I might as well learn something instead. Around the second or third round of interviews, I noticed I would get a little bit of hesitation from employers, and I wanted to understand why that was happening. Was it me, my experience, my résumé, or that I needed a visa? I used Claude as a career coach I used Claude almost like a partner and built this tracker for my applications. I'd take a job description and ask Claude to identify the main skills, keywords, and themes. Then I built another automation agent into that same project. Basically, it was my own version of what people call an ATS score. I'd paste the job description and my résumé together and ask, "What top keywords am I missing?" I didn't want AI to invent experience or make me sound like everyone else . I wanted it to show me where my experience wasn't being communicated clearly enough. Sometimes that meant changing one bullet. Sometimes it meant realizing that applying would be a waste of time. As I went along, I became more intentional about who I wanted to work under and what types of jobs I applied for. I used Claude to act like a career coach and figured out I liked three things: talking to people, making things pretty, and finding patterns. As a result, I made three résumés: one for analytics, one for sales and marketing, and one for consulting. Eventually, I used Claude to turn that into a simple dashboard , so I could see what was happening: 186 applications, 44 cold outreaches, 19 interviews, six take-home assignments, three final rounds, and one offer. Seeing it that way made the process feel less like 185 personal failures, and more like a funnel I could keep improving. I treated an interview like a conversation During the process, I started treating every interview like a real conversation instead of an audition. I also really wanted to find someone who was not just a good boss but also a good mentor. When recruiters said they were using an AI note-taker, I'd ask if I could record, too. Most said no. With the yeses, I would scrape the notes and use a sentiment analysis to figure out where I hesitated or used filler words, where the interviewer asked me to get more specific, where they seemed engaged, agreed, or laughed. Even when I couldn't record, I'd write down what I remembered right after — what they asked, where I rambled, what seemed to interest them. I also used AI to research the people I was interviewing with. I built a skill in Claude to scrape LinkedIn profiles. I copy and paste everything on their page, and by now, Claude knows who I am because I talk to it a lot. So I ask it to find similarities to me . In one case, I connected with a recruiter over a cheese club we'd both been part of, years apart. That got me further than any cover letter or résumé font choice ever did. I also think the questions at the end of an interview can make or break it. I would ask how they got to where they are, and what advice they'd give someone just graduating. I think when you stop letting the interviewer drive the entire conversation and actually engage back, you go further. It's easy to have imposter syndrome, but I tried to remember that this is a process, and I know my experience. I've done my research. I know why I want to apply to this job, and if they don't see my value, someone else will. Everyone has access to AI now, so that isn't a differentiator. What makes the difference is knowing what to ask, how to interpret what AI gives you, and where judgment still matters. AI can help you see patterns, but you have to decide what they mean. It can help you get your foot in the door, but it can't make you want the job or make someone remember you . Do you have a story to share about your job search? events.title: These 5 states will pay you to build a tiny home in your backyard
events.summary: An ADU built by Villa in a California backyard. miller.photo for Villa Building tiny backyard homes can be expensive . The units can range in cost — from under $100,000 to over $300,000.  These states will help with the cost by providing homeowners with grant money.  Here are the programs, how much homeowners can receive, and who is eligible to apply.  If you've looked into building a  tiny home  in your backyard, you've probably discovered what many have: While they may save you money in the long run, they can be expensive to build. These homes, called accessory dwelling units , or ADUs, are small housing units ranging from 150 square feet to 1,200 square feet, depending on where you live. While detached backyard units are popular, ADUs can be incorporated into many parts of a property, including as a garage or basement conversion, an above-garage unit, or an attic or upper-level apartment. The average cost of a unit can range from  $100,000 to $300,000,   not to mention the permit cost, and securing a loan to build an ADU can be challenging . In California, where most backyard homes are being built, ADU building permits cost anywhere from $450 to $15,000 — even before construction starts, Backyard Unlimited, a company that builds ADUs, said. That's not all: Other costs could include site preparation, which includes anything from inspections to running utility lines.   To put it another way, if you don't have cash easily available or the ability to access financing for the project, it can be cost-prohibitive,  making it harder  for middle- and low-income homeowners to actually build one, studies have shown. To combat this disparity, promote equity, and ultimately propel the construction of much-needed housing, some states — as well as nonprofits in specific cities — have established loan and or grant programs to provide assistance. The deadlines for these programs vary from state to state. Those interested in building an ADU should be prepared for next year's application cycles, as they often experience high demand. Here are the ADU programs launched nationwide. Colorado: A new grant program is still rolling out A tiny home in Colorado. Ray Wise/Getty Images In 2024, Colorado passed HB24-1152 to assist homeowners in building ADUs. The Colorado Department of Local Affairs (DOLA) works directly with local governments as they implement regulatory changes to comply with HB24-1152. DOLA also runs the Accessory Dwelling Unit Grant Program (ADUG), which provides $5 million to jurisdictions that bring their codes into compliance and support ADUs. Who can apply? For ADUG, jurisdictions can apply for funding to provide technical assistance to low- and moderate-income homeowners. The Colorado Housing and Finance Authority (CHFA) is also establishing programs that directly support homeowners. Total funding available: The state has set aside $5 million for ADUG. The primary homeowner-directed effort channels $8 million into CHFA's ADU Finance Programs, providing lender support through loans, credit enhancements, and interest-rate buydowns to help homeowners. When are applications open? Applications for the third round of funding opened on September 28 and will close on Friday, October 23, 2026. Requirements: Local governments — including those not covered by HB24-1152 — must be certified by DOLA as an ADU Supportive Jurisdiction under the legislation. Agency or Department in charge of distribution: The Colorado Department of Local Affairs, Colorado Housing and Finance Authority Hawaii: A couple of counties provide grants or incentives for ADU construction Maui, Hawaii. Brandon Colbert Photography/Getty Images To help expand the supply of workforce housing, Maui County launched the ʻOhana Assistance program to aid homeowners in building attached or detached ADUs on their properties. The County of Kaua'i also offers financial assistance for homeowners who build a second unit on their property through the Affordable Additional Rental Unit (ARU) program. Who can apply? Owner-occupants with qualified residentially zoned property are eligible to apply for both the ʻOhana Assistance program and the Kaua'i Affordable Additional Rental Unit program. Total funding available: The ʻOhana Assistance Pilot Project provides grants of up to $100,000 for qualifying homeowners. Kaua'i's ARU program waives certain county development and permitting fees for homeowners who agree to keep the unit affordable to households earning up to 90% of the area median income for at least five years. Kaua'i's website states that the combined fee waivers and subsidies for an ARU certified through the program can total nearly $20,000. When are applications open? Applicants should consult Maui's Department of Housing and Human Concerns for the ʻOhana Assistance program. Kaua'i accepts applications year-round. Requirements: The Ohana Assistance program: Grant recipients must set ADU rents in line with the county's workforce housing requirements. The ADU must also be rented to full-time residents of Maui County for at least 10 years. Kaua'i's Affordable Additional Rental Unit program: Homeowners must own property in a zoning district that allows ARUs. The ARU must be no larger than 800 square feet, and one additional parking space is generally required, subject to zoning and County standards. The ARU cannot be used as a short-term rental and must be rented for long-term residential use. Agency or Department in charge of distribution: The County of Maui Department of Housing, Kaua'i County Housing Agency Massachusetts's ADU incentive program is in its first phase An A-frame tiny home in a backyard. Aleksei Isachenko/Getty Images Under Massachusetts' Affordable Homes Act, homeowners in most parts of the state—excluding Boston—have the right to build ADUs of up to 900 square feet on their property. To help homeowners build them, Massachusetts has launched a statewide incentive program. The program is in its first phase and focuses solely on property owners. Who can apply? Any homeowner in Massachusetts living in an area that allows residential ADU construction. Total funding available: Massachusetts's ADU Incentive Program pays approved professionals up to $500 to conduct feasibility studies for homeowners. These studies are designed to help property owners make informed decisions about their ADU projects and include: Details about a property's specific conditions and limitations Zoning and permitting requirements in the local municipality Utility needs, including water, sewer, and energy Key ADU design considerations, though the study does not provide architectural designs, engineering plans, or construction documents Estimated project costs and budget considerations; the program does not provide permit application services When are applications open? The program launched in July 2026, and applications remain open. Requirements: The property must be located

events.title: Real-estate investors who started with little savings share 4 creative ways they bought property
events.summary: Grace Cary/Getty Images Four investors share how they used existing assets to fund their first rental properties. Their approaches included borrowing from their 401(k), home equity, and a paid-off truck. The strategies lowered the cash barrier but added debt. It's easy for prospective real-estate investors to get discouraged by sticker shock. Many lenders require a down payment of at least 20% for an investment property. With the median US home price hovering around $400,000 , that can mean coming up with $80,000 — and that's without factoring in closing costs, repairs, and cash reserves. If you don't have tens of thousands of dollars in cash at your disposal, investing in real estate isn't necessarily out of reach. Business Insider spoke with four investors who found creative ways to use assets they already had — from retirement savings to a paid-off truck — to help finance their first deals. Lucy Zheng borrowed from her 401(k) Lucy Zheng and her husband bought their first investment property by tapping into retirement funds. Lucy Zheng When Lucy Zheng wanted to buy her first rental in 2023, she was cash-strapped and living in California, where prices felt unaffordable. She began looking at cheaper Midwest markets, eventually focusing on Detroit, where she found homes selling for about $60,000. To fund the purchase, Zheng put in about $15,000 of her own money and borrowed the rest from her 401(k), allowing her to buy the property in cash. Under the rules of her employer-sponsored plan, she could borrow up to $50,000 or 50% of her vested account balance, whichever was less. For Zheng, the appeal was speed and cost. She said she received the money within a few business days, paid a $75 fee, and closed on the property within two weeks. She also liked that the interest on the loan went back into her own retirement account. To make the monthly repayments manageable, she temporarily reduced her regular 401(k) contributions so the loan payments roughly replaced what she had already been setting aside from each paycheck. The major caveat, she noted, was the job-related risk: If she left or lost her job, she would have had to repay the balance immediately. Mark Kearney used a HELOC to buy his first rental Mark Kearney used a HELOC to help buy his first rental. The income from his real-estate portfolio eventually allowed him to retire early. Mazske Finance Florida-based investor Mark Kearney never earned more than $52,000 a year and didn't think real-estate investing was a viable path to wealth, but he was able to use a home equity line of credit , or HELOC, to help fund his first investment property. A HELOC lets homeowners borrow against the equity in their primary residence — the difference between what the home is worth and what they still owe on it — and it works similarly to a credit card: The lender approves a maximum credit line, and the homeowner can draw from it as needed during a set period. Kearney said his paid-off home was worth about $200,000 at the time. Rather than borrow close to the maximum amount available, he opened a $30,000 line of credit — about 15% of his home's value — to help purchase a $100,000 single-family house in Virginia's Shenandoah Valley. After finding a tenant, Kearney said the rental generated about $220 a month in profit. He used some of that cash flow to pay down the HELOC balance and put some into savings. Kent He took out a home-equity loan to fund a short-term rental Kent He used a home-equity loan to buy a short-term rental property. Courtesy of Kent He Kent He tapped into the value of his San Diego home using a different product: a home-equity loan . He and his wife bought their primary residence in 2019. As it appreciated, they built substantial equity and eventually took out a home-equity loan, which provides a fixed amount of cash upfront. "When we bought, our home was $800,000, but it went up $200,000 in value," he said. "Because we're able to take out 80% of that, we could take out up to $160,000 of home equity to use it towards whatever we wanted." They chose to use the money to invest in a short-term rental. A home-equity loan is similar to a HELOC in that both products let homeowners tap their home equity, but they distribute the money differently. A home-equity loan provides a lump sum upfront, while a HELOC provides a credit limit that borrowers can draw from during a set period. Think of your primary home as "another tool in your tool belt," said He. "With all this equity, maybe you can take it out and put it into an investment, as long as the investment makes sense and it fits your risk appetite." Mike Savage took a loan against his paid-off truck Mike Savage is a former firefighter and EMT who now invests in real estate full-time. Courtesy of Mike Savage Mike Savage used a more unconventional asset to fund his first deal: his paid-off truck. After using retirement savings to relocate his family to Charleston, South Carolina, Savage said he and his wife had little left in the bank, but he owned his truck outright. When he found a three-bedroom, one-bath house in South Carolina for $49,000, he took out a loan against the truck to cover the roughly $10,000 down payment. It gave him a way to enter the market without waiting years to save the money in cash. Like borrowing against a home or retirement account, the strategy created another debt obligation tied to an asset he already owned. Still, Savage was determined to find a way into real estate. His mindset, he said, was: "This is what I want to do. I just have to figure out how to make it happen." Read the original article on Business Insider
