events.title: As a French woman, I cherish my 'French Sundays.' I wouldn't change this weekend routine for anything.
events.summary: The author spends her Sundays relaxing and reconnecting with friends and family. Courtesy of Virginie Romary "French Sundays" are a trend that seems to be gaining popularity in the US. Being French, they have been one of my routines throughout my life. They're a day to completely unwind and a chance to recharge before the week begins. I grew up in France , where Sundays have their own distinctive feeling. It's not just another day of the week for us — and even though I've moved to the US, it's something I've taken with me. On Sundays, most traditional shops and services are closed, with only a few exceptions in tourist areas. It's a day dedicated to slowing down and resetting. I haven't lived in France for 10 years, but I still continue to uphold the tradition of unwinding on Sundays, and I have no intention of changing it. Sundays are for slowing down and relaxing When I was living in France , I couldn't go grocery shopping on Sundays or buy a new pair of jeans as the shops were closed. Now that I reside in the US, I maintain this habit of organizing my time so that I can run errands on the other days of the week, even late at night, but never on Sundays. I don't do chores either. Vacuuming can wait until another day — responding to emails can, too. Sundays are dedicated to reconnecting with my family, my friends, and myself. The key is to savor the day without rushing from one activity to another while prioritizing self-care . My mornings at home are always relaxed, spent enjoying slow moments with my family, listening to jazz, practicing slow-flow yoga, or playing games. In the afternoon, I like to have friends over to share a glass of wine. I don't even cook on Sundays, since it's not my favorite activity and I handle it during the week. I'm perfectly happy with a plate of pasta and sometimes even skip the salad. French Sundays are not a waste of a day When I moved to the US , I noticed a different approach to Sundays; there, they are often viewed as a catch-up day for everything that wasn't done during the week. My American friends tend to prefer their Sundays to be productive. I believe French Sundays are even more beneficial than a day focused on productivity . It doesn't mean lying on the couch all day scrolling on the phone, but rather engaging in activities that restore my mind and body. My brain cannot remain in productivity mode constantly; it requires some downtime. By allowing myself to slow down on Sundays, I feel less anxious and stressed. This gives me a chance to recharge, and I know I will have more energy and be more productive for the coming week. The author's daughter loves slowing down on Sundays, too. Courtesy of Virginie Romary Even my daughter enjoys French Sundays My 9-year-old daughter appreciates that on Sundays, she doesn't have to rush to anything, which is a relief. She has time to wake up and enjoy breakfast. There is no homework to worry about, as she was responsible for doing it beforehand. She can go at her own pace to do what she wants, like reading or crafting. That's also the perfect occasion to have some slow time with her parents. I do not schedule any structured activities for her, aside from having free play with her friends. If she is invited to a big birthday party, I don't decline, but I'm careful to give her enough time afterward to relax and reset for the week. When her friends' parents asked me what we did on Sundays, and I replied, " Nothing special, we stayed at home," they often looked at me as if my daughter was missing out. They typically went to soccer practice, then to the mall or a theme park. However, I discovered that having a quieter Sunday allowed my daughter to rest and concentrate better at school in the following week. French Sundays is a mindset. Being able to let go is not for everybody. However, it's certainly worth a try. For me, they are essential for a less stressful week. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: AI was supposed to kill tech jobs. The data on job openings says otherwise.
events.summary: Mechanical systems expert Chris David leads a tour of Meta's data center in Temple, Texas. Mikala Compton/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly AI Insider newsletter here . Fears that AI will wipe out tech jobs aren't showing up in the data. Job openings at tech companies are climbing, while layoffs continue to ease after a brutal industry reset following the pandemic, according to new data from TrueUp , a hiring platform that tracks more than 9,000 technology companies. TrueUp is currently tracking more than 280,000 open tech jobs across startups and big tech firms, up strongly from the start of 2026. Layoffs haven't disappeared, but they're no longer happening at anything like the pace of the post-pandemic downturn. About 190,000 tech workers have been laid off so far this year, putting 2026 on track to finish well below the roughly 430,000 job cuts recorded during the industry's layoff peak in 2023. The recovery isn't happening evenly across the sector. Demand for hardware engineers has surged this year, fueled by massive spending on AI infrastructure. "It's not surprising given the interest in GPU innovation, AI robotics, US manufacturing startups, and SpaceX," Amit Taylor, TrueUp's founder, told Business Insider. Software engineering job listings, meanwhile, have held up surprisingly well despite predictions that AI coding tools would sharply reduce demand for programmers. The numbers suggest AI is changing what tech companies hire for, not eliminating the need to hire. Demand is shifting toward engineers building the physical foundations of AI — chips, servers, robotics, manufacturing, and data centers — while software hiring remains resilient. Taken together, the data points to a tech job market that is finding its footing. Companies are still cutting jobs in some areas, but they're also hiring aggressively where AI investment is booming. events.title: Her family kept getting cancer. At 33, a saliva test explained why.
events.summary: Michelle York, 43, was diagnosed with Lynch syndrome 10 years ago. Lynch syndrome heightens her risk of developing multiple cancers, especially colon cancer. Michelle York Michelle York, 43, had family history of multiple cancers on her mom's side. York tested positive for Lynch syndrome, an underdiagnosed, symptomless condition that increases cancer risk. York and her other family members who tested positive get more frequent cancer screenings. On her mom's side, Michelle York has a long family history of cancer. Her great-grandmother died from colon cancer. Her grandfather had stomach and brain cancer, and his sisters died from liver, ovarian, and breast cancer, respectively. Her mother's cousin died from pancreatic cancer. Then, when York was 33, her mother came across a possible explanation: Lynch syndrome . An inherited genetic mutation, Lynch syndrome is underdiagnosed, symptomless, and increases the risk of cancers, including colorectal, uterine, stomach, ovarian, pancreatic, among others. With colon cancer in particular, it can increase lifetime risk as high as 80%, and is sometimes associated with more aggressive forms of the cancer. About 1 in 300 Americans is estimated to have Lynch syndrome, though many don't find out until after they've been diagnosed with cancer . York's mother, who was a nurse at the time and had read about Lynch through her work, decided to get tested. "She thought: 'Well, what if I do have this and what if my daughter has this?'" York, now a 43-year-old content creator in Los Angeles, told Business Insider. At the time, York was also dealing with pelvic pain caused by complex ovarian cysts — cysts containing either solid tissue or irregularities that could mask growing tumors. If she also had Lynch, her cysts would warrant an even closer look, given her heightened ovarian cancer risk. Both York and her mom tested positive for Lynch, as did both of York's siblings and other family members on her mother's side. Now, they get annual screenings to catch any potential cancers earlier. "In the beginning, it was a little bit more anxiety-inducing," York said. But after about a decade of regular screenings, she feels reassured that she's lowering her risk of developing late-stage cancer. "I think knowledge is power — now, it almost feels comforting because I know that I started doing this young." A quick saliva test York (second from left) with her mother, sister, and brother — all of whom tested positive for Lynch syndrome. Michelle York There are three ways to get screened for Lynch syndrome : a saliva, cheek swab, or blood test, with blood yielding higher-quality DNA samples. After York's mother got tested, York and her two siblings were all offered the saliva test by their physician. "I spit in a tube — it was a very easy test," York said. Because her mom had already tested positive for Lynch syndrome, she said her insurance covered the test. All three siblings tested positive, as did York's aunt, uncle, and cousin on her mom's side. (York's father did not take the test because he doesn't have a family history of cancer on his side). Afterward, York and her siblings met with a genetic counselor who explained which cancers they were predisposed to and the average population age for developing them. At first, the information made them nervous, especially given how young they were. York was 33, her sister was 31, and her brother was 22. "Does this mean I'm going to get cancer at a young age?" York said. "Does this mean every time I don't feel well, I'm going to immediately think I have cancer?" At the same time, she understood that her family members all knowing their risks could prevent serious, surprise cancer diagnoses later. Her mother, in particular, has had precancerous polyps removed during multiple annual colonoscopies. "None of us have had cancer yet, but we've had lots of scares," York said. She gets annual colonoscopies and other cancer screenings York makes sure to get screened for multiple cancers every year. Michelle York After getting diagnosed with Lynch, York and her family members started getting annual colonoscopies, regardless of their age. At first, York thought she could at least go every other year, since the common recommendation for people with a family history of colon cancer is getting screened every five years. But because colon cancer can develop so rapidly in people with Lynch, her doctor advised annual screenings. "Doing it every year kind of sucks — it's really just the preparation for the colonoscopy," York said, which involves fasting the night before and drinking laxatives. For her complex ovarian cysts , York started seeing a gynecologist-oncologist and would get each cyst reexamined every 3 months. Eventually, due to complications with her cysts, York ended up getting a hysterectomy and oophorectomy, removing her uterus and both ovaries, thus reducing her ovarian and uterine cancer risks to practically zero. Because of her specific Lynch variant, York also gets annual skin cancer screenings and annual mammograms, as some newer studies indicate that her mutation is linked to a slightly elevated risk of developing breast cancer. (For average-risk women over 40, the general breast cancer screening recommendation is getting one every two years.) She said having a Lynch diagnosis also made it easy to get screenings like colonoscopies covered by her insurance plan. Without a family history of colon cancer, opting for a colonoscopy under the age of 45 can cost hundreds — even thousands — of dollars out of pocket. Prior to her hysterectomy, she said a CT scan was initially denied by her insurance because it wasn't deemed "medically necessary." The CT scans were later approved by her insurance after her doctor told the insurance company that York had Lynch. "The Lynch diagnosis absolutely does help, in that respect," York said. She believes doctors listen to her more York, pictured with her family, wants her kids to test for Lynch syndrome when they're old enough. Michelle York Some young people who get diagnosed with colon cancer recall feeling dismissed by doctors because of their age, lack of family history, or overall health. York said that having Lynch changed how her doctors responded to her pain, particularly when she was still dealing with ovarian cysts. "I think people take you a little bit more seriously, people look a little closer," she said. "If there is a pain or a lump, you are treated differently because of Lynch syndrome." Lynch syndrome is still rare and only accounts for about 2% to 5% of all colorectal cancer cases. Still, York says Lynch immediately comes to mind when she hears of another young colon cancer case . "My first thought is 'I wonder if they've been tested for Lynch,'" she said. events.title: Thousands of Glasgow council workers face pay cuts in one of UK’s biggest fire-and-rehire plans
events.summary: Unison union refuses to ballot members on offer that would make 11% of council employees worse off Thousands of Glasgow council workers face being sacked and reappointed under less favourable terms in one of the UK’s biggest ever “fire-and-rehire” exercises, after union negotiations broke down once again this week. About 23,000 workers – all of the council’s non-teaching staff – first heard they were affected last week when talks between the SNP-led council and the GMB, Unison and Unite unions fell apart. Those negotiations concerned a new pay and grading system designed to resolve historical pay equality issues. Unison refused to ballot its members on an offer that would mean pay cuts for 11% of council employees, prompting the council to begin issuing fire-and-rehire letters. At the beginning of this week the fire-and-rehire plans were temporarily paused when Unison returned to the negotiating table. But when discussions collapsed again midweek, the council’s leader, Ricky Bell, suggested Unison members could still be fired and rehired while negotiations with GMB and Unite continued. Unison said it was seeking advice on the legality of its members being treated differently based on union membership. An emergency motion by Green councillors to block the scheme was also rejected on Thursday by the council’s city administration committee, with the Glasgow Greens co-leader Anthony Carroll saying the city was “facing a genuine cliff-edge of one of the largest fire-and-rehire schemes in the UK being implemented”. “We are angry and shocked that the SNP administration moved to fire and rehire all 23,000 staff last week despite its own government’s position,” he said, calling on Bell to personally rule out the move. The deputy first minister, Jenny Gilruth, reaffirmed the Scottish government’s view on fire-and-rehire last week, saying “our position is that such a practice does not align with the principles and expected practice of fair work”. On Friday, Gilruth chaired mediation talks between the council and Unison, securing a further pause to fire and rehire for the weekend. But the union said it must be taken off the table permanently for negotiations to be “productive and in good faith”. For those affected, the week’s tumultuous events have caused anger and uncertainty. “It’s been handled terribly,” said one worker affected. “It’s like a rollercoaster ride of anxiety; we can’t plan for anything and nobody knows what’s going to happen next. We are all furious about how we’ve been treated.” One person close to the negotiations said the unions were particularly aggrieved by “the blatant cynicism” of the council’s fire-and-rehire plans, which were communicated to staff in letters sent at the end of September, meaning a required 12-week notice period expires shortly before the practice becomes illegal in January under UK-wide changes to employment law. “We’re talking about a so-called progressive administration who have spent years taking credit for ending the equal pay dispute,” they said. “It beggars belief they would treat workers who are already undervalued and overworked like this.” In 2019, the council agreed to pay more than £500m to 8,000 mostly female workers who had been discriminated against by unequal pay structures. As seen in Birmingham in 2023 , the authority risks financial ruin if it cannot agree a new pay structure after almost a decade of negotiation. “We know equal pay is still an issue local authorities across Britain need to solve,” one union source said. “Council workers everywhere will surely be looking at what’s happening here and feeling very worried about what might happen to them next.” Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Glasgow city council agreed in earlier negotiations to protect the pay of those facing wage cuts for an extra year, but Unison said they wanted a further year of protection alongside a number of other concessions. Bell said in a statement: “I’m deeply disappointed that, despite the council putting a further year of pay protection on the table, Unison has once again chosen not to put this offer to its members. Taken together with improvements made since August, this represents a package well over £100m in extra pay for our staff.” Bell said some of Unison’s remaining demands were “simply unworkable”. Unison’s Glasgow city branch said: “We want workers who have waited decades for equal pay to receive every penny they are due. But we will not abandon workers facing devastating losses, or the thousands who still don’t know their outcome.” They called for “a properly funded settlement that delivers equal pay without leaving thousands of other workers behind”.

events.title: After about a year of using the scooter, I sold my car.
events.summary: Gary Brown sold his car and now uses his gas-powered scooter to commute to work. Gary Brown The costs of car ownership have been increasing, from new car prices to gas. One commuter ditched his car in favor of a gas-powered scooter. It's a practical, money-saving alternative when paired with apps like Uber, he said. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Gary Brown, an architectural visualization artist in Charlotte, North Carolina. It has been edited for length and clarity. My wife and I own a townhouse here in Charlotte. It's about four miles from where I work. We actually closed on the house as the city shut down due to COVID in 2020. We entered that period where everybody was working from home for about two years. Then, as I started going back to working in an office, I realized that I hadn't really driven much because I've been working from home. I'm spending $700 a month on a car payment, insurance, parking fees at my office, and all the other costs of a car just to drive four miles down the road. That started to get me thinking: How else can I get there? At first, I got an electric Segway scooter, but after about six months, I realized that it was too hard on my back. I also considered taking the bus or the light rail, but the routes don't go quite close enough. I ended up getting a gas scooter. I had seen them while studying abroad in Europe and realized that this problem has already been solved by just about every other country except ours. It checked all the boxes: It's fuel-efficient. I could park in a garage downtown and not pay anything — a huge deal, given that I was spending thousands of dollars a year parking my car there. It also gets 60 miles per gallon and has some storage and heated seats. Owning a scooter is cheaper than owning a car I bought my scooter used for $3500 cash. A helmet and other gear cost another $1000. The operating costs are much lower than a car: My insurance is $35 a month, and gas for the month averages to about $15. Yearly maintenance that runs about $300. Riding in the heat and cold can be rough at times, but that's a tradeoff I can accept. If the weather is really bad, I'll ask my wife to drive me to work, or I'll take a rideshare. Uber and all those apps have helped facilitate my turn to a scooter. After about a year of using the scooter, I had barely used my Tesla, so I sold it. When I first started this experiment, there was only ever my scooter, a motorcycle or two, and a handful of bicycles where I parked at work. Now, sometimes I have trouble finding a parking space because there are four or five scooters, several motorcycles, some electric scooters and bikes, and fewer bicycles. I read predictions that one day, everyone will rely on Uber rides or robotaxis instead of owning a vehicle. I don't think that's going to happen. We are a country where freedom is based on your car, and our cities and highways are designed around that. There may come a time when owning a car is old-fashioned, but I don't think driving will be. Scooters like mine are a sort of gateway drug to alternative modes of transportation. Do you have a story idea about Uber or Lyft? events.title: I thought a recruiter had found me the perfect job — then he asked me to pay. These are the warning signs I missed.
events.summary: Alyshia Hull. Alyshia Hull Alyshia Hull was approached by a recruiter with a job opportunity that seemed like a good fit for her. After sending her résumé, she was told she would need to pay for a résumé service before she could progress. She realized the offer was a scam. Other indicators could be asking for overly personal information. I've spent six years writing about the workplace, and though this job market has been unexpectedly difficult, I thought I had learned its ins and outs. I've seen readers go through this, and as a freelancer open to a full-time position, I've experienced it, too. Apply online, post on LinkedIn, get contacted by a recruiter, interview, take a test, interview again— and then get ghosted . Repeat. When hope began to feel scarce earlier this year, I woke up to an email from a "recruiter." His message was long, detailed, and complimentary. He praised my writing and portfolio and explained how closely my experience aligned with a role he was hiring for. At first, all he asked for in return was my résumé . The email was kind, detailed, convincing — and a scam. The scam was convincing I received this from the recruiter: "I'm currently partnering with the recruiting team supporting a confidential Senior Editorial Strategy Lead Workplace & Career Content opportunity with Indeed, and I wanted to reach out personally because your profile is unusually aligned with what this team is trying to build." His email included a photo of himself, and his signature linked to a LinkedIn profile that he claimed was his. The verified profile was filled with endorsements, an image of himself, and years of experience listed on his page. I'd heard of recruiter scams before, but I didn't see any harm in his email. I agreed to send him my résumé. His next email didn't ask for anything either He complimented my work again, gave me a more detailed overview of the role, and laid out the pay range of $125,000-$165,000. I was excited to see the range, especially because it was higher than I had anticipated and more than I had earned in my previous roles. I thought, He's not asking for anything. Maybe it's real? Then came the third email After a few days had passed, he told me the hiring team had reviewed my candidacy and, though "the feedback was positive overall," my résumé needed improvement before we could proceed. To move forward, I'd need to have my résumé redone through a service he worked with. Otherwise, he couldn't advance me. He said: "My intention is simply to connect you with a resource that can help present your experience at the level the hiring team is looking for. You can then decide for yourself whether the service and investment make sense for you." I was now almost certain it was a scam I replied and asked him if there was a fee for the résumé service. Within the hour, he replied: "The service does involve a fee. I don't want to quote a specific amount on their behalf because I'm not directly involved in their current pricing structure, and the cost may depend on the level of support and tools you choose." The next day, I forwarded the exchange to Indeed They confirmed the recruiter was not affiliated with the company and that the job opportunity was not real. I received this from Indeed: "Regarding the outreach you received, it appears to be a fake recruiting email from an impersonated recruiter. Our People team has confirmed that we are not hiring for this position, and that Indeed does not work with outside agencies to fill open roles. We've also found that this email domain has recently been involved in other fake recruiting schemes." I stopped replying. Fake recruiters are becoming harder to spot My experience is far from unusual. LinkedIn's 2026 Job Search Safety Pulse found that 36% of recruiters say they've been victims of impersonation, and 67% say job scams are making it harder to build trust with candidates. How can job seekers tell the difference between a real recruiter and someone pretending to be one? Erica Rivera , a career coach and former recruiter at Indeed and Meta, said these scams can be hard to spot — but there are signs. Green flags: What a legitimate recruiter should do If a recruiter reaches out about a job opportunity, applicants should be able to find the position somewhere outside the recruiter's message, ideally on the company's website or a reputable job platform. It can also be a good sign when the recruiter or their colleagues are actively sharing the opening on LinkedIn, she said. You might also be able to tell by their email address. "If they have their email included, and it's truly a company email," that's another green flag," she said. To check, she suggested looking at the company's website for an official email address. Yellow flags: Proceed with some caution Not every unusual recruiting practice means someone is trying to scam you, but some situations should prompt applicants to verify who they're dealing with. A recruiter's LinkedIn profile can offer some clues about whether they are who they say they are. Rivera said applicants should be cautious if a recruiter has very little activity or only a few connections. A suspicious-looking LinkedIn profile photo, a newer profile, or a lack of verification can also be reasons to take a closer look. "I'm always suspicious when I see a recruiter reaching out that isn't endorsed, because if you're going to be reaching out to people, you should validate your profile," Rivera said. Text messages from a recruiter can also warrant some caution. Recruiters are more likely to call a candidate unexpectedly, she said, although texting can happen in some circumstances. For example, recruiters may text someone like a CDL driver because they may be difficult to reach by email. If a recruiter reaches out via text, Rivera recommends moving the conversation to a phone call and asking them to send the job information by email. Red flags: Cut off communication If a recruiter starts asking for sensitive personal information or money, Rivera said applicants should cut off communication. "Anything tied to Social Security, date of birth, bank account information, marital status, anything like that should be an automatic flag," she said. Recruiters may reasonably ask for a résumé, portfolio, work samples, or other information directly related to the position, but requests that go beyond that should raise immediate concerns. Being asked to pay for something is another major warning sign. Rivera said legitimate recruiters should not require candidates to pay for résumé services, equipment, or other costs as part of the hiring process. If you're asked to pay for something, stop communicating. She also recommended reporting the account on the platform the recruiter used to contact you and, when appropriate, reporting suspicious activity to Google. If you're comfortable doing so, Rivera suggested sharing your experience to warn other job seekers. I knew the signs, but I wanted to believe it w

events.title: Own a mobile phone? Then you’re paying the ‘app tax’. It’s a racket and it’s time the UK faced Apple and Google down | Chi Onwurah
events.summary: Own a mobile phone? Then you’re paying the ‘app tax’. It’s a racket and it’s time the UK faced Apple and Google down A deep-seated duopoly allows the tech giants to exploit the public and developers. But the regulator has powers to stop this abuse – it should use them Chi Onwurah is the Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West and chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee D ebates around big tech and digital regulation can sometimes feel distant from the everyday concerns of voters. But the power that a small number of global tech companies hold over our lives goes far beyond what most people realise. As chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee, I have spent years raising concerns about this: from the data they harvest and the digital “twins” they build of us, to the algorithms that decide what our children see. But there’s a much less visible example of this imbalance of power sitting in the pocket of almost every smartphone user in Britain: the app tax. Apple and Google control the two app stores through which almost every mobile app in this country reaches its customers, and that position lets them set terms for app developers that most businesses would never accept from a supplier. Sell a subscription, game or piece of software through either app store and both companies now charge a commission of up to 30% on purchases made inside apps , regardless of what the product is or what it costs to make. With no alternative platforms, developers simply have to accept the terms set by Silicon Valley. Developers are also prevented from telling users that a cheaper option exists elsewhere, known as “steering”. That restriction is enforced by Apple and Google to protect their own profits. For small British developers who might struggle to absorb the cost, that could be the difference between hiring their next engineer or not, investing in a new product or shelving it, or growing their business here or uprooting and building overseas instead. Consumers pay the price, too. Research commissioned by the Coalition for App Fairness, as reported in the Daily Mail, indicated that British consumers pay approximately £700m per year to Apple and Google, a full £232m more than the companies paid in UK corporation tax last year combined. This is equivalent to around £55 annually for a household with four smartphone users. It is a cost built into the price of the product, invisible on any receipt, that has far more to do with market control and bolstering profits than anything the companies actually did to earn it. My last job before coming into parliament was with Ofcom, the regulator for communications markets. I was responsible for assessing the competitiveness of markets, because it is through competition that consumers get choice. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has found that Apple and Google’s mobile platforms hold an effective duopoly, with at least 90% of UK mobile devices running on their mobile platforms. App developers have no choice but to distribute their product through the Apple App Store or the Google Play Store. If a developer happened to dislike Apple’s terms and another app store existed, they would take their app, and their customers, elsewhere, and the price would fall. But there is no alternative app store on an iPhone, and no practical route for Android users outside Google Play either. Apple and Google set the rules unchallenged. Parliament anticipated this problem when, in 2024, it passed the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act (DMCCA) with cross-party support, giving the CMA genuine powers to force dominant platforms to change their behaviour. But, so far, the CMA has resorted to weak, voluntary commitments from Apple and Google rather than requirements it is actually obliged to enforce. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Its consultation on “steering”, which would finally let developers point users to cheaper options elsewhere, has now closed and a decision is due soon. Many are rightly nervous that this could end up with another voluntary gesture, rather than a binding rule, deemed acceptable. But this moment also represents an opportunity. It will be one of the first serious decisions this government makes on big tech, and will likely determine the direction it takes on this issue. The prime minister has been clear, both before and since entering Downing Street, that tech sovereignty means reducing our dependence on a handful of overseas platforms. I want to see that instinct applied to decisions such as this. This is not about being anti-technology or anti-growth. It is about whether British consumers, British developers and British regulators are able to shape the terms on which technology operates in our own market and influences our society. I urge the CMA to use the powers we gave it, and I urge my colleagues in government to back it in doing so.

events.title: Lack of inspections at fish slaughterhouses a ‘disgrace’, says Animal Equality UK
events.summary: Charity calls for faster progress on humane slaughter laws for farmed fish in England and Wales Up to 77m fish are slaughtered each year in the UK but there are no routine or mandatory inspections of fish slaughterhouses in England and Wales, it can be revealed. Concerns within government about the way fish are slaughtered date back decades but all of the official bodies responsible for animal welfare and food standards in England and Wales said they do not undertake regular inspections. When Animal Equality UK contacted the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA), it referred the charity to the Fish Health Inspectorate (FHI). In response to a previous inquiry, the APHA had said it does not carry out mandatory inspections of fish slaughterhouses and suggested contacting the Food Standards Agency (FSA). Both the FSA and the FHI told Animal Equality UK that they did not carry out routine or mandatory inspections. Abigail Penny, the executive director of Animal Equality UK, said: “Fish are thinking, feeling beings, capable of pain. It is a disgrace that not a single government agency will take responsibility for checking on their welfare at slaughter. This is a huge blindspot, and it leaves these animals all the more vulnerable behind closed doors.” In 1996, the government’s expert advisory body, the Farm Animal Welfare Council – now called the Animal Welfare Committee – suggested there should be legislation governing the slaughter of farmed fish . The committee returned to the issue in 2014 and again in 2024 . On the latter occasion it urged governments across the UK to legislate for fish to be stunned before slaughter, and for inspection systems to be put in place to enforce those standards. In its Animal Welfare Strategy for England , published in December 2025, the government committed to introducing humane slaughter requirements for farmed fish but draft legislation has yet to be published. Penny said: “For 30 years, people in power have known that farmed fish need legal protection when they are slaughtered, yet for 30 years decisionmakers have failed to act.” She added: “The government promised to change the law, and we welcome that promise, but promises don’t protect animals. Every month of delay leaves millions of fish at risk of prolonged, painful deaths. Ministers must bring forward species-specific slaughter legislation now, backed by a proper inspection regime, so that what happens to these animals is no longer left to chance. It’s the least they deserve.” Animal Equality UK estimates that about 7,742 tonnes of trout a year are killed in England and Wales. The British Trout Association says the UK has almost 290 trout farms, including hatcheries, concentrated in northern England, southern England and southern Scotland. An APHA spokesperson said: “It is incorrect to suggest fish farms aren’t regulated or inspected by government bodies. APHA investigates reports of suspected cases of poor welfare at fish farms, and the Fish Health Inspectorate inspects them on behalf of the government. We do not hesitate to take further action if we find evidence of cruelty or neglect.” The best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said. events.title: OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’
events.summary: David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technology A safety leader at OpenAI has quit the company, warning that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology. David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, explained his resignation in an essay headlined: “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken.” Robinson wrote that a cultural overhaul was needed at cutting-edge AI firms and incidents such as a “swarm” of OpenAI agents – AI programmes operating autonomously without human oversight – attacking the AI startup Hugging Face were “typical of the industry, given the speed and flexibility with which people operate”. Writing in the Atlantic magazine , Robinson wrote: “I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture.” Referring to OpenAI’s pace of development, he wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.” OpenAI has shown signs of caution in recent weeks, after the Hugging Face incident and the revelation that it has notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity. This week it announced it was scrapping the release of a next-generation ⁠AI model after researchers raised safety concerns ⁠during internal testing. OpenAI has also paused training of its most advanced models. Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and was chief scientist at the UK government’s AI Safety Institute before joining the AI safety researchcompany Resolution, also issued a warning on AI on Saturday. Writing in Time , he said: “Recent warnings about the potential destructive power of AI are understating the severity of the situation. I believe there’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems, and that our actions over the next two to 10 years will determine the outcome.” The warnings follow the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at the OpenAI rival Anthropic, who quit the Claude chatbot developer last month. He said he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade” – and was backed up by an Anthropic employee warning there was a more than 10% chance AI would wipe out humanity within the next decade. Critics of such warnings have cautioned, however, that they are unscientific because they cannot be verified or falsified. Robinson wrote that Silicon Valley lacked an awareness of “how to handle dangerous technology” and “what it means to care for people”. Warning that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose, he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems became more capable. “Imagine ‘rogue’ agents that work like teams of hackers (for example, holding hospital computer systems for ransom) but never need to sleep,” wrote Robinson. Robinson called for two safety changes: that AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation, and that they develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives “Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster,” he wrote. An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs. “We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” said the spokesperson. events.title: ‘They call every week’: the phishing attacks targeting past victims
events.summary: Scammers reuse personal details harvested from fake Esta websites – and texts and calls can keep arriving for months W hen the British actor Lisa Riley was preparing to travel to the US last year, she applied online for an Esta so she would not need a visa. After finding the site through a Google search she filled in her passport, bank and personal details and waited for the confirmation, which normally takes just under an hour. When it failed to arrive, she emailed an address from the site where she had paid and got back a message unlike any she had seen before, with a link to a website that displayed a jumble of words and letters. It was then she realised she had been scammed. But that was just the start of her problems, which persist to this day. She has been repeatedly targeted by criminals, receiving text messages and calls many times every week. Riley was the victim of a fraud where criminals create websites similar to the legitimate one run by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). After fooling unsuspecting applicants they pocket a fee and use the personal details of victims for later scams. Riley lost £16 – the cost of an Esta back then – but says there has been a huge increase in the number of scam calls and texts she has received in the 17 months since the fraud happened. Often the person claims to be from her bank with queries about a money transfer. “Calls are once a week, easy – sometimes twice a week,” she says. “And the texts even more often.” Research from Nationwide building society suggests that 15% of people have given personal information to something who later turned out not to be genuine, leaving them open to future frauds. “Criminals do sadly retarget people after an initial scam,” says Annya Burskys, head of fraud operations at Nationwide. “They take the personal information they have gained and either sell it on to other scammers or use them to make follow-up bank impersonation calls , texts and emails appear more convincing.” The fake Esta site that stole Riley’s personal details looked very similar to the official one and showed up high in search results, she says. “The webpage was absolutely identical so there was nothing that would remotely make me fearful up until [I realised],” she says. Criminals can use AI to recreate legitimate government sites and will frequently use key words such as “Esta”, in the domain name to try to portray legitimacy. A spokesperson for the US CBP says some sites may demand action by the applicant quickly, a common tactic by criminals to try to get people to act without thinking something through. Only use the official Esta website, which has a .gov address, or the mobile app. “Applicants should protect their Esta confirmation number and payment details, retain application records, and review financial statements for unauthorised charges,” says the CBP spokesperson. “Suspected fraud should be documented and reported promptly to the applicant’s financial institution and appropriate local government reporting channels.” In the UK that means telling your bank and Report Fraud . If you have inadvertently handed over your personal details you are at risk of future scams, so be alert to unexpected calls, texts or emails, says Burskys. “Don’t feel pressured to act. A genuine call or message from your bank will never ask you to move money, never ask you to share codes, and will never tell you what to say to your bank or friends, family,” she says. “Take a moment to verify who you’re speaking to and contact your bank directly using trusted contact information from your bank card or search for the official website if you’re unsure.”

events.title: Ministers explore how to stop regional leaders misusing planned new spending powers
events.summary: Labour wants to make sure mayors and council chiefs in England can be held to account for extra revenues devolved to them Ministers are mulling over how to ensure that England’s regional leaders do not misuse their newfound spending muscle, as Whitehall prepares to devolve more revenue to local levels. Ideas under consideration include a new select committee in Westminster, enhanced reporting rules and a new audit body focused on local and regional government. The Guardian understands the idea has even been mooted of allowing spendthrift mayors to be recalled by the electorate, as can happen to rule-breaking MPs. The government will publish a white paper on “rewiring the state” later this month, setting out detailed plans to hand over more income tax revenue to regional mayors. Rachel Reeves suggested the idea in her Mais lecture earlier this year , and it has been adopted by Andy Burnham’s government, which sees devolution as a big part of its growth policy. However, officials are concerned about how to ensure local leaders are fully accountable for what they do with the additional cash – including in between elections. Meg Hillier, the chair of the Treasury select committee, said she believed hers would be the right body to scrutinise the use of the additional spending powers. “It’s clear that one of the prime minister’s key ambitions is to take spending power out of Westminster and hand it to local leaders,” the Labour MP said. “It is absolutely critical, though, that strong, clear scrutiny structures are established which match this move to localism. It would be reckless to hand out new powers without ensuring there are transparent mechanisms to hold mayors to account for their decisions.” Hillier added: “One way to do this is to establish clear lines of authority running through departments and up to ministers, which will allow existing select committees to judge this work. “A core role of a select committee, particularly the Treasury committee which I chair, is to ensure politicians are publicly held to account for how they decide to spend taxpayers’ money. That is just important at a local level as it is on a national scale.” The Audit Commission, which had the specific task of overseeing local government spending, was abolished in 2015, with its role split across several other bodies. As well as shoring up accountability, it is understood there have been lengthy discussions in government about how to balance the need to incentivise local leaders to encourage economic growth, with the imperative to ensure funding is stable over time. The Institute for Fiscal Studies said last week that the government should use “equalisation payments” to prevent the funding of areas with the highest share of income tax, such as London, pulling ahead of other regions. David Phillips, the IFS’s devolution expert, said: “With more skin in the game of economic growth, mayors will be more incentivised and empowered to support growth through local policies and investments. But careful design will be needed to prevent richer areas’ funding unfairly pulling ahead. “The government must also decide how big a gap in funding it is willing to see between ‘winners’ and ‘losers’ in the years ahead.” Burnham has made clear his intention of accelerating devolution, with his new No 10 North office focusing on the regional aspects of growth policy.

events.title: UK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU markets
events.summary: Britain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measures Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China and Europe , as manufacturers struggle to balance the benefits of both markets ahead of looming trade measures that could restrict UK exports to the EU. The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely , and the EU imposes duties of up to 45% . EU officials reportedly warned Andy Burnham last month that the UK must put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicles otherwise Brussels would impose protectionist “made in Europe” barriers on British exports to the bloc, hitting British carmakers in their largest market. Ministers have so far resisted such calls, with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, arguing any levies would “probably be reciprocated” – costing UK manufacturers sales in China . Tariffs would also raise prices for British drivers, who have flocked to cheaper Chinese models , and could deter brands such as Chery, which is in talks to build cars at Nissan’s Sunderland plant , from investing further in the UK. “There is a difficult trade-off,” said Emily Sawicz, of the consultancy RSM UK, adding that the UK “cannot afford to drift between the two indefinitely”. Chinese investment could be a “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers. “Being excluded risks UK suppliers becoming increasingly shut out of those European opportunities,” she added. “Manufacturers need clarity on which direction the government intends to take so they can make long-term investment decisions.” Ian Plummer, commercial director at Autotrader, said competition from Chinese brands had made cars more affordable and “is encouraging more people to go and buy a new car”. Brands such as BYD, Omoda and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in the first eight months of 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to industry figures. Figures released on Friday showed that British new car ⁠registrations rose 12% in the year to September, the best month for annual growth since 2017. The preliminary data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showed the boom was powered by a demand for electric vehicles and Chinese brands, with the Jaecoo 7 and BYD’s ​Sealion ‌7 among the top sellers. The trade body said on Wednesday that the European Commission’s made in Europe rules, which restrict subsidies, tax breaks and public procurement contracts to vehicles built within the EU, pose an existential threat to British car production. The EU accounted for 58% of UK car exports in the first half of the year, compared with about 4% for China. Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The UK and EU automotive industries are deeply integrated, so effectively excluding British-produced vehicles from their largest market would assure mutual damage.” Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s chair in Europe, said last month: “Europe cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market through the UK.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Victor Zhang, the deputy UK chief of Chery, which owns the Jaecoo and Omoda brands, rejected that claim, saying: “Most of what we sell are super-hybrids, not the cars that those tariffs are about, and the cars we sell here stay here.” He added: “Tariffs can come and go, but we won’t change our ongoing investment in the UK.” Brussels raised its own tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024, triggering a decline in what was then an accelerating sales trajectory. It is now facing calls for fresh barriers to be imposed on importing hybrid electric vehicles, potentially quotas or price floors. Imports of plug-in and battery hybrid cars rocketed after the EU tariffs were imposed on EVs, underlining China’s ability to pivot its export efforts when hit by trade barriers. Others in the industry believe tariffs could help protect the UK’s manufacturers, whose market share in Britain continues to be eroded Chinese firms. Tim Tozer, a former chair of Vauxhall, said that tariffs were “vital” to stop Britain’s car sector “atrophying”. He said: “We are at last knockings now, trying to save the industry.” He added that Reynolds was “whistling in the wind” with hopes of continuing to export to China en masse, arguing the market had become “fiercely nationalistic,” with buyers increasingly loyal to domestic brands “because they’re bloody good”.

events.title: 'Debris field' found in search for missing medical flight from Bermuda
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 'Debris field' found after 6-person medical flight goes missing over Atlantic The US Coast Guard is continuing the search. ( US Coast Guard via AP ) The US Coast Guard has found a "debris field' in its search for an air ambulance that went missing over the Atlantic. The Canadian-registered aircraft was carrying six people from Bermuda to Boston in the United States. The Coast Guard said the search would continue. Searchers have found debris from an air ambulance that was carrying six people when it went missing over the Atlantic during a flight from Bermuda to Boston. The "debris field" was found off the coast of Nantucket, in the US state of Massachusetts, following the disappearance on Saturday, the US Coast Guard said. Four Canadians and two Bermudian nationals were aboard, the Coast Guard said in a statement. It added that the next of kin of those missing had been notified and one of its cutters would keep searching the water overnight and into Sunday. According to the Coast Guard, the Federal Aviation Administration reported that the Gulfstream G100 aircraft lost contact very early on Saturday morning. Air traffic audio indicates that it may have been "coming in blind" when a storm loomed ahead shortly before it disappeared. The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net. "Roger, you said you're coming in blind. Is that what you said?" a controller can be heard asking the pilot. The plane may have lost its navigational instruments as a storm seen on radar moved across its path, former US Department of Transportation inspector-general Mary Schiavo said. The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 7.3 kilometres to around three kilometres, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24. "Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm," Ms Schiavo, an aviation attorney, said. "It's a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind. "It's very easy to get disoriented and not know if you're turning, climbing, descending, etc." The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew and two passengers aboard when it departed Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport for the night flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport's operator, Skyport. Transport Canada was closely monitoring and working with authorities on search and rescue efforts, the country's Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon said on X. The Bermuda government is in contact with US authorities and the families of the passengers, Bermuda Premier David Burt wrote in a statement posted on Instagram. "We are praying that all six people will be found safe," the statement said. The US National Transportation Safety Board said it was gathering information about the situation, but it did not say immediately if it would investigate.

events.title: ‘We are in a kind of war’: row over viral Amsterdam chip shop lands in court
events.summary: Neighbours say crowds drawn by TikTok to Fabel Friet are clogging the picturesque canal street and attracting litter, gulls and rats People living in one of Amsterdam’s most exclusive neighbourhoods have taken the city to court for licensing a chip shop that has gone viral on TikTok . On busy days, the queue for Fabel Friet on Runstraat stretches across a bridge on the Keizersgracht – one of Amsterdam’s most famous canals – a court was told last week. The narrow street itself is crowded by tourists waiting for their orders seven days a week. And loitering with intent – on parked cars, on the street itself, and on steps and porches – gulls wait to swoop. “We are in a kind of war where a very unwelcome chip shop has polluted the whole area,” said Thomas van Leeuwen, who lives nearby. “Eating in the street is a shameful behaviour. It gets filthy food on our doorsteps and mayonnaise in the beautiful stone. The herring gulls have moved in as residents, and the worst thing is the rat infestation.” Nineteen neighbours have formally protested against the business licence for Fabel Friet, whose signature product is fries topped with parmesan cheese and truffle mayonnaise. Niek van der Heijden, the lead plaintiff, said the problem was the takeaway’s small size. “What we call the ‘TikTok queue’ for Fabel Friet causes the most nuisance,” he said. “The business takes place on the street: waiting to order, waiting to be served, eating. We want Fabel to go to a place where there is enough room to have clients inside.” In a packed courtroom on Tuesday morning, a lawyer for Amsterdam city council acknowledged that the city’s mayor, Femke Halsema, can refuse a licence to operate if the “residential and living environment” is negatively affected by a business. While the chip shop, she said, sticks to its licence obligations to manage the queue and clear litter “it has been going on for a long time, the impact remains severe, and you have to ask: how long can we tolerate this?” For the current licence, she said, the city would be guided by the court’s ruling. The shop’s owners, Abel Klatser and Floris Feilzer, said they employed a cleaning service seven days a week, four times a day, and that year-on-year visitor numbers had dropped by 23% this August after they opened four new locations . “A few neighbours have experienced nuisance, but other people enjoy eating chips,” said Gertjan Teeuwen, their lawyer. “It can be busy, but there are peaks and troughs.” Klatser and Feilzer said in a public statement that they felt unfairly attacked while doing their best to be good neighbours. “Fabel Friet is our child, and we have put our heart and soul into it,” they said. “It is painful if people talk about our business negatively.” The case goes beyond irritations about so-called performative tourism, where tourists flock to a place to post images on social media. “The tiny streets might be charming, but actually the space is not designed for so many people,” said Lisa-Bobbie Kamp, a lawyer for the neighbours. “This is a question of taking space, who owns the place and whether you can just use public space.” Marije Peute, a PhD student at the University of Amsterdam, has studied the effects of “viral urbanism” in the neighbourhood. “The municipality should really think about how they want to act, because this is about the public space. A lot of much older retail spaces have lost their local clients because they don’t want to go there any more,” she said. Rogier Havelaar, a councillor from the Christian Democratic Appeal party, said that, while Fabel Friet should probably be offered a “flagship store” licence in a more suitable location, the benefits of tourism to the city should not be overlooked. “Amsterdam would never have as many museums, restaurants, going-out spots and theatres if they were only for the residents,” he said. “And tourism provides 70,000 jobs. Amsterdam would have a gigantic financial problem if tourism went away.” Standing on the bridge over the Keizersgracht, some German laboratory apprentices drawn by TikTok were enjoying their chips. Natalie Stübben said crowd managers had just asked them to move away from people’s houses. “It’s pretty hard to get through here with a car or just by walking,” she said. “I don’t think we were thinking about annoying the neighbours, but it makes sense.” Some of those neighbours will be pleased if the business location has had its chips after the court verdict on 12 November. “There’s something very alarming about the fact that these people are all led by their higher power – influencers – and call themselves followers,” said van Leeuwen. “It’s Orwellian. This court case is part of the parasitic industry that lives on tourists.”

events.title: Quality over quantity: China’s AI microdrama producers battle viewer fatigue
events.summary: Challenge has shifted from making videos at low cost to standing out in a market saturated with lookalike productions, creators say Two decades after stepping away from the spotlight, iconic actress Joey Wong made an unexpected return to the screen – not through a traditional production, but via artificial intelligence-powered reconstruction. In a two-minute video by NetEase this summer, Wong, one of the most well-known actresses of the 1980s and 90s, had some of her most celebrated roles recreated, including the beautiful ghost in A Chinese Ghost Story and an alluring snake demon in Green Snake . More than 90 per cent of the 430,000 microdramas launched online in the first eight months of the year were AI-generated, according to the National Radio and Television Administration, China’s broadcasting regulator.

events.title: Regional audiences to lose Network 10, as licensee warns of TV's future
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Network 10 to disappear in parts of SA, NSW's Riverina, after no deal made Network 10 channels will disappear from Mount Gambier, Riverland and Griffith TV screens. ( ABC News: Jak Rowland ) Audiences in Mount Gambier and the Riverland in SA, and Griffith in NSW, will lose terrestrial Network 10 channels on Friday. Network 10 and license holders WIN failed to come to a new agreement after months of negotiating. WIN says it will be "challenging to maintain services", due to the economics of regional broadcasting. Viewers in parts of regional South Australia, and parts of the Riverina in New South Wales, will lose access to Network 10's terrestrial channels, after the network and license holder, WIN Network, failed to reach an agreement. WIN has announced it will stop broadcasting 10, 10 Drama and 10 Comedy in the Mount Gambier, Riverland, Griffith and Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area, with the final broadcasts to be on Friday, October 9. The network had flagged its agreement with Network 10 would expire in July, and that the channels would be pulled. However, local audiences were given a three-month reprieve , with Network 10 saying it would provide its feed "free of charge" to WIN while the parties worked on a deal that has not eventuated. WIN Network says the decision reflects the economics of regional broadcasting. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) In a statement, a WIN Network spokesperson said providing Network 10 services to the impacted markets was "no longer viable". "This is a business decision that reflects the realities of regional broadcasting," they said. "Regional markets carry high transmission and infrastructure costs, while digital disruption continues to erode audiences and advertising revenue. "These economics will continue to make it challenging to maintain services across regional Australia. "WIN recognises this will be disappointing for viewers and thanks them for their understanding." The move follows a similar loss of Seven Network channels to the same markets, after Seven and WIN failed to reach an agreement before Seven's deal expired last year. The channels were eventually restored after a multi-day shutdown that saw the channels replaced with red screens advising they were "no longer available". Audiences in Mount Gambier, the Riverland and Griffith temporarily lost Seven Network channels last year. ( ABC South East SA: Eugene Boisvert ) Job cut fears at one of Australia's largest toilet roll manufacturers How a 'piece of rural propaganda' became 'compulsory listening' for Aussies Soccer player with broken leg endures 70km car trip between hospitals Regional women share postpartum journeys to create change A Network 10 spokesperson said audiences could continue to access the network's channels online and via its app. "WIN holds the broadcast licences in the Riverland, Mount Gambier and Griffith regions and although Network 10 has worked closely with WIN to explore options to maintain local access to its content, WIN has advised that continuing to operate them is no longer commercially viable," they said. The WIN Network holds the broadcast licenses in Mount Gambier, the Riverland and Griffith. ( ABC South East SA: Eugene Boisvert ) It is not the first time a regional market has lost Network 10 channels due to the financial challenges of regional broadcasting. In 2024, audiences in Mildura, Victoria, lost their Network 10 channels when Mildura Digital Television (MDT), which carried 10's signal to the market, was closed by co-owners Seven and WIN. The networks said "it did not make commercial sense" to keep MDT going, as it had been unprofitable throughout its existence. A government spokesperson said the decision was a "commercial matter" and that it was up to the networks to explain it to the community. "The government continues to support Australian broadcasters through a range of measures including the deferral of the Commercial Broadcasting Tax, which will deliver an estimated $111.3 million in savings for the sector," they said. "We know how important free-to-air TV is and are examining ways to ensure it continues to be delivered in a sustainable way in the future, with public consultation now underway.

events.title: Houthis target Saudi oil facility as hostilities escalate in Yemen
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Iran-backed Houthis target Saudi oil facility as hostilities escalate in Yemen Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis say they targeted a Saudi Arabian oil company in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen. The fighting has worsened the already appalling humanitarian conditions in Yemen. Iraq's state-owned Oil Tanker Company says it has transported 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude aboard a large crude carrier through the Strait of Hormuz. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis say a targeted attack on a Saudi Arabian oil company facility near the capital Riyadh is retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen. The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen's Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait in a lightning offensive last month. Houthi-affiliated channel Al-Masirah TV reported that Saudi aircraft hit Sanaa with 26 strikes, after earlier reporting "Saudi aggression" against the Yemeni capital. Houthis say they targeted a Saudi oil facility, south of Riyadh. ( AP ) Two correspondents in Sanaa reported hearing loud explosions and seeing warplanes firing missiles at the city. In Saudi Arabia, flames and smoke were seen rising on Saturday afternoon from an Aramco facility south of Riyadh. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted an oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones. They said the attack sparked fires at the targeted sites. Al-Masirah also reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in Yemen's north-western governorate of Saada, one of the group's strongholds. After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war in July, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of north-west Yemen, including Sanaa, against Yemen's internationally recognised government. The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country's south and east, a region that is larger but much less populated. A big, expensive, global excursion into hell What so many of the current major global conflicts have in common with the debacle in Iraq is their undefined, or sometimes not truthfully defined, missions. Hostilities were reignited after four years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation. The flight did not seek authorisation from Saudi Arabia, contravening a decade-old practice. Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022. Since then, fighting has intensified, with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive in which they seized control of coastal regions along the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Houthi fighters took over the Red Sea port of Sanaa in Yemen. ( AP ) They have also struck multiple Saudi targets, including oil infrastructure and Riyadh, while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea. The renewed fighting has worsened the already appalling humanitarian conditions in Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, with the World Food Programme warning on Friday that three-quarters of the population was unable to meet its basic food needs. Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where dozens of combatants were reported killed on Friday by sources on both sides. The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed, while government sources said 26 troops had died. The Houthis have moved on strategic islands in the Red Sea and are now putting one of the richest and most powerful nations in the Middle East in a tricky spot. The Houthis said on Friday Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the previous 24 hours. Saudi authorities reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemeni border. Riyadh has reportedly requested help from the United States, a call so far rebuffed by US President Donald Trump . Meanwhile, Iraq's state-owned Oil Tanker Company transported 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude aboard a large crude carrier through the Strait of Hormuz, in what its director general described on Saturday as the company's first such operation in decades. A week of Houthi attacks threatens oil and markets The Iran-backed Houthi rebels have made their biggest land grab in years, reigniting Yemen's 12-year long civil war and pushing up global fuel prices. The announcement means the company is transporting the crude through the strait rather than delivering it at the port of Basra, giving state oil marketer SOMO greater flexibility in how and where it sells the crude.

events.title: Ethiopian federal forces retake Mekelle airport from Tigrayan fighters, residents say
events.summary: Ethiopian federal forces have retaken Mekelle’s airport from Tigrayan fighters KAMPALA, Uganda -- Ethiopian federal forces have taken the airport in Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region, according to people in the city who spoke to The Associated Press on Saturday, reversing a takeover by Tigrayan fighters that prompted the suspension of commercial flights last month. It wasn't immediately clear when federal forces recaptured Alula Aba Nega Airport. Those who provided the information declined to be identified for fear of retribution amid uncertainty over who controlled the city. Severe disruptions to internet and cellphone networks have made gathering and verifying information from Tigray difficult. Details of how the airport changed hands, including whether fighting took place there, remained unclear. “The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm,” an Ethiopian general said on condition of anonymity. Neither the Ethiopian government nor the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, had issued an official statement on the airport’s reported capture. It wasn’t clear who controlled Mekelle itself. An AP contributor in the city said residents feared looting amid the uncertainty. “Many reports indicate that the government and allied forces have begun to control Tigray’s capital,” said Jalale Getachew Birru, an Ethiopia analyst for ACLED, an independent global monitor that collects, analyzes and maps data on conflict. The AP could not independently verify those reports. TPLF fighters seized the airport on Sept. 23, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to Mekelle and the Tigrayan cities of Axum and Shire. The African Union urged restraint, warning that renewed tensions threatened the peace agreement signed in 2022. Federal troops are fighting alongside allied Tigrayan forces against the TPLF. The AP previously reported that the Tigray Peace Force, a breakaway faction of the Tigrayan rebels, was operating alongside federal forces in the neighboring Afar region. The reported change in control follows a sharp deterioration in relations between Ethiopia and neighboring Eritrea. Ethiopia on Thursday ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave and announced the closure of its embassy in Eritrea. Eritrea said that it would sever diplomatic ties. Ethiopian authorities have accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF , an allegation Eritrea has denied. The U.S. State Department in a statement Saturday urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to show restraint and return to talks. Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' “Increasing cross-border tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea have the potential to affect the entire region,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said. “The Horn of Africa cannot sustain another military conflict and humanitarian crisis. A conflict jeopardizes ongoing U.S. collaboration on shared interests with both countries.” The government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed , if it takes control of Mekelle, is very likely to leave regional security in the hands of the Tigray Peace Force, which comprises former members of the Tigray Defense Forces, Birru said. Abiy has tried and failed to subdue Tigray’s rebellious leaders in recent months, with TPLF Chairman Debretsion Gebremichael openly challenging him. Renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 peace deal that ended a devastating two-year war between federal troops, backed by Eritrea and allied militias, and the TPLF. “This is an extraordinary and largely unexpected turn in a war whose direction looked very different only days ago,” Getachew Temare, an independent attorney and human rights defender who is from Ethiopia, said of the possible fall of Mekelle in an analysis posted on X. “But the most consequential question is not whether Mekelle falls. It is what this fall means politically.” He said the emergence of the Tigray Peace Force makes the current conflict different from the previous one. When Mekelle fell to federal forces in November 2020, the TPLF “retained something far more important. A substantial political and social constituency for armed resistance remained intact. Within months, Tigrayan forces returned to Mekelle and the military balance was dramatically reversed.” The fighting has brought renewed hardship to civilians still recovering from the previous 2020-2022 war. Residents of Mekelle told the AP earlier this week that communications, banking and other essential services had been disrupted. In September, residents described fears of renewed isolation following the suspension of flights. They also reported that roads connecting Tigray and Afar had been closed to civilian traffic, although the AP couldn't independently verify the closures. Kiyaro reported from Hamburg, Germany.
