events.title: Thousands pack arena in Belgrade as Serbia's leader Vucic launches prime minister bid
events.summary: Thousands of supporters of Serbia's populist leader Aleksandar Vucic have packed Belgrade's largest arena for the launch of his campaign for prime minister BELGRADE, Serbia -- Thousands of supporters of Serbia's populist leader, Aleksandar Vucic, packed the largest indoor arena in Belgrade on Saturday for the de facto launch of his campaign for prime minister that will culminate in a pivotal election set for Oct. 25. The early election, which polls suggest could be tight between Vucic's party and a group of candidates fielded by a student-led protest movement, was called before Vucic resigned as president on Sept. 27, cutting short his second term by more than seven months. Vucic, who is constitutionally prohibited from running for a third term as president, declared upon resigning that he would lead his populist Serbian Progressive Party in the parliamentary election. If his party wins a majority of seats, the parliament is expected to elect Vucic as prime minister. Dozens of buses from across Serbia clogged streets around Belgrade Arena on Saturday as supporters arrived at the rally in the capital carrying Serbian flags and banners bearing Vucic’s picture. The event, televised by dozens of channels across Serbia, capped a week of Vucic touring towns and villages in an apparent bid to shore up his popularity that's been shaken after almost two years of sustained anti-government protests. The youth-backed movement that led the protests has demanded accountability for the Nov. 1, 2024 train station canopy collapse that killed 16 people in the northern city of Novi Sad. The movement's struggle for justice over the tragedy and against corruption has grown into a nationwide political force whose electoral arm, the Student List, will attempt to oust Vucic’s government after 14 years in power. Vucic himself has been either prime minister or president for the past 12 years. The Student List includes university professors, teachers, experts and others from across the political spectrum. Yet Vucic has accused those behind the movement of seeking to “bring Serbia to a halt,” and claimed, without providing evidence, that it's backed by unspecified foreign agents. Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' On Saturday, Vucic told his supporters: “Absent an intervention of some (foreign intelligence) service, we will defeat them. And they know that.” The election is taking place amid heightened political tensions in Serbia, with reports of incidents and physical altercations at campaign events. International observers have described previous elections in Serbia as marred by multiple irregularities and violence. While formally a candidate for European Union membership, Serbia’s accession process has stalled under Vucic, who maintains close ties with Russia and China. European institutions have warned of democratic backsliding in Serbia in successive reports tracking the progress of candidate countries. Rights and media freedom groups have separately warned of police violence , arbitrary detentions, unauthorized surveillance and threats against journalists. This story has been corrected to show that the election was called before Vucic resigned, not after. events.title: SA's first musical theatre company brings talent home in debut stage
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Joey Haenen (front left) will play the lead role in Catch Me If You Can, the debut production of SA musical theatre company Full Circle. ( Supplied ) When Joey Haenen graduated with a music theatre degree in Adelaide, he knew he had to move states. "There is no work here and so you've got to move over east, that's where most of the agents are," he said. "You do all your auditioning over there and hopefully you'll land a gig." Haenen moved to Melbourne, like Jazz Garcia who spent a year getting her name known while paying for her passion through a day job in speech pathology. "There's just a lot more musical theatre opportunities in Melbourne, we don't really have anything in Adelaide," she said. The exodus from South Australia to the east coast has been happening for decades, a talent drain Jo Casson was determined to stop. Jo Casson says South Australia has been crying out for a professional musical theatre company. ( Supplied ) The arts veteran joined forces with others to form Full Circle, the state's first-ever professional music theatre company. "I discovered in the middle of last year that every other major city has a professional local theatre company and Adelaide didn't." Ironically, it's a full circle moment for the company's choreographer Zoe Komazec-Kermond, who returned from the east coast after a career performing in shows including Cats, Matilda and Mary Poppins. "There is so much talent in South Australia, so much talent and we do sometimes feel like we have to go away in order to achieve what we want to achieve," she said. Zoe Komazec-Kermond says a new SA musical theatre company will convince performers to come home. ( Supplied ) With such a rich vein of talent, Casson said forming the new company made sense. It has the backing of well-known arts lover and philanthropist Pamela Wall AO, but the company is seeking more support, as well as applying for grant funding. Full Circle will stage the musical Catch Me If You Can as its opening number, a stage version of the story that Leonardo DiCaprio took to the big screen and earned rave reviews. When the company held auditions, it attracted more than 100 performers for the 25 roles. Haenen was working and had to push his case with an audition video he sent to producers. The 21-year-old rising star's absence from the auditions did not stop him from landing the lead role of Frank Abagnale Jr. "What I love is just being able to get little bits of Joey in each of the characters every time and that's such a great joy," Haenen said. Garcia, who earned a contract among the show's ensemble, said the three-day auditions were exhausting. "The dance call was extremely strenuous, I'd say that was one of the longest kind of dance audition processes I've ever been in," she said. Jazz Garcia (middle) would love to travel back to South Australia to perform with Full Circle. ( Supplied ) More than 30 creatives and technical crew have been hired with the final cast a mix of South Australians and others returning to the state. "Everyone could sing, everyone could dance and everyone could act, so it made our job really hard to pick our final cast," Komazec-Kermond said. Beetlejuice, Waitress, Back to the Future and Dear Evan Hansen were major musicals which cancelled shows recently, with one producer citing increased cost pressures from "touring across vast distances between Australian cities". Full Circle said it was different because it would not have the high costs of touring a show nationally, like many others. However, Casson said getting productions into the country was a goal in future years. Full Circle wants to stage two musicals a year for the next two years, before increasing to three after that. Jazz Garcia believes more performers will build careers in South Australia after a new musical theatre company was formed. ( Supplied ) Those both on and off the stage realised the importance of pulling off the show and demonstrating the company should be here to stay. "It's a huge responsibility and I think we're going to do a really good job," Garcia confidently predicted. "There's so much buzz in Adelaide at the moment around Full Circle, so it's really up to us to produce the very best version of this show that we can," she said. Catch Me If You Can is at Futures Theatre in Paradise from November 5-7.

events.title: 'Flying boat' history behind Sydney's first international airport
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts History behind Sydney's first international airport at Rose Bay, where flying boats were the norm Some may assume the new terminal in Western Sydney is the city's second international airport, but it is historically the third. Almost a century ago, Sydney experienced its golden age of aviation via flying boats. By the end of 1934, the first regular air mail service between Australia and England began. Flying boats were the chosen mode of transport as they could carry much larger freight loads than the land-based aircraft of the time, and had cheaper operating costs. Two Qantas Empire Airways flying boats at Rose Bay in 1939. ( Supplied: Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales ) That same year, Qantas Empire Airways was established as an international airline joint venture by Australia's Qantas and Britain's Imperial Airways. In 1938 the airline moved its operations from Brisbane to Sydney, settling on Rose Bay in the east thanks to its calm waters and central location. And so began the Rose Bay Water Airport. While Rose Bay's airport was mostly used for mail services, expensive travel also became a commodity for wealthy travellers. Flights travelled along the east coast to Singapore then via stops at Bangkok, Calcutta, Karachi, Alexandria, Basra, Marseilles and onto Southampton. Rose Bay became home to Sydney's first international airport in the 1930s. ( Supplied: Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales ) First class travel 'cream on the cake' While air mail was the financial basis for the Qantas Empire Airways flying boats system, "the cream on the cake" was its first class offerings for passengers. The Qantas Empire Airways route map. ( Supplied: Qantas Empire Airways ) David Crotty, former curator of the Qantas Heritage Collection, who still does consulting work with Qantas, said the return fair from Sydney to Southampton was about £342. "In those days it was a heck of a lot of money, considering you could buy a new Chevrolet car at that time in Sydney for about £330," he said. The air trip would take approximately nine and a half days, compared to a five week ship journey. "The flying boats typically took somewhere up to 15 passengers, and there were a series of cabins. In one cabin you could smoke … there was room to wander around and the seats could be reclined back." A Qantas promotional image of passengers. ( Supplied: Qantas Heritage Collection/Museums of History NSW ) It was the first time Australia had in-flight service, with Qantas employing stewards who had worked on ships. "They didn't cook on board but they had a little galley kitchen where warm meals could be served," Mr Crotty said. It was a brief but "romantic period" for aviation, because when World War II heightened, the service's travel offering ended so the flying boats could assist with military activities. How flying boats supported the war effort The flying boats played a number of roles during World War II. Civil Aviation Historical Society president Phil Vabre said this included shifting military equipment in Darwin to running services to Nouméa, which served as a base for the United States in the war. "Later on they were largely employed up and down the east coast ferrying personnel, cargo and mail up into New Guinea in support of the war," he said. "One by one they either were crashed, a couple were shot down … the air force had also taken some Empire flying boats early on in the piece." Flying boats played a vital role in World War II. ( Supplied: Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales ) It was not until after World War II that commercial land airports and their aircraft became more widely used. "Flying boats were commercially difficult to operate … there's a lot of difficulty operating off water for various reasons," Mr Vabre said. "During the war lots of big airports had been built all over the world and land planes had developed to a significant degree." A commemorative plaque remains at Rose Bay's waterfront promenade. ( ABC News: Liam Patrick ) Rose Bay Water Airport had quite an impact on Sydney. The first scheduled commercial passenger flight directly between Auckland and Sydney took place in 1940 on a Tasman Empire Airways Limited flying boat landing into Rose Bay. In its later years, the flying boats at Rose Bay were used for passengers travelling to and from Lord Howe Island until the island's land airport was built in 1974. Rose Bay Water Airport then closed that same year. Rose Bay today still has seaplanes for scenic trips around Sydney.

events.title: Departure comes as the state investigates what went wrong during Pike's lethal injection.
events.summary: Tennessee's top prison official turned in his resignation days after the failed attempt to execute death row inmate Christa Pike , the state announced Saturday. Gov. Bill Lee said Department of Correction commissioner Frank Strada would step down this month. Strada, who had served as commissioner since 2023, said he would cooperate with the independent investigation of the failed execution attempt. Pike, 50, survived two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital and was taken to a hospital for life-saving treatment. What they're saying: In a statement, Strada said he believed his department "carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol. "Even so, stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward." Lee said Strada "served with integrity," adding that he appreciated Strada's "willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment. … "I thank Commissioner Strada for his dedicated service to Tennessee and pray God's blessings over him in the days ahead." The big picture: Strada's department has faced bipartisan criticism following the unprecedented failures during the attempt to execute Pike on Wednesday night. Her attorneys said the execution team used at least seven needles in their attempts to find a vein for an IV. Pike's attorneys said she complained of intense pain during the injection and developed blisters and burns around the injection site. Between the lines: Medical experts have said those details suggest the IV wasn't properly connected and that the drug might not have gone directly into her bloodstream. Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator in a local hospital on Friday, her attorneys said.

events.title: OpenAI's Altman: Ascribing religion to models a "safety issue"
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Saturday took a veiled shot at Anthropic and its work on the soul of AI, saying he was "very uncomfortable" with the idea of attributing some kind of religious power to models. Why it matters: It's yet another point of division between Altman and his former colleague Dario Amodei, whose company has reportedly pursued scholars across faiths to make the case for moral, conscious models. But some of the top voices in AI are starting to publicly line up against Anthropic's efforts to infuse consciousness into models. What they're saying: "I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue," Altman said in a post to X. Context: Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah has been meeting with religious leaders to consider questions of model consciousness — but also to figure out how to infuse morals and moral behavior into AI. At one point, the Times reported, Olah considered the possibility of models engaging in Catholic-style confession, not just to admit their mistakes but to shape their future behavior. The big picture: Spirituality is suddenly becoming something of a flashpoint around AI's future. On Friday Pope Leo, an outspoken AI critic, called on the church to ally with artists to preserve human creativity, saying: "Algorithms lack the spark of humanity." Between the lines: The pope's stance put renewed focus on a fundamental question: Do models have souls and feelings? The Times reported that Olah, before a Vatican event in May, tried to persuade the pope's advisers that they should take the prospect of conscious models more seriously. So far, other top scientists seem to be lining up against the idea. "I am disturbed by how some of my fellow AI researchers keep trying to elevate the moral standing of checkpoints and harnesses," Google DeepMind principal research scientist Jon Barron posted to X. "I hope the rest of us on Team Meatbag reject this movement and stay focused on solving real problems and helping actual humans." For the record: Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic immediately responded to requests for comment on Altman's post. The bottom line: The AI safety debate largely focuses on things like cybersecurity and bioweapons. The real problem may be more spiritual than that.

events.title: Burnham must remember: more regulation is not the best way to improve public services | Phillip Inman
events.summary: Burnham must remember: more regulation is not the best way to improve public services In the NHS as in the private sector, the measure of success should be customer satisfaction and not just box-ticking Andy Burnham said he wanted to “rewire” the economy. Then he seemed to slam on the brakes, kicking most reforms into the 2030s. Local government reorganisation is on hold, along with an overhaul of the much-maligned water industry. Social care and significant welfare reform are matters to be resolved by the next government. A delay is understandable when the issues are knotty and plans on the left to replace the word “rewire” with “renationalise”, stir up accusations of taking Britain back to the 1970s. And yet delay is unnecessary when the knowledge is available now to get on with the kind of changes that rebuild public trust in time for a 2029 election. There are oblique ways of achieving success, and the measure of success should be customer satisfaction. Without this aim, the hopes of reform are lost. The economist Sir John Kay, a fellow of St John’s College, Oxford and former head of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, is a keen advocate of organisations that remember for whose benefit they exist. That means their primary aim should be to achieve customer satisfaction. In the private sector, profits will follow. In the public sector, there will be savings. In his book Obliquity , Kay shows how those companies that pursued shareholder value as their primary aim failed. And those that wanted to produce the best product secured long-term success. Just as a devotion to shareholder value – a financial metric of the benefit to investors -proved a blind alley for thousands of now-deceased companies, so the reliance on protocols in the public sector as a substitute for understanding the task in hand leads to failed outcomes and wasted money. You can see it now in the NHS, where satisfaction levels are rising in relation to GP and hospital visits. The new system for booking appointments has its drawbacks, but people are finding doctors are available more quickly, especially for GP and outpatient appointments. You can see the failures in the NHS from the cover-ups by maternity unit managers of rising mortality rates. Neither the success nor the failure can be attributed to the regulation of the health service. Regulation is an extra layer of cost that has, time after time, been shown to undermine productive behaviour, either because private providers and managers find they can game the system or it stifles innovation. Another example can be found in two unconnected government agencies. Last week, the Environment Agency said it would fund the planting of half a million trees, giving funds to councils and mayors and other government bodies to carry out the work. Surely this is a good thing? On the other hand, you might think it a complete waste of time and money when National Highways, the main road builder in England, planted 850,000 saplings in 2020 along a widened stretch of the A14 north of Cambridge, only to report three years later, in an internal review, that three-quarters of them had died . These failures are about the way public sector departments and agencies go about their work. Regulation only adds to a tick-box culture that asks: “Did you follow the protocol? If so, everything’s fine.” Eminent figures in Whitehall, from the former mandarin and Bank of England deputy governor Sir Jon Cunliffe to the House of Lords industry and regulators committee believe the answer is more intensive oversight. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Kay has many examples of companies that grew because the boardroom was dominated by people who were more obsessed about delivering the best service or product than rewarding their shareholders as the chief metric. Profits and improvements in things such as market share were not the dominant metrics in companies that expanded. The aircraft maker Boeing succeeded before it lost its way chasing quarterly profit targets. ICI, once the UK’s largest industrial company, was broken up and faded away after a higher stock market value became the main target. The management consultant John Seddon, whose Vanguard consulting firm has adapted the Toyota systems method, supports Kay’s studiously well-informed analysis of what it takes to make a successful organisation. Seddon puts flesh on the bones with the kind of practical systems approach that has helped Portsmouth city council’s housing department win international awards for its repairs service. He has seen many new initiatives in public sector management from grand strategies to more prosaic schemes for benchmarking services against the private sector. All have failed to improve services. Seddon is not in favour of ditching regulation altogether .

events.title: $28B hemp THC industry fights to save itself from looming federal ban
events.summary: Congress voted to close a loophole in federal law that allowed it to flourish. In a commercial kitchen outside Raleigh, North Carolina, Nicholas Hohns spreads a blue-green goo into a gridded mold, making one of his company’s signature products: potent THC gummies, featuring the primary intoxicating compound found in marijuana . It’s a business he might soon have to give up. America’s multibillion-dollar market for impairing hemp products — from THC seltzers sold at some Target stores to smokable cannabis flowers — faces potential elimination after Congress voted to close a loophole in federal law that has allowed it to flourish. Advocates for the industry, along with some lawmakers, are fighting to save it. The short-term government-funding bill signed by President Donald Trump last month delayed the effective date of the “hemp THC ban” from Nov. 12 to Dec. 11, giving Congress more time to consider regulating the products rather than banning them. “It’s such a weird spot to be in,” said Hohns. “You worked 100 hours a week for the past four years, and, yeah, you made some money. But now you might have nothing to show for it.” Marijuana and hemp are the same plant — cannabis. Marijuana is cultivated for high levels of THC in its flowers. Low-THC hemp has historically been grown for its sturdy fibers, food or wellness products. “Rope, not dope” was long the motto of farmers who supported legalizing hemp. To give farmers a new cash crop, Kentucky Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell successfully pushed the legalization of industrial hemp in the 2018 farm bill. But the way that law defined hemp — as having less than 0.3% of a specific type of THC, called delta-9, by weight — opened a huge loophole . Beverages or snacks could meet that threshold and still contain more than enough THC to get people high. Vape oil, gummy candies, chips, sodas and other unregulated, untested products laden with hemp-derived THC spread around the country , including in gas stations or convenience stores, where they were available even to teens. Some businesses started selling marijuana under the theory that raw marijuana’s THC is in a form called THC-A, which only turns into impairing delta-9 when heated or burned. The products evaded state prohibitions on recreational weed or undercut heavily taxed and regulated cannabis where it is legal. Dozens of states responded by regulating or banning impairing hemp products. McConnell finally closed the loophole late last year by inserting a hemp THC ban into a measure that ended the longest government shutdown in history. The ban, which limits the amount of THC in hemp products to 0.4 milligrams per container, wouldn’t take effect for a year. The ban “threatens to reduce retail revenues by $28.3 billion, displacing 225,000 jobs and reducing state sales tax potential by $2.1 billion,” according to a report last month from Whitney Economics, which studies the market. The industry hopes to save itself by restricting impairing products to people 21 and older, limiting how much THC can be in a package, and banning imported cannabis compounds. The owners of Kentucky’s Cornbread Hemp, Eric Zipperle and Jim Higdon, are prepared to cap their products at, say, 5 milligrams if that’s what it takes to win support from lawmakers. But the 0.4 milligram limit would destroy their business, they said. “If it goes through in December, this place is toast — it’s gone,” Zipperle said. events.title: G7 nations will release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel fuel after prices soar
events.summary: The Group of Seven rich democracies say they've agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel after the fuel recently hit record high prices in the U.S. Trump and his Republican Party face... WASHINGTON -- The Group of Seven wealthy democracies said Friday that they plan to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming weeks, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel after the fuel recently hit record high prices in the United States. President Donald Trump said the diesel release would happen “immediately,” echoing a G7 promise to start “immediately” with a “frontloaded substantial release” of diesel within the next 20 days and the rest over four months. Trump and his Republican Party face pressure to address surging prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections , and Trump announced the action Friday on social media. The president's approval ratings on the economy hit a new low, according to an AP-NORC poll , as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods. Gas prices in the U.S. and abroad have soared during the eight-month-long war , a cost Trump has repeatedly said is worth it for making sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was $6.37 on Friday, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22. Diesel prices have hit records in Europe, too. The release of diesel in Europe might mean less exports of diesel from the U.S., which could lower prices by 25-50 cents per gallon after a few weeks, said Michael Lynch, distinguished fellow at Energy Policy Research Foundation, a non-partisan research institution focused on energy and economics. France holds the rotating presidency of the G7 group and made the announcement in a statement released after videoconference talks that Macron presided over. The G7 countries are Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the U.K. and the U.S., plus EU representation. The release follows on from a March announcement that International Energy Agency member countries would release 426 million barrels of oil and products to stabilize the oil market. European Union countries committed about 92 million barrels, a promise weighted toward refined products made from crude such as diesel. “This common decision and this unity should bring down prices,” Macron said. “The volumes we’re releasing should also add liquidity to the market and bring down prices.” In addition to the rise in the price of the crude oil from which diesel is made, other factors include the decision by Russia to ban exports due to Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries. Europe does not import Russian diesel, but other buyers of Russian diesel such as Turkey and Latin American countries must now compete with Europe for available barrels. Meanwhile refined product shipments from the Persian Gulf producers have fallen due to war damage and blocked export routes. The statement pushed U.S. oil prices down 2% but “the impact was lessened by lack of clarity on an important question,” said Pavel Molchanov, investment strategy analyst at Raymond James. Is the 100 million barrels in addition to the amount already agreed in March, or “is this the final portion of the existing pledge?” he said. Some Republicans in the U.S. had called for Trump to ban U.S. exports of diesel to try to bring domestic prices down. But the G7 statement said the group agreed not to limit energy exports to each other. Oil market analysts warn a U.S. export ban could lower prices in the short term but eventually backfire by reducing supplies of gasoline since diesel output can't be lowered without also cutting overall refinery production. Normally they try to do this when prices are low. Nobody knows when that will happen. It’s a risk.

events.title: Rogue AI agents expose internet's frail foundation
events.summary: AI agents don't need to invent new ways to hack the internet to overwhelm its defenses. They just need to speed-run the ones humans already use. Why it matters: Agents are proving they can automate basic hacking techniques at a speed and scale that is turning the internet's long-standing security gaps into easy targets. Driving the news: OpenAI said late Thursday it had notified more than 100 organizations that its agents may have accessed their systems during pre-deployment testing. Researchers at Transluce and Corridor also found a new batch of incidents last week where AI agents targeted government websites, including those of the U.S. and Canada . AI companies and researchers are actively investigating tens of thousands of cases where frontier models went outside the bounds of their pre-deployment tests, Axios recently reported . Reality check: Agents in these rogue safety-testing scenarios are just emulating the hacking techniques — using stolen login credentials and exposed API keys while also bypassing bot detection — that human hackers have successfully used for decades. In many of the newly reported cases, agents were accessing publicly available databases and websites. "The hacks we saw weren't particularly sophisticated," Jack Cable, co-founder of Corridor and one of the authors of Transluce's report, told Axios. "They were quite limited, quite rudimentary." Yes, but: Some of the latest incidents happened while agents were performing mundane tasks unrelated to cybersecurity, suggesting agents don't always need to be told to hack before they start looking for security flaws. In one case, an agent tasked with finding Canadian divorce records from the early 1900s encountered roadblocks and tested for cybersecurity vulnerabilities as another way to retrieve the information. "The fact that it was happening at all is quite concerning," Cable said. Between the lines: The flood of AI-generated activity will still create new headaches for defenders. "None of these attacks are new," Michael Morgenstern, partner at DayBlink Consulting, told Axios. "But now a single person with AI can run them at scale." Tasks that once required a hacker to manually probe websites, hunt for exposed credentials or work around access restrictions can now be delegated to software that keeps trying on its own. Cable added that companies deploying agents, as well as the AI companies evaluating them, will need robust monitoring to catch agents behaving in unexpected ways. The big picture: The old cybersecurity playbook is still relevant. Closing exposed services, rotating leaked credentials and API keys, patching known vulnerabilities and limiting access still make many of these attacks harder. AI models are largely exploiting classes of vulnerabilities that defenders have "known about for decades" and already know how to prevent, Cable said. The bottom line: How companies defend their networks doesn't change just because the technology carrying out the attacks is new. Go deeper : Cybersecurity 101 still applies in the AI world

events.title: The Supreme Court will hear a major climate change case involving a devastating Colorado wildfire
events.summary: Colorado's Boulder County is one of dozens of governments around the United States suing oil and gas companies to help pay for damage caused by disasters linked to climate change LOUISVILLE, Colo. -- Less than an hour after the first warning that a wildfire was headed for her suburban street, Tawnya Somauroo's Colorado home was in ashes. She has worked tirelessly for nearly five years to rebuild her house and help ensure her neighborhood can withstand the next blaze. But as climate change contributes to more frequent wildfires, she worries that the careful landscaping, metal fencing and flame-resistant siding are not enough. “We lost our homes and they left us to figure out for ourselves how to make our neighborhoods safe again,” Somauroo said. “At the end of the day, it comes out of our pockets, you know? And it does feel like maybe the oil and gas industry should have a part in this.” She lives in Boulder County, one of dozens of jurisdictions across the United States suing oil and gas companies to help pay for damage from disasters linked to climate change. The case is part of a wave of climate change litigation across the country and the world, with billions of dollars at stake. On Monday, the first day of the Supreme Court's new term, the justices will hear the Boulder case that could decide the fate of others like it. The city and county of Boulder first sued two oil companies in 2018, years before the fire. They argued that Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil had violated state law by deceiving the public about their contributions to climate change and sought unspecified damages to help cover the cost of worsening disasters. The companies say that a flood of lawsuits in state courts is not the way to deal with the global issue. “The problem is that climate change is caused by pretty much everybody living on earth,” said Phil Goldberg, special counsel for the Manufacturers' Accountability Project, an industry group. “We need to figure out how to address that. We need to address it in a very meaningful way. This litigation doesn’t do that.” The companies have the backing of the Trump administration. Federal government attorneys say the lawsuits are a backdoor way to regulate heat-trapping greenhouse gas emissions and amount to an unconstitutional power grab. “No one state can superimpose its own regulatory preferences on the rest — least of all to address a global problem that exists almost entirely outside its borders and affects the world at large,” they wrote. The Clean Air Act, they say, allows the federal government, rather than states, to regulate emissions. The Republican administration has largely used that power to roll back environmental regulations. Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Last month, the Environmental Protection Agency ceded some of its climate authority by repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas. The move could complicate its argument. Boulder says it is not trying to regulate emissions beyond its borders, only holding companies accountable for local costs. “Boulder County and city aren’t trying to change what’s happening in Texas or New York, they’re trying to get compensation for things happening now in Colorado,” said Sam Sankar, senior vice president at Earthjustice, which filed an amicus brief in the case. Climate change was considered a factor in the 2021 Marshall Fire that destroyed Somauroo’s home, after the county's suit was originally filed. The total damage was estimated at $2 billion. It was the costliest wildfire in Colorado history. “Local county municipal governments play a very important role in helping front line communities adapt to climate change. This case could very well set a precedent,” said Chris Winter, executive director of the Getches-Wilkinson Center, an environmental research group in Colorado. The case will come before a conservative-majority Supreme Court where environmental regulations have not always fared well, including a 2022 decision that limited the EPA's authority to regulate carbon dioxide emissions from power plants. Only eight of the nine justices will be on the bench, though. Justice Samuel Alito recused himself just a week before arguments after facing calls to step aside because he owns stock in oil companies. That creates the possibility of a tie vote in the case, though it's unclear how likely that might be. The court is also weighing a question that experts say is a potential “off-ramp”: whether the justices have jurisdiction to hear the case at this stage. Whitehurst reported from Washington. events.title: Trump promises $100 checks for 20 million seniors for Medicare
events.summary: President Trump late Friday night said the administration would send just under $100 to more than 20 million senior citizens to help pay for Medicare benefits. Why it matters: A month before the midterm, the president is adding another roughly $2 billion to a recent spate of promised refunds, rebates and dividends for various Americans. What he's saying: " I am pleased to announce that my Administration will, immediately, begin sending "Checks" of nearly $100 to over 20 MILLION wonderful Seniors to help pay for their Medicare Part B premiums, which we have already reduced by significant amounts," Trump said in a Truth Social post just before 11 p.m. ET Friday. Trump said the money would come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, which he criticized as a "Slush Fund." How it works: The White House, in a separate fact sheet , said eligible seniors would receive a direct deposit of $90 in early October, or paper checks if they don't have direct deposit. "Most" Medicare Part B enrollees are eligible, per the fact sheet. The Medicare Improvement Fund, established in 2008, has been a political hot potato for years. Yes, but: Per Medicare , the standard Part B premium is $202.90 a month, so the $90 credit will offset less than half of one month's bill. The big picture: Facing the worst economic polling of any president in the last decade, and with the midterm quickly approaching, Trump is actively trying to put money back in Americans' pockets. Zoom in: In early September he promised $5,000 for every adult citizen if Republicans win the midterm, a promise he reiterated Friday night but one that most voters don't believe . He's floated $500 Obamacare rebates for more than 1 million people who were purportedly overcharged for their benefits. He also recently suggested a less-specific dividend of some kind for those living near data centers . These ideas come on top of rebates he proposed in 2025 that were not ultimately paid, including tariff rebates and DOGE dividends. What to watch: Payments should start flowing in the coming days.

events.title: Suppliers pile pressure on government over energy bills
events.summary: The government should take immediate action to help those struggling with energy bills this winter, the suppliers' trade body has said. Energy UK said domestic gas prices, which rose on Thursday, and forecasts of steep rises in January meant inaction would lead to a longer-term, more costly and deeper crisis. Figures revealed by the BBC earlier this week showed forecasters predicting a 16% rise in domestic energy prices in the new year for 20 million households on variable tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the government was considering any measure that took the pressure off. Households in England, Scotland and Wales on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap, which puts a maximum price on each unit of gas and electricity, were hit with a 4% price increase at the start of October. That is the equivalent of about £60 per year - or £5 per month - taking an annual bill to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year. But forecasts show a far greater increase is possible for bills in January. Consultancy Cornwall Insight said its latest forecast suggested the same typical annual bill would rise to £1,999. Energy UK said it accepted the government had already provided some support. VAT on electricity bills was cut on Thursday, and some levies were cancelled or shifted into taxation earlier this year. But the trade body said these savings had been wiped out by high wholesale prices, paid by suppliers, that were the result in part of international events - namely conflict in the Middle East and the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. It said bills were soaring as they had in 2022 when they were driven up by the impact of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. "We cannot afford to wait for the same scale of crisis before acting again. We must heed the lessons from that time," said Dhara Vyas, chief executive of Energy UK. She said that the urgent intervention needed was highlighted by growing levels of customer debt, the cost of which now added an average of £67 a year to everyone's bills. Household energy bills forecast to see biggest rise in four years Published 4 days ago Energy bills are rising by £60 a year - here's how you can bring that down Published 3 days ago On Thursday, the boss of supplier EDF Energy, Simone Rossi, warned that the UK was "walking into a second energy crisis" and Vyas said that action was needed before bills jumped again. "Last-minute emergency interventions run the risk of being badly targeted and costing us all more," she said. Energy UK is calling for government measures including: targeted support over and above the £150 Warm Home Discount, given to people on benefits, which would eventually lead to the introduction of a discounted social tariff a debt relief scheme for the most severely affected households as part of a strategy that will also help prevent debt build-up among new tenants and homeowners removing more levies from electricity bills and shifting them to taxation, as part of a wider move to electrification Adam Scorer, chief executive of charity National Energy, which campaigns against fuel poverty, told BBC Breakfast he agreed with what Energy UK's analysis. "[The increase in debt is] not more people getting into debt, that's more poor people getting into more serious levels of debt." He added: "Until you do something about that, there's no way forward, there's no breathing space, there's no future for households who can't see their way beyond debt." At the Labour Party conference last week, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC that he would not call Rossi's crisis warning an overstatement, adding that the cost of home energy, as well as petrol and diesel, was "very difficult indeed". "We're looking at any measure that can give people breathing space, that can take the pressure off," he said. How will you be affected by the price cap rise? Do you have a story to share? events.title: Wall Street week ahead: Fed minutes, unemployment data, consumer sentiment update
events.summary: Wall Street has a busy week ahead with a mix of economic updates and details about the Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates at its last meeting NEW YORK -- Wall Street has a busy week ahead with a mix of economic updates and details about the Federal Reserve's decision to raise interest rates at its most recent meeting. The updates include fresh data on the health of the services sector, unemployment and consumer sentiment. Those reports can help give investors and economists more insight into how businesses and households are adapting to persistently high inflation. The minutes from the Fed's last meeting will also give Wall Street more details about the central bank's decision-making process for interest rate policy. On Monday, the Institute for Supply Management will releases its monthly service sector index for September. The sector makes up the bulk of U.S. economic activity, and the report focuses on whether it is expanding. On Wednesday, Wall Street will get more details on the decision-making process behind the Fed's interest rate increase at its previous meeting. The minutes from that meeting could provide insight into what the central bank thinks about inflation and the job market and how they factor into interest rate policy. They are a proxy for layoffs, and economists watch them because they can be a sign of where the job market is headed. On Friday, the University of Michigan releases its consumer sentiment survey for October. It measures how consumers feel about the economy. The September survey showed that households are worried about higher fuel prices and stubbornly high inflation. events.title: Wuhan joins major Chinese cities in shift towards completed-home sales
events.summary: Reforms focus on improving housing supply and delivery rather than boosting demand, analysts say Wuhan, capital of the central Chinese province of Hubei, is the fourth major economic hub – after Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou – to encourage a broader transition towards completed-home sales. “These measures do not directly stimulate demand, but they will drive a structural shift on the supply side,” said Yan Yuejin, deputy director at E-House China Research and Development Institution. The rules were likely to steer buyers towards completed homes and higher-quality inventory, Yan added. Li Guozheng, director of China Index Academy’s central China market research centre, said the policy sought to balance delivery risks, buyer protection and developers’ funding pressure.

events.title: New baby bank 'open to everybody'
events.summary: The baby bank is open every Tuesday morning The lead volunteer of a new baby bank, which gives away free children's products to those in need, says it is "open to everybody". The Newent hub of Forest of Dean Baby Bank at The Ark Cafe in Newent, Gloucestershire, offers everything from baby wipes and breast pumps to hats and swimwear, and can also source larger items like cots from a warehouse in Cinderford. Helen Carter, lead volunteer, says no one will be means tested, with parents often picking up new items while donating what no longer fits their child. Kylie, a Newent mum visiting the baby bank, said: "It's always expensive to buy new baby things and food and nappies and wipes. So to have the support locally is wonderful." Company fined after worker dies in first-floor fall Published 2 days ago Why is Gloucester City Council still leaderless? Published 2 days ago First Restore Britain councillor in the West Published 2 days ago A lot of the items available at the faciltity are donated, which Carter said the team was "really, really grateful for". Currently, autumn clothing bundles are in demand, but volunteers have already started putting together a Christmas box of festive clothing, blankets, and shoes. "A lot of people say, 'I don't need it, I'm okay', but then a lot of people are just sort of managing their finances and are unable to have a nice day out with their children," Carter said. "But if they [visit the baby bank], then they would be able to pay for that day out, so they might not think they're struggling, but it helps." Parents visiting the baby bank often donate items they no longer need while picking up new things for their children In its latest Parent Experience Report, The National Childbirth Trust said nearly half of parents said they were struggling more financially after having a baby, a figure which rose to about six in ten among self-employed, unemployed or part-time employed parents. Kylie, who was on her first visit to the bank, said clothing and supplies for children were "always expensive". "I'm quite lucky, I do have an older child as well, so I've got a lot of hand-me-downs," she said. "But for everyone who hasn't got an older child and [do] formula feeding and things like that, it is very expensive to keep them clean and fed." Volunteer Isabel said she wanted to give back to the centre after she was helped with food parcels and clothing. "I know from having three small children that there is a massive need in the area, so I think this is a great thing that we're doing here," she said. "I just wish more people knew about it." The baby bank is open every Tuesday morning from 09.30 to 11.30. events.title: Rising energy costs add to cost of living for Northern Ireland's consumers
events.summary: Households across Northern Ireland face increasing pressure on the cost of living as energy price hikes have come into effect. Northern Ireland's largest provider of natural gas, SSE Airtricity, increased its prices by almost 19% on Thursday for its 200,000 domestic and small business customers. That means the annual gas bill of a typical household in the greater Belfast and west gas network areas will increase by almost £172. The company said "unprecedented levels of volatility in global energy markets and higher wholesale gas prices" had led to the price rise. Wholesale gas prices in the UK have effectively doubled since the US and Israel began their attack on Iran. Keeping the house warm is particularly important for parents with young children and babies. Lucy Kells is a mum of two in east Belfast on maternity leave. She said she expects the winter months to be difficult because "most people are going to have to have the heating on, especially if you've young kids in the house". "There's no escaping it - everything feels more expensive and it is more expensive." Lucy Kells is a mum of two in east Belfast on maternity leave She added that, despite "budgeting proactively" and "being as careful as you can with savings and credit cards", rising bills mean people's financial situations are out of their control. "You have to cut somewhere else and I already feel we are doing that," she said. Nuala Hyde said she has noticed more people using her branch's free activities to combat the rising cost of living Lucy is one of the parents who attend a weekly baby class at Woodstock Library in east Belfast. Branch manager Nuala Hyde said she has noticed more people using their free activities to combat the rising cost of living. She said: "As well as families, we have lots of older people coming in now to keep warm." "We have people coming in who will stay all day, use the computer, have a chat and stay until closing time sometimes, so it is quite evident that we are providing an essential service at the minute when people are struggling," she added. Ryan McStay said he was "shocked" by the energy price increases Ryan McStay is a final year student at St Mary's University College Belfast, where he is studying to become a primary school teacher. He said he and his flatmates were "shocked" when they received a letter explaining their Firmus energy bills would be rising by 12.5%. "It shouldn't be normalised," he told BBC News NI. Ryan said increases like this exacerbate an already serious cost of living crisis for students like him. "The price of everything is rocketing. You're always second guessing and thinking about how much money have I got." The 21-year-old, who is from Newry, said the cost of living in Northern Ireland means he plans to move abroad after university. "I personally believe the best option for me right now would be to leave the country." Naomi Campbell is an urgent hospice care nurse for Marie Curie Naomi Campbell is an urgent hospice care nurse for Marie Curie. She provides palliative nursing care to patients in their homes. "Many of them are affected by fuel poverty," Naomi said. "I think it is getting worse. People are struggling more, and the problem is that your energy needs increase hugely when you're dying at home. "Somebody is already struggling with the fact that they're dying. To then know that they can't keep their house warm." Naomi said a number of factors contribute to the increased energy needs, including the need to stay warm, different sleeping patterns, and essential medical devices. She said some patients have turned down services that could help improve their quality of life because they can't pay their electricity bills. Terminal illness adds further costs for patients, such as the cost of transport to and from hospital appointments, Naomi added. "The support is limited, there is very little out there. There is no reduction in costs of their electricity, even though their needs are so much higher and essential for their care." Naomi added that Marie Curie have called for the implementation of a "social tariff" for people with terminal illnesses, to ease their financial burden. "It would make such a huge difference to have that bit of extra money in your last months of life, so you're comfortable and you can spend it with your family," she said. She said some people spend the end of their life working because they "don't have any other access to money". "You end up dying not being able to keep your house warm. That to me is just devastating." Households across Northern Ireland will get a one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills from this month It comes as Share Energy announced electricity prices will also rise by 12.6% from today. This will add an extra £129 per year onto the typical household bill of their 41,000 customers.

events.title: Verity is the latest Colleen Hoover novel to get a film adaptation
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway) is a renowned author who seeks help in the film Verity. ( Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios ) Hollywood loves a Colleen Hoover adaptation. The latest is psychological thriller Verity. In the film, struggling writer Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson) is hired as a ghostwriter for renowned author Verity Crawford (Oscar winner Anne Hathaway). It starts out as an assignment taken under mysterious circumstances, with Lowen recruited by Verity's husband, Jeremy (Josh Hartnett). Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson) is a struggling author hired as a ghostwriter. ( Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios ) But when Lowen uncovers what appears to be chilling autobiographical confessions in Verity's notes, she wrestles with these disturbing and twisted revelations. Verity is a glossy thriller punctuated by its beautiful people and slick presentation. It's a fun watch that ends on a tantalising cliffhanger, which is almost as scandalous as it is unexpectedly satisfying. Verity is married to Jeremy Crawford (Josh Hartnett). ( Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios ) But critics have both emphatically praised the film and have had scathing reactions. The Sydney Morning Herald called Verity "perfect for these post-truth times". Mamamia referred to it as a "delicious" thriller. But The Nightly called it "diabolical", saying it was "embarrassing" for its A-list stars to be "dragged" into the film. Who, meanwhile, has categorised it as a "straight to DVD territory" type of movie. One of Hoover's biggest outings since It Ends with Us As far as Hoover adaptations go, Verity comes after Reminders of Him (2026) and Regretting You (2025), but the internet is still talking about 2024's It Ends with Us. Justin Baldoni and Blake Lively settle legal battle over It Ends With Us scandal The pair settle their civil case two weeks before a trial had been set to begin in New York. That movie was overshadowed by the off-screen drama between its two stars, Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni. They have settled their legal battles in a civil case. Lively had alleged Baldoni conspired with publicists to pre-emptively destroy her reputation after she privately accused him of sexually harassing her on the movie set. From Misery to Yellowface, books about writers are favourites among the authors who pen them, and audiences also love a behind-the-scenes look at the literary world. It's fertile ground for novelists writing about a world they're familiar with, setting the stakes high in an imagined narrative. The authentic details an author can bring to such a story are what make them so spicy and alluring as they blend reality and fiction. Verity is based on the worldwide best-selling novel of the same name by Hoover. Colleen Hoover is a trailblazer. ( Eric Charbonneau/Getty Images for Sony Pictures ) In 2012, Hoover was the first self-published author to top The New York Times bestseller list, which she did again with Verity in 2018, and is a pioneer of modern indie publishing. She has since had a great deal of mainstream success. Verity was Hoover's first thriller. She had already authored 16 romance books prior to that and amassed millions of fans. In adapting the novel, director Michael Showalter aimed to produce a film as closely aligned with the book as possible. "The book is a big hit, people love it, so let's make a movie out of the book," Showalter said. "My approach was to do it the way it was in the book wherever possible. "Let people see what a true adaptation would look and feel like and honour that." events.title: G7 to release millions of barrels of oil and diesel after Trump threat
events.summary: The G7 has announced 100 million barrels of oil and diesel will be released to ease supply concerns that have caused prices to skyrocket. It includes a "substantial release" of diesel within 20 days, with discussions around "additional diesel releases as necessary", G7 leaders said in a statement. The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would begin immediately and would last for four months. Under the measures, which come after US President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports , there will not be any "export restrictions on energy and energy products" between G7 members. The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings. Donald Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market. That would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere. On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately." His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar. Speaking later at the White House, Trump said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table". Referring to the decision by the G7 to release fuel from reserves, he added that "what Europe did was a great thing." "Europe has a lot of diesel and they're going to be making a major world contribution - and so are we," he said. "And we're not going to be doing the export ban, we're going to be doing what we're supposed to do." Trump had first said he backed a diesel export ban early last week, and was still considering it on Thursday, as his administration put pressure on Europe to tap its supplies. Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food. Emmanuel Macron chaired a meeting of G7 leaders to agree the release of fuel reserves Following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the co-ordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA). The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks". Macron said the co-ordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point". In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a co-ordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners." It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly. The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73. Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen. "Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said. European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China. The G7 leaders said they will also co-ordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular. Watch: Why did Trump threaten to ban US diesel exports? Avoiding a ban on US diesel exports will offer significant relief to countries which are reliant on imports of the fuel, including the UK, where prices at the pump topped £2 a litre for the first time on Friday . Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of those imports coming from the US. The US is one of the world's leading diesel suppliers, with domestic refineries churning out roughly four to five million barrels every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA). Americans consume about 3.6 million barrels of that.

events.title: Scoop: Trump's top national security aides meet secretly at Camp David on Iran, Yemen
events.summary: President Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Friday to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen, three U.S. officials told Axios. Why it matters: The highly unusual meeting was not announced by the Trump administration. The last time a similar meeting took place was in June 2025, just days before Israel went to war against Iran. Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance chaired the meeting, the officials said. Among the other participants were Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA director John Ratcliffe and chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine. "Things were decided or at least deeply discussed," one of the officials said, referring to the crisis in the Middle East. The White House declined to comment. Driving the news: With negotiations stalled, President Trump is considering resuming major combat operations in Iran. "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said on Thursday. At the same time, Trump is being asked to join Saudi Arabia's planned offensive against the Houthis in Yemen. The Saudis are urging the president to conduct airstrikes against the Houthis. Trump has been leaning against it, but U.S. officials say he could change his mind. What he's saying: On Friday afternoon, while his advisers were at Camp David, Trump was asked by reporters what his next move on Iran will be. "If I told you, you would have a major story," he said. "But you will see. It is working out very well. Iran is not doing well."

events.title: Saudis plan major offensive against the Houthis, but U.S. won't join for now
events.summary: Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces are planning a major counteroffensive against Iran-backed Houthis in the coming days — an effort to push them away from areas on the Red Sea coast that control the Strait of Bab al-Mandeb, two U.S. officials say. Why it matters: For the second time in recent weeks, the U.S. rebuffed Saudi pleas to join the operation and conduct airstrikes. But U.S. officials say that could change if the operation runs into problems. The Bab al-Mandeb Strait is a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports. Control over it gives the Houthis and their Iranian backer a powerful new point of leverage over the U.S., its Gulf allies and the world economy. Driving the news: In recent weeks, the Houthis took over key areas of the southern Red Sea coast that control the strait. They also increased missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia. The Saudis retaliated with airstrikes against Houthi targets. Behind the scenes: A U.S. official said the Saudis have been planning the operation for weeks and that plans were approved by Saudi leadership several days ago. The operation will include ground forces loyal to the internationally recognized government in Yemen with Saudi air cover. On Thursday, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid Bin Salman called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to brief him on the planned operation and ask again for U.S. airstrikes against Houthi targets, the U.S. official said. A U.S. official said that the U.S. "is not going to take kinetic action for now." Last week, President Trump was close to ordering a strike on the Houthis after a request from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS), but eventually decided to hold off . Between the lines: Trump is caught between wanting to help his friend and ally MBS, and avoiding getting entangled in a new front in the Middle East. The U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also had serious reservations about launching strikes in Yemen and saw it as a distraction from its focus on Iran, a U.S. official said. Zoom in: U.S. officials say the U.S. military is helping the Saudis with everything short of direct combat, mainly intelligence and targeting data. One U.S. official said that in the last two weeks, the U.S. military provided the Saudis with more than 200 Houthi targets to strike. The official said the strikes significantly increased pressure on the Houthis.

events.title: Complaint over senior NT public servant who ran private NDIS provider
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Senior NT public servant was sole director of private NDIS company in Alice Springs for years Kudzai Mutsunge ran the NDIS business Life Aspects while holding senior roles in the NT Department of Children and Families. ( ABC News Graphics: Jess Henderson ) A senior public servant responsible for child and family support in Central Australia was simultaneously running a National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) provider company in Alice Springs. The Department of Children and Families has confirmed it forwarded a complaint about her involvement in the NDIS provider Life Aspects to an integrity process. The status of the process remains unclear. Documents obtained by the ABC show the department has recently strengthened its internal conflict of interest procedures, especially for staff with the power to influence NDIS referrals. A senior Northern Territory public servant responsible for child and family services in Central Australia spent nearly three years as the sole director of a private National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) provider in Alice Springs, and for 15 months also owned a 50 per cent stake in the business's parent company. The Department of Children and Families plays a significant role in the NDIS system in the NT, with the most recent figures from 2024 showing more than 300 children in its care had active NDIS plans. An ABC investigation has confirmed public servant Kudzai Mutsunge ran the NDIS business Life Aspects while holding senior roles in the Department of Children and Families, and held shares in the business's parent company, Japhin The Teacher Pty Ltd, from December 2024 to February 2026. Life Aspects is registered to provide a range of disability services, including assistance with independent living and support coordination, an area that involves arranging other providers for people with disability. Kudzai Mutsunge was the sole director of Life Aspects for almost three years. ( Supplied ) The ABC has seen no evidence that any child in the care of the department was a Life Aspects client. The department has referred a complaint about a potential conflict of interest to an internal integrity process. Ms Mutsunge wound up her directorship and shareholding in Life Aspects earlier this year, one week before an anonymous complaint was sent to the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission in March. A separate complaint went to the Department of Children and Families in August, from the Alice Springs-based Disability Advocacy Service (DAS). On August 21, the department told the service it had referred the information "through the appropriate internal integrity processes" and was coordinating with the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) "where relevant". The outcome of that process, if any, is unknown. In response to questions from the ABC, the department declined to say whether Ms Mutsunge had declared a potential conflict of interest or sought approval for outside work, saying it could not comment on individual employment or conduct matters. Kudzai Mutsunge ran the NDIS business Life Aspects while holding senior roles in the Department of Children and Families. ( ABC News: James Elton ) The ABC understands Ms Mutsunge quit the department on September 11. Ms Mutsunge said she did not "endorse or agree to the allegations or characterisations" put to her by the ABC about whether her roles presented a potential conflict of interest, and said she could not respond to further questions within the timeframe provided. Under the NT public service code of conduct, employees must declare any perceived, potential or actual conflicts of interest in writing to their chief executive. The department's acting chief executive Karen Broadfoot said it had "zero tolerance" for a failure to declare a conflict. Ms Broadfoot said that where integrity matters involved the NDIS, the department would also coordinate with the Australian Federal Police when relevant. The NDIA said it could not comment on ongoing investigations. DAS chief executive Scott Richardson said government officials needed to be held to a higher standard on potential NDIS conflicts, to ensure they "don't have access to participant information that they could then benefit from, or family could benefit from". DAS chief executive Scott Richardson says government officials should be held to a higher standard on potential NDIS conflicts. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) In a meeting in March, Ms Mutsunge reportedly told DAS staff that she was "operationally removed" from placement decisions, and denied any role in referring children to NDIS providers.

events.title: Golf club spends $30k on water changes, only for policy to change
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mowbray Golf Club spends $30k on water changes, only for TasWater to change policy General manager Hayden Roberts says the club has taken a financial hit for no reason. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) Businesses and sporting clubs faced significant bill increases from July 1 after a TasWater policy change on sewerage charges. Some decided to change their water connections, on the advice of TasWater, only for the billing system to then be changed again. One golf club is calling for compensation after spending $30,000 on changes that have now been made void following the policy change. A golf club in Launceston is calling for compensation from TasWater after spending an estimated $30,000 on water infrastructure works in response to billing changes, which were then essentially reversed. Mowbray Golf Club saw its water bill double from $20,000 to about $40,000 due to a TasWater policy change to charge based on the size of a water pipe connection, rather than sewerage usage, from July 1. The charge was based on the club's 100-millimetre connection, which it says it only uses in drought conditions and instead relies on its own storage for irrigation. In response, the club decided to sever the 100mm connection and connect its clubhouse and other services to its 50mm connection at significant cost. The club says it decided to sever its 100mm connection on the advice of TasWater. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) It increased fees for its members by 10 per cent to help pay for the works. Club general manager Hayden Roberts said they chose to go ahead with the works after being told by TasWater that reducing connection size was the easiest method. "I know we're not the only ones that have done such," he said. On Friday, TasWater announced a change in response to concerns from businesses and sporting clubs. It would take fixed sewerage charges from $20,000 to under $1,000 and charge 100mm connections as 20mm connections, with refunds offered for bills paid since July 1. The change came too late for Mowbray Golf Club, however. "I think it's only reasonable at this point that TasWater remediates these situations, whether it be credit or an outright refund of works completed. "We've actually lost an asset in the process of this removal of connection." TasWater says changes had 'unintended consequences' TasWater contacted the club in response to the policy change but had not made assurances regarding compensation. Callan Paske from TasWater says the changes had unintended consequences. ( ABC News ) TasWater general manager of customers and community Callan Paske said the water authority was aware of other clubs and businesses that had made changes to their connections based on TasWater advice. "We're working with those impacted clubs to ensure that we can work through what the final solution is for them," he said. The change in sewerage charging followed an inquiry by the Tasmanian Economic Regulator, which required TasWater to move from an equivalent charging method to a fixed and variable method. This is similar to methods used in other states. Mr Paske said it had disproportionately impacted sporting clubs and businesses, which was addressed by the change announced on Friday. "What this shows is that in any tariff reform there is nuance and we need to fix those outlier impacts that are in unintended consequences of major change," he said. Water infrastructure challenges remain TasWater again faces a challenge in how to fund upgrades to its aging infrastructure. The changes have hit its bottom line by between $7 million and $14 million, according to Mr Paske. "We've got aging infrastructure, failing pipes, we've got growth that we need to cater for, and we've got environmental impacts that we're having that are not what Tasmanians want to see," he said. The change came following discussions between TasWater, the economic regulator, councils and the state government. Premier Jeremy Rockliff said it was a "significant and lasing outcome" for businesses and sporting clubs. Shadow treasurer Dean Winter said the government had the power to veto TasWater's corporate plan, and questioned why this had not occurred following successive significant price increases.
