events.title: How employees forced OpenAI’s president to back down
events.summary: The Scoop On June 1, OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon gave employees a preview of a blog post denying the company had any connection to Leading the Future, a super PAC established to defend AI from regulation. OpenAI president Greg Brockman’s support for the super PAC “has been in a personal capacity, not on behalf of the company,” Kwon wrote in an internal Slack message. Not everyone on his staff bought it. One OpenAI employee took to Slack to warn of a dangerous trade-off: The company’s aggressive political activity threatened to drive researchers to Anthropic, and hamstring OpenAI in the all-out race to recursively self-improving AI. The post earned 24 “agree” reactions and a solitary eyes emoji. The next day, Kwon gave ground to a different internal critic: The company, he said on Slack, was “taking reputational hits.” They had drawn “some clear public lines,” but “I wish we’d done it even sooner.” Ten days after Kwon’s post, Brockman backed out of the second half of his public $50 million commitment, saying he felt “terrible about the fact that LTF keeps reflecting on the company” in a post first reported by The New York Times. Brockman’s message received 40 hearts, five checkmarks, and three thank-you emojis. The episode, part of a set of Slack messages shared with Semafor, offers a window into the complex internal politics of the handful of companies shaping the global future of artificial intelligence. Outsiders observing the tribal world of San Francisco frontier labs often see OpenAI as the “accelerationist” cousin to the safety-oriented Anthropic. The rare glimpse inside the company’s Slack illustrates a more complex reality: Many of OpenAI’s developers, engineers, and researchers — whom the company is fighting to keep in intense talent wars whose bidders also include Meta, Google, and an array of startups — aren’t sanguine about unregulated AI. And they dislike being associated with the political group’s aggressive tactics. A spokeswoman for OpenAI declined to comment. One employee initially placated by Kwon’s post followed up two days later flagging that Brockman’s money would be used to fund an X account the employee described as “an LTF sockpuppet ( confirmed here ) that posts stuff like “ [sam altman is] a caterpillar that murders insects and stitches their dismembered body parts onto its back as armor .” (Twenty-two other employees responded, “WTF.“) A source familiar with the situation told Semafor that employee pushback was definitely part of Brockman’s decision, but that he had his own qualms that began with LTF targeting New York Assemblymember Alex Bores, an AI safety advocate running for Congress in New York. The person said that Brockman had expected the PAC to focus more on supporting allied candidates. The people running LTF appeared not to understand the complex internal dynamics of frontier safety policy — and how the whole industry would react to attacking someone running on that platform. At different points, the person added, Brockman gave pointed feedback to LTF; the source noted they hadn’t heard of the PAC attacking candidates since Bores. Since then, the PAC has overwhelmingly donated to front-runners in congressional races. And candidates LTF has endorsed or implicitly supported have come out in favor of a bill from Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar that would pause frontier AI development and criminalize attempting to build superintelligence, OpenAI’s stated goal . Leading the Future LTF launched in August 2025, well before AI became a major public issue. The group boasted more than $100 million in commitments, with $50 million to come from Brockman and his wife Anna. OpenAI’s global affairs chief Chris Lehane had helped set up the PAC, which followed a model he pioneered for the crypto industry. OpenAI sought to characterize the PAC as a totally independent entity, but employees — encouraged by critics on X — were skeptical. Staff were complaining about the connection in February, Wired reported, and Transformer reported that employees confronted Lehane in a meeting in May, pushing the company to explain its relationship with LTF. Kwon’s June 1 Slack message sought to defuse the controversy. “Many have posted questions,” he wrote, about the nature of the relationship between OpenAI and LTF. At the end of the multi-paragraph message, he concluded, “Thank you to everyone who has given feedback on this topic and pushed for a stronger company statement, in particular” before tagging three employees. It worked — for about an hour. More than 80 employees reacted with approving emojis, and the first reply was excited and appreciative. But then others questioned the group’s independence, highlighted LTF’s controversial and backfiring track record, and worried about the super PAC’s toxic effect on OpenAI’s brand and retention of senior researchers. The messages were shared with Semafor on the condition that they not be quoted directly out of concern that employees would feel uncomfortable seeing their messages reproduced verbatim, potentially chilling future Slacktivism. The dispute flared up again on June 11. One worker posted a Transformer article in which the director of LTF’s sister lobbying group, Build American AI (BAAI), which does not disclose its donors, texted journalist Veronica Irwin, “For this project I’m funded by four separate entities … OpenAI is just one of them” (OpenAI told Irwin and other journalists that the company had not provided funding to the groups). Just over an hour later, Brockman weighed in for the first time, denying the story’s claim that OpenAI backed BAAI and assuring staff that he’d given nothing to the organization (though as employees noted later in the thread, LTF gives money to BAAI). He then apologized for how LTF reflected on the company and abandoned his additional $25 million donation. Initially, responses in the thread under Kwon’s post ping-ponged between appreciation and recrimination, with approving Slack reactions hovering in the 20s and 30s for each variety. But skepticism and pointed questions mounted. A day later, Kwon weighed in again, addressing a disappointed employee. “I generally agree with what you’re saying, including the part about taking reputational hits for their activities. This is one of the reasons it made sense for us to draw some clear public lines about what we don’t condone. I wish we’d done it even sooner,” he wrote. “I don’t think we are asking people to believe that separation of scope and control means no accountability. I can’t speak for Greg but it does seem like LTF is in the process of adjusting. I interpret that as accountability in action.” Kwon also noted that Brockman had only provided “a fraction” of LTF’s funding. “Critics stick it on him / us because we are visible, and what that means is that we have to be even more visible about our own things,” he wrote. “That includes what we’re for and the types of political tactics we do not condone. events.title: Fishers warn snapper, kingfish prices could soar under proposed catch limits
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Snapper, yellowtail kingfish price could soar under proposed catch limits Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Fishers say stricter limits would see snapper and kingfish prices rise. ( ABC Coffs Coast: Claire Simmonds ) Stricter limits have been proposed for snapper and yellowtail kingfish to help rebuild stocks in NSW fisheries. Commercial and recreational fishers are opposed to the changes. The NSW government has extended the consultation period for the proposed changes until February 15. Seafood shops and fishers are warning snapper and yellowtail kingfish could become unaffordable if catch limits are tightened. Both species are popular menu items, but stocks of kingfish in particular were described as "dangerously low" in a recent statement from the NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty. The state government has proposed reducing the annual kingfish catch from 250 tonnes to 120 tonnes a year. The snapper take would remain at 300 tonnes a year, but the proposal would include commercial monthly catch limits and a bag limit of three, with only one over 70 centimetres for recreational fishers. Naeco Blue Seafood's Adam Hambley says he cannot see people willing to pay any more for snapper and kingfish. ( Supplied: Adam Hambley ) Adam Hambley, who owns a seafood shop in South Grafton in northern NSW, said stricter limits would lead to higher prices. "If we see a $5 increase on the whole fish, we're going to see a $20 increase in the fillet, so you're going to near $80-90 a kilo for snapper fillets… I don't believe that anyone here will pay that much," he said. On a regular day, Noel Gogerly would pull in up to 40 kilograms of snapper while commercially fishing at Tuncurry on the NSW mid north coast. Under the proposed reforms, he would be allowed 10 kilograms, which he estimated would cost him up to $300 a day. Fisherman Noel Gogerly says the changes could cost him hundreds of dollars a day. ( ABC News: Lauren Bohane ) Mr Gogerly said any fish thrown back were unlikely to survive due to internal damage caused by the pressure change when pulled from the deep ocean. "You're going to have snapper just laying on top of the water," he said. Charter operators and recreational fishers are also worried. Under the changes yellowtail kingfish limits would drop from five per person to one per boat. Charter fishing operator Craig McGill said the proposed changes would ruin his business. Craig McGill says if the proposed changes to catch limits for yellowtail kingfish are implemented it could destroy his business. ( ABC News: Supplied ) "That would probably be the end of me," he said. "I get four guys on board; for me to have to tell them that they've got to share one kingfish, or that one guy gets to take one kingfish and the others can't catch one … they all pay a premium to come charter fishing with me." Michael Mashado estimated the proposed changes would cost his tackle store in Eden, on the NSW far south coast, up to $200,000 in sales per year. "Nobody's going to come and buy the quantity of gear to go and catch one kingfish or three snapper," he said. Mr Mashado said fishing was one of the south coast's biggest tourism industries. Michael Mashado says the proposed changes could have a broader impact on local towns where fishing is a major tourist attraction. ( Supplied ) "If you look at a family that comes here with a big boat, they spend [money] in the tackle shop, they spend it at the pub, they spend it at the supermarket," he said. The DPIRD said the proposal aimed to allow historically depleted fish stocks to recover, while still allowing some commercial and recreational catch. "We know approximately recreational fishers take about 50 per cent of the catch, as do commercial fishers, for both of these species," DPIRD director of fisheries management Heath Folpp said. Public consultation on the proposed changes was extended until mid-February in response to industry concerns. Fishers have warned any snapper thrown back would likely not survive.

events.title: Big Bend border wall construction blocked by judge
events.summary: A federal judge blocked the Trump administration from pursuing border wall construction in the Big Bend region in Texas on Friday. The big picture: The construction inside the national park sparked local outrage and environmental concerns, with Friday's decision handing the Department of Homeland Security a loss in its quest to rapidly expand the Southwestern border wall. Driving the news: The administration is barred, for now, from building border barrier or infrastructure — or engaging in any " construction or ground disturbing activities" — in the Big Bend sector, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone said in a brief order . The administration paused border wall construction in the park back in August, with U.S. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott saying he'd visit and discuss with local stakeholders. DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Catch up quick: The local challengers urged the court to prevent the administration to restart construction, alleging the administration overstepped its authority on multiple fronts and warning of harm to the environment and recreation. "Once bulldozers clear vegetation, roads are cut into previously undeveloped terrain, lights mounted, and steel barrier infrastructure is effected, those qualities cannot be restored through monetary compensation or after-the-fact relief," they argued in an August motion. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: One Nation makes election promise to revive Victoria's timber sector
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts One Nation promises to revive Victoria's native timber industry but cannot cite the cost Topic: Forestry, Logging and Timber Industry One Nation has pledged to let loggers back into native forests in Victoria if it wins the state election. ( Supplied: Victorian National Parks Association ) One Nation has promised to resume native timber logging in Victoria if it wins the state election, but has not said how the policy would be funded or achieved. The party says its policy also includes provisions to protect old-growth forest and native habitat. The Victorian Coalition is finalising its timber policy ahead of the election. Two years after sawmills fell silent in Victoria's native forests, the logging industry could be revived if there is a change in government at the November election. While the Coalition and One Nation have committed to restarting native forest logging, which was shut down by the Labor government in January 2024 , it is unclear what it would take to get the industry back on its feet. One Nation's Narracan candidate Ben Lucas said the policy supported country-of-origin labelling laws on timber and wood products, and a self-funding model in which harvest revenue supported forest improvement and fire prevention. He said the party would consult industry leaders and audit the millions of dollars Labor spent on the logging industry transition fund before settling on a new approach. He said the party would incentivise the use of Australian timber in construction through a "local wood first" policy in government procurement and would ensure timber was extracted using a selective harvesting model. "You can't take away the forestry industry from a town like Noojee and replace the economy with a truffle festival once a year," Mr Lucas said. Pauline Hanson with Ben Lucas during a visit to Gippsland in August. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) But when pressed for details, Mr Lucas would not clarify how much it could cost or what would be involved in reopening native forests to logging. "This is a broad policy and it's very open-ended, but with clear guidelines on how we want to do it and why we want to do it," Mr Lucas said. "We've got the words on paper and if we get in, we can have some influence on how that happens." The Liberal-National Coalition is still working through the details of its policy, but Nationals leader Danny O'Brien previously vowed to restore native forest logging. Nationals MP Melina Bath, whose portfolio includes timber, said the coalition was finalising its policy but also backed a return to logging. "We will be announcing a suite of packages and policies in relation to this," Ms Bath said. "They're still going through a parliamentary process and we make sure … that we've done our costings correctly." Victoria's Regional Development Minister Michaela Settle said restarting native forestry under a Coalition or One Nation government would cost Victorians. "Labor is backing forestry workers into new jobs, growing local plantation timber and keeping forestry skills and experience in our forests to reduce bushfire risk and support better forest management," she said. According to a 2026 Victorian Auditor-General's report, the Victorian government's decision to shut down the industry affected 1,000 workers and 200 businesses. It found the Victorian government spent $1.5 billion on transition arrangements and 87 per cent of workers had retired or found new jobs. But it found many had moved into part-time, casual or contract roles and it was "not clear if workers' new jobs meet their needs or are sustainable". Ms Bath said a revived industry would "look different to what the Labor government shut down in 2024" and would need to overcome challenges, such as rebuilding the workforce. Orbost District Chamber of Commerce and Industry secretary Garry Squires said any move to revive the forestry sector would be well received in the regions. Garry Squires says rural towns like Orbost would love to see a return of native forest logging. ( ABC Gippsland: Natasha Schapova ) "The reality is you can't just start big harvesting operations right across Victoria in a hurry, but start off slowly with thinning operations," he said. "We've got this great resource of eucalypt forests across Victoria. Victoria has more than 380,000 hectares of plantation forest, totalling more than 20 per cent of Australia's plantations. Victoria also produces about one-quarter of Australia's plantation-grown wood, at a gross value of about $550 million each year.

events.title: Qld government rejects petition to change stop signs to give way
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Queensland government rejects petition to change all stop signs to give-way signs Topic: State and Territory Government The petitioner argued stop signs offer "no safety significance". ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) The Queensland government has rejected a petition to swap all stop signs with give-way signs in the state. A petition signed by 391 Queenslanders argued that stop signs provide "no safety significance" and cost drivers more in fuel. Transport Minister Brent Mickelberg said the safety benefits outweigh any operational impacts associated with stopping. The Queensland government has rejected a petition to change every stop sign in Queensland into a give-way sign. The petition was signed by 391 Queensland residents and was tabled to the government late August. It argued "requiring vehicles to come to a complete stop is almost always of no safety significance". "Collectively, it wastes a significant amount of fuel or electrical energy," the petitioner said. Minister for Transport and Main Roads, Brent Mickelberg, responded to the petition confirming the Crisafulli government would not be making the change. The petition was signed by 391 Queenslanders. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) The petitioner said petrol, diesel and LPG powered vehicles use more fuel to come to a complete stop. They also stated stop signs could create more traffic accidents by drivers rear ending cars that have come to a complete halt. "It is important to note up front that stop and give-way signs are not interchangeable traffic controls," Mr Mickelberg wrote in his response. "They serve different road safety and traffic management functions and are installed in accordance with nationally recognised engineering standards and traffic control guidelines." He said stop signs are more often used on intersections where visibility is restricted, in an attempt to limit crashes. The minister admitted bringing vehicles to a complete stop "may result in some additional fuel or energy consumption compared with giving way". Brent Mickelberg said the signs are not interchangeable traffic controls. ( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) But he wrote that despite that, the safety benefits outweigh any operational impacts associated with stopping. "I recognise that unnecessary traffic controls can impose costs on road users and that traffic control devices should be proportionate to the level of risk. "Installation of stop signs is based on an assessment of site-specific conditions, including sight distance, intersection geometry, traffic volumes and safety performance. He finished his response by reminding any Queenslander that if they feel an intersection may be incorrectly signed, to contact the relevant council. events.title: Christa Pike survived lethal injection. How your state carries out executions
events.summary: Data: Death Penalty Information Center ; Note: New Hampshire abolished the death penalty but retains one prisoner on death row; Map: Erin Davis/Axios Christa Pike 's survival after two lethal injection doses has put state execution protocols nationwide under new scrutiny. The big picture: How prisoners are executed varies by state , with lethal injection, electrocution, lethal gas and firing squads among the methods authorized. Lethal injections are the most common U.S. execution method , accounting for roughly 89% of the 1,683 executions carried out since 1976, per the Death Penalty Information Center . By the numbers: More than two dozen states have lethal injection as a primary method. Lethal gas is authorized in Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Oklahoma and Wyoming. Electrocution is allowed in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Tennessee. Firing squad is allowed in Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah. Idaho is the only state where it is the primary method. Context: Some states let prisoners choose among the different execution methods. Zoom out: The Supreme Court requires states to keep the death penalty only for the most heinous murders. Pike , convicted of killing a classmate three decades ago, survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs earlier this week in what would have been the first execution of a woman in Tennessee in 200 years. Pike was still alive as of Friday, remaining on a ventilator and unconscious, AP reports.

events.title: Australia's power supply forecasts have never been rosier. Experts are worried
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts The 'fantasy' underpinning Australia's rosy power supply forecasts Experts fear the way Australia's energy operator assesses future power reliability obscures problems. ( ABC News ) In the chaos and complexity of energy in Australia, one topic has always cut through the noise: blackouts. Or, more precisely, the need to avoid blackouts at seemingly any cost, so untenable are the political consequences. It is for this reason that so much of Australia's energy planning goes towards making sure there is always enough capacity to keep the lights on. "When people say, 'Oh, we've breached the reliability standard, therefore blackouts', the reliability standard that we have is incredibly, incredibly tight," Tristan Edis of Green Energy Markets says. Powerlines are a much bigger source of outages than lack of energy. ( ABC News: Keana Naughton ) To be exact, Australia's "reliability standard" prescribes that consumers should expect their electricity needs to be met 99.998 per cent of the time. In other, albeit simplified, words, no more than 0.002 per cent — or 10 minutes — of their demand should go unserved across an entire year. This does not include power lost because of outages on the poles-and-wires network, a much more common occurrence. For more than two decades now, one document has been central to ensuring Australia's onerous reliability standards are maintained. It's called the "electricity statement of opportunities" and it's handled by the body that runs the country's biggest electricity system — the Australian Energy Market Operator. Dylan McConnell from the University of New South Wales says it's called a statement of opportunities for a reason. He says it shows where there are likely to be supply gaps in the decade ahead, thereby signalling where new energy projects would be most needed. "It says everything will be fine if we do these things," McConnell says. "It's essentially supposed to provide guidance to the market on where reliability issues may emerge in the future. The cost of building wind projects has ballooned in the past five years. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) There's just one problem, according to McConnell, Edis and several other respected energy market observers canvassed by the ABC. The statement of opportunities is now counting on projects that may not be built on time. Many, they say, may never be built at all. And they warn that fundamental changes to the way the reliability assessment is carried out are hiding major problems with Australia's energy transition. "At the moment, it's probably the case that we're downplaying some pretty significant risks and challenges ahead of us, and that has consequences," McConnell says. Among those consequences, he says, are higher wholesale energy costs in the event forecast generation and storage does not arrive in time or is simply not built. Partly, he says this is a function of supply and demand. If there's less supply than was forecast by the end of the decade, McConnell says prices will inevitably increase to reflect that scarcity. Equally, he says the market operator will turn to emergency measures to ensure supply is sufficient. These measures could include paying big energy users a premium to turn down or turn off their use at times of stress on the system. Or it could be shelling out small fortunes to the operators of diesel-fired generators to provide critical back-up power. Either way, McConnell says, the measures are not cheap. On top of this, he says governments themselves would step into the breach to stave off any shortfalls in supply. The lever most likely to be pulled would be the extension of ageing coal-fired power plants such as Yallourn in Victoria and Eraring in New South Wales. "At the end of the day, blackouts and unreliable electricity is politically untenable," he says. AEMO did not always publish such a rose-tinted view of reliability. If anything, Edis of Green Energy Markets says the agency used to take a much harder line that was arguably too conservative in its assumptions. He says it effectively underestimated forecast supply because of "silly rules". The next coal-fired domino to fall will be Victoria's Yallourn in 2028. ( ABC News: Freya Michie ) "And now it's probably gone too far the other way," Edis says. Key to the change is the way AEMO includes projects in the reliability outlook. Historically, he says it was only those projects which were either existing or committed that got a guernsey. Put another way, the plants had to be in the ground already or under construction to be used in the forecast.

events.title: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil in bid to curb soaring prices
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts G7 countries to release 100 million barrels of diesel and oil to curb fuel prices The G7 talks were convened by Emmanuel Macron after a conversation with US President Donald Trump. ( Reuters: Axel Schmidt ) G7 countries are set to release up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil reserves. It comes amid soaring fuel prices and after clashes between European leaders and Donald Trump. The US president is under political pressure in America over rising energy costs, which have been sparked by the US-Israeli war with Iran. G7 countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from their reserves over four months to ease global energy supply concerns. The leaders also pledged not to impose export restrictions on energy products. The announcement came after G7 leaders held a video conference, chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron, as the United States stepped up pressure on Europe to release strategic reserves and threatened a diesel export ban. The talks, convened by Mr Macron after a conversation with US President Donald Trump, focused on coordinating a response to soaring fuel prices among the other G7 economies of Britain, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. The US-Israeli war with Iran has sent energy prices skyrocketing, coming back to bite Mr Trump at home with high fuel costs that have become a key issue ahead of midterm congressional elections in a month. Analyst warns diesel prices could top $4 a litre Analyst warns export ban the most worrying development since the Middle East conflict began. Mr Trump has floated the possibility of banning US exports of diesel, which is used in farming machinery, trucks and other hauling vehicles, an alarming prospect for the EU, which relies heavily on fossil fuel imports. The seven countries agreed to a coordinated release through the International Energy Agency (IEA) of 100 million barrels "to begin immediately over four months, including a front-loaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days", the leaders said in a statement released by Mr Macron's office. Emmanuel Macron, flanked by two French ministers, spoke after convening the G7 meeting. ( Reuters: Ludovic Marin. ) They also said there would be no ban on diesel exports between them. "We reaffirm our commitment to refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products between G7 countries and call on all producers to refrain from imposing bans that could exacerbate market tensions," the leaders said. Mr Trump said European countries had agreed to release a "massive amount" of diesel from their reserves. "The process will begin immediately," he posted on his Truth Social network. Earlier the EU pushed back hard against US threats to impose a diesel export ban, something Mr Macron also warned against during his conversation with Mr Trump. A taxi driver says he is driving 12 hours a day to make ends meet amid rising fuel prices. "We fully reject any ban on diesel," European Commission spokeswoman Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said, warning it would "undermine our trust in the United States as a reliable partner". The flurry of diplomatic activity came a day after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent cranked up the pressure on European nations. The 32 members of the IEA agreed last March to unlock 400 million barrels of oil from reserves, their largest release ever.

events.title: It's October, but Republicans are already retreating in N.C.
events.summary: With one month until Election Day, some big GOP spenders are giving up on North Carolina and prioritizing other states. Why it matters: It's a sign that Republicans believe Michael Whatley can't win and that the seat will flip to Democrats, who need four pickups to regain control of the Senate. Driving the news: Several key Republican super PACs have canceled October ad campaigns in North Carolina as polls show Whatley several points behind former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper. By the numbers: Last month, Republicans spent $53 million on North Carolina's Senate race, while Democrats spent $44 million, the firm AdImpact tracked . PACs backing the candidates had reserved ads totaling over $33 million for each candidate in October. Yes, but: That calculation was made on Thursday. The latest: On Friday, Senate Leadership Fund said it would redirect money meant for Whatley, Semafor and other national outlets reported. It's a major blow for the campaign. Senate Leadership Fund dropped $17 million on North Carolina in September, nearly a third of Whatley's total, according to AdImpact analysis. The PAC paid for the misleading ad that tied Cooper to a South Carolina murder suspect's release from prison, The News & Observer reported. What they're saying: Whatley campaign spokesperson DJ Griffin said they were betting on undecided voters breaking for Republicans. "We feel confident we have the resources to highlight Career Politician Roy Cooper's 40 Years of Failures and win in November," Griffin said in an email. An unidentified source told Semafor it was Senate Leadership Fund's job to "maintain the majority and this move reflects the most effective and efficient use of resources." State of play: Neither Prosperity Action nor Old North Action plan to spend in North Carolina in October, Politico reported. Money is needed in races in Kansas, Texas and Alaska, a GOP operative told the publication, calling Whatley "a good man who took one for the team." Between the lines: The reduced spending could affect down-ballot Republicans in North Carolina. Several congressional races and North Carolina General Assembly seats are in play. The bottom line: It's been over a decade since a Democrat represented North Carolina in the U.S. Senate, and Republicans are bracing for that to change this election cycle.

events.title: Environmental groups sue Trump administration over eased vehicle fuel economy rules
events.summary: A group of environmental organizations sued the Trump administration on Friday over its recent relaxation of key vehicle fuel economy rules, a move the group says will make vehicles less efficient, contributing to more pollution and increasing gas cons... DETROIT -- A group of environmental organizations sued the Trump administration on Friday over its recent relaxation of key vehicle fuel economy rules, a decision that the group says will make vehicles less efficient, contribute to more pollution and increase gas consumption. On Monday, the Trump administration lowered Corporate Average Fuel Economy, or CAFE, standards that set out how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline. The announcement was made as the Trump administration negotiated with Iran over reopening the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's oil passes through the strait on a typical day, and the fight over its control has sent energy prices soaring across the globe. The environmental groups filed the petition for review Friday in the U.S. Court of Appeals against Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Jonathan Morrison, the administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which sets the rules. “We’re taking the Trump administration to court for this reckless rollback that prioritizes Big Oil and automaker profits over American families,” Katherine Garcia, director of Sierra Club’s Clean Transportation for All program, said in a statement. “It is unlawful for Trump to turn back the clock on fuel-efficient cars, forcing drivers to waste more money on gas and communities to breathe toxic air.” The Center for Biological Diversity, the Conservation Law Foundation, the Environmental Defense Fund and Public Citizen, along with the Sierra Club, filed the suit. The Transportation Department and NHTSA earlier this week lowered the standards to an industry fleetwide average of roughly 34.9 miles per gallon for passenger cars and light trucks in the 2031 model year, down from a projected 50.4 miles per gallon under rules set by the Biden administration. The administration said the change would provide Americans more vehicle choice and encourage consumers to buy newer, safer vehicles. Experts say reducing fuel economy requirements in vehicles does not necessarily lower their cost, nor would it automatically translate to new vehicle sales. Duffy said the new rule also cuts the “illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want.” There has never been a mandate that manufacturers sell EVs or Americans buy them; the rules and other cleaner vehicle standards incentivized automakers to sell a mix of electric, hybrid electric and increasingly-efficient gasoline-powered vehicles. When reached for comment, a DOT spokesperson referred to statements made by Duffy: "This administration understands the freedom of every American family starts with affordable cars. That’s why our new standards will make that dream more achievable by letting auto manufacturers produce the cars that fit families’ needs at a lower price.” Auto companies and industry groups broadly welcomed Monday's change, saying the rules under the Biden administration were too stringent and did not benefit consumers. But environmental organizations decried the changes. Trump administration set to roll out lower fuel economy standards for cars, light trucks Co-pilot in FlyDubai attack is identified, and other Mideast developments A gut punch in Ohio: Nearly 1,400 laid off at truck factory just days before Trump rally “With gas prices at historic highs, Trump picked the worst possible time to roll back federal mileage standards,” David Pettit, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity’s Climate Law Institute, said in a statement. “Oil companies will profit from less efficient cars, but drivers will take a hit to their wallets and our kids will breathe dirtier air. We’ll all pay the price for more tailpipe pollutants spewing everywhere from playgrounds to wild places. We’re asking the courts to put a stop to this callous giveaway to Big Oil and Big Auto.” Gas prices have hovered around $4.50 and diesel has hit unprecedented heights in recent weeks, according to AAA. The DOT said Monday that the rule would cut yearly oil consumption in 2050 by about 1.3 billion barrels as compared with yearly oil consumption in 2024, but NHTSA had estimated the 2024 standards would have saved 14 billion gallons of gasoline from being burned by that year. Fuel economy requirements have been in place since the 1970s energy crisis, and over time, have led to improved average efficiency in vehicles. President Donald Trump has made a number of moves to undercut cleaner vehicles in the U.S. These include eliminating electric vehicle tax credits ; scrapping vehicle emissions standards ; repealing the fines for automakers who don’t meet mileage rules; and attempting to block the nation’s EV charging buildout .

events.title: Senate crushes House on congressional work days
events.summary: Source: Ballotpedia, Congressional Record; Chart: Stef Kight/Axios The Senate is well on its way to claiming the congressional attendance trophy this year, spending 32 more weekdays in session so far than the House. Why it matters: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) have been torched by members for all the time off — not to mention Democrats, who taunt them for their truancy. The Senate left town late Wednesday — two weeks after its House counterparts — putting both chambers out of town until after the Nov. 3 midterms. "I suppose I left the House two years too soon," Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) told Axios, joking about how many fewer days the House has worked compared to the Senate this Congress. By the numbers: The Senate has been in session for 104 weekdays so far this year, compared with just 72 for the House, according to an analysis of congressional calendars by Ballotpedia and Axios. The Senate has spent nearly 664 hours in session, compared with about 378 hours for the House as of Sept. 14, according to data in the Congressional Record . The House isn't catching up anytime soon: Under the chambers' current calendars, the Senate is on pace to finish the year with about 126 weekdays in session, compared with 92 for the House. Zoom in: Some of the House's time off was unplanned. Johnson has repeatedly sent members home early when his razor-thin majority has run into trouble on the floor, or GOP rebels have blocked passage of a procedural "rule ." Decisions to cut D.C. workweeks short have been met with some backlash. "Canceling yet another day of votes is unacceptable," Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) wrote on X after Johnson canceled a session day. "The founders did not envision taking this much time off and still getting paid." The other side: Johnson repeatedly argues that his chamber has already done its job. "This House has been the second most productive in terms of legislation in the history of the institution since 1789," Johnson told reporters this month, saying the House had passed more than 900 pieces of legislation and roughly 700 were awaiting Senate action. Johnson's 900-plus figure includes resolutions that can't become law. The Washington Post found the House had passed 732 bills capable of becoming law through Aug. 31. By the numbers: The House passed more measures than the Senate (380 to 269), but the Senate held more "yea" or "nay" votes (231 to 216) between Jan. 3 and the end of August. House members introduced more legislation overall, but the Senate was more productive per capita — 22 pieces of legislation per senator compared to nine per House member. The House has passed 21 bills sent over by the Senate, and the Senate has passed 20 bills sent by the House. The Senate spends significant floor time confirming nominees — which is outside of the House's portfolio.

events.title: House Democrats want to win big. It could cost them.
events.summary: Democrats' dream election scenario risks becoming a nightmare as their candidates in Republican-leaning districts strain to assert their independence from party leadership. Why it matters: Add them to the sizable cohort of outspoken leftists promising to be a thorn in the side of House Democratic leaders, and you get all the ingredients for an unruly majority. "When I see things that I don't think are right, whether they're within my own party or within another party, I'm going to call it out," Jake Johnson, a Democratic House candidate in Minnesota, told Axios in an interview. Montana Democrat Sam Forstag, when asked about the approach he would take on Capitol Hill, said showing a willingness to work across the aisle and "buck your own party" have "got to be a part of it." "There is a tremendous amount of frustration with the D.C. political establishment, and ... a lot of cynicism that things aren't going to change," said Colorado candidate Eileen Laubacher. State of play: Democrats got an early taste last month when Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) repeatedly broke with party leadership on key procedural votes. The defections from a pair of independent-minded frontliners unlocked a new fear for House Democrats: That safe-seat progressives aren't the only rebellious freshmen they will have to worry about next year. It's a salient concern as Democrats put more Republican-leaning seats on their radar in anticipation of a "blue wave" on Election Day. There has been a huge spike in ads from Democrats in those districts repudiating their own party or the two-party system as a whole, Axios reported last week . What they're saying: "I will stand up to Republicans, I will also stand up to Democrats. I talk a lot about this," said Michigan swing-district candidate Christina Hines. Johnson said it's "no wonder people have historically low levels of confidence in Congress" because they "see a bunch of people put on red shirts and blue shirts ... and it's just not working." Forstag pointed to housing as an issue where he has broken with Democrats in his state, telling Axios: "When it comes to zoning reform, you know who I've seen be the biggest impediment to progress? Oftentimes, Democrats." "You bet your ass I'm going to work with Republicans," he said. Between the lines: This swing-district independent streak is bound to come in conflict with the rebellions that safe-seat insurgents are planning. Left-leaning Democratic lawmakers and candidates have told Axios they want votes on core policy issues such as Medicare for All, abolishing ICE and cutting off aid to Israel. The kind of candidate that gets elected to a seat President Trump carried by double digits in 2024 is not going to want to take those votes — in fact, they may be more likely to fund ICE and Israel. Yes, but: Some of these red-seat candidates are quite openly progressive and partisan. The common denominator: They're hearing voters' frustration about party leadership and, if elected, they would arrive on Capitol Hill with a mandate to shake up the system and remain independent. Missouri candidate Fred Wellman, who told Axios he is "very Democrat" and "fairly progressive," said he was "disappointed" that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) met with Jared Kushner in August. Wellman said he will "make a decision when I get there" about whether to vote for Jeffries as speaker and doesn't "intend to be a rubber stamp." Zoom in: Democratic operatives told Axios that this leadership-skeptic attitude extends, in some cases, to candidates not wanting party leaders to come campaign for them. "There's very little appetite for anyone in Democratic leadership," said one consultant of the battleground-district House campaigns they are working with. Matt Herdman, an adviser to Maine Democrat Matt Dunlap, offered Axios a curt response when asked if they would welcome Jeffries to their district: "They haven't offered and we haven't asked." The bottom line: None of this rebelliousness has thus far turned off the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which Jeffries and his leadership allies control. The House Democratic campaign arm has been spending heavily to support Gluesenkamp Perez even after some of her colleagues called for her to be cut off. Fittingly, Gluesenkamp Perez declared in a coordinated ad with the DCCC released Tuesday: "I don't answer to any political party or any president."

events.title: AI costs are rising for organizations, reports warn
events.summary: The AI bill is coming for governments and businesses, and no one knows whether the money will be there to pay it. Two new reports from consulting giants show how the AI adoption conversation has shifted from whether it works to whether the spending on it is sustainable, as pilot programs pile up and agentic applications take off. The debate over AI safety in recent weeks has somewhat dwarfed the still very urgent discourse over AI’s macroeconomic impacts. Those stakes were made clear in a Bain & Company report this week that found that the industry’s compute demand will require $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 — including about $4.2 trillion from new markets and products that don’t exist yet. At the same time, buyers of AI are coming under pressure. A McKinsey report focusing on American government entities — a large and fast-growing customer for enterprise AI — warned that the per-token price of AI is collapsing, but the total bill is rising , as agents require much more compute. For many governments, until now, “usage might have been essentially near-zero cost,” McKinsey Senior Partner and Global Public Sector Leader Tim Ward told me. Very soon, “it won’t be.” The coming IPOs from Anthropic and OpenAI will surely bring more debate over whether their revenue can catch up to the labs’ lofty valuations. But “ the complete disruption of the economy is all but certain, ” credit rating agency Egan-Jones wrote Wednesday, in a note titled . — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Amazon launches new data center commitments
events.summary: Amazon today announced new commitments to generate buy-in for US data centers and rebutted criticism about the facilities. The tech giant vowed to publish its energy and water use annually, and spend more than $1 billion over five years on free community college, trades training, and home energy-efficiency upgrades in data center counties. Desperate for compute, tech companies have been pouring resources into responding to community and political pushback to data centers, countering what they see as misinformation. In a roughly 3,000-word post, AWS CEO Matt Garman directly responded to what he described as “myths floating around,” including that the facilities consume too much water, drive up energy costs, and emit pollution. Some cities and towns across the US are ultimately earning concessions as hyperscalers come under pressure: Teachers in Louisiana got bonuses thanks to Meta, for example, and NorthPoint Development proposed giving $10,000 to every household in a Pennsylvania township. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Microsoft Digital Defense Report: How AI is reshaping the cybersecurity landscape
events.summary: Discover what’s coming to Microsoft Ignite, Nov 17-20, 2026. Register now. Insights from the 2026 Microsoft Digital Defense Report Every year, the Microsoft Digital Defense Report gives us an opportunity to step back from individual threats and look broadly at what Microsoft’s security and threat intelligence teams are seeing. Today, we released the 2026 Report , which reflects a security environment that continues to grow more interconnected. We see that across the report. Threat activity can span infrastructure, identities, applications, cloud environments, and software supply chains. AI systems and agents increasingly interact with data, tools, and business systems. And activity that looks incomplete in one part of an environment can become clearer when separate signals are considered together. That makes the connections across an environment increasingly relevant to how we understand both cyberthreats and defense. The pace of change also matters. AI models are becoming more capable, automation is expanding, and new connections are forming across the systems organizations rely on. These developments can change the speed and scale of security activity even as the underlying security fundamentals remain familiar. Several findings in this year’s report illustrate that. Threat actors are incorporating AI into reconnaissance, social engineering, malware and exploit development, and post-compromise activity. For now, much of their use remains focused on specific parts of existing attack workflows, even as more advanced applications of AI continue to develop. AI can give threat actors greater speed, scale, and ability to tailor activity more efficiently. We see that in social engineering, where AI can make campaigns more targeted, and in technical work, where automation can compress parts of the attack process. The underlying methods often remain familiar. People, identities, exposed systems, and trusted access continue to feature prominently in the threat activity Microsoft observes. AI is also becoming more connected to the systems and processes organizations already rely on. That brings another dimension to the security work. Securing AI as part of the enterprise Agents are a good example of these observations. They can interact with enterprise data, applications, APIs, and tools, with different levels of access and autonomy depending on how they are designed and deployed. Those connections are what allow agents to perform useful work, and they are also part of what security teams need to understand. That makes it increasingly important to look at AI as part of a broader system. A model may be one component, but its security also depends on the data it can reach, the tools it can use, the identities and permissions involved, and the infrastructure and services around it. The report looks at agent identity, appropriate access, authentication between agents, attribution, and the ability to revoke access. It also examines security considerations specific to AI, including prompt injection, memory, models and data, agent behavior, and the integrity of software and services around AI systems. There is a lot we are still learning as these technologies develop. Security teams do have a strong foundation to build from. Identity and authorization, data protection, least privilege, monitoring, testing, and secure software development all remain relevant. AI puts those disciplines into new systems and increasingly connected workflows. Advances in the application of AI toward code analysis are making it possible to examine software and identify weaknesses more effectively. That creates new opportunities to find vulnerabilities earlier and strengthen software before weaknesses are exploited. Those same advances can give threat actors more capable tools for vulnerability discovery and exploit development. This is an important area to watch as capabilities develop. AI is giving defenders new ways to find and address weaknesses while giving cyberattackers new ways to look for them. The work on both sides continues to advance. The same interconnectedness that shapes how activity moves across systems also shapes how defenders understand it. Security teams work with information from endpoints, identities, cloud environments, applications, email, networks, and threat intelligence. The report shows why those signals become more useful when they can be considered together. Threat activity spanning several systems may leave a pattern that no individual source shows on its own. In a more connected environment, the ability to relate activity across systems becomes an important part of understanding what is happening and where attention is needed. The same principle extends beyond an individual organization. Trusted sharing of intelligence and information across organizations and public-private partnerships can connect pieces of activity that no one organization sees on its own. AI can help with that work. Established techniques and repeatable tasks are increasingly candidates for automation, including bringing relevant information together and giving experienced defenders more capacity for deeper investigation. The discussion of red teaming in this year’s report captures the balance well. Connecting known information and running established techniques can increasingly be automated. Finding an undocumented attack path, or recognizing how weaknesses that appear unrelated fit together, continues to benefit from experienced operators staying close to the work. That balance will continue to evolve. There is substantial opportunity to use AI to help defenders work more effectively while preserving the human judgment, context, and expertise that remain essential to security work. The 2026 Microsoft Digital Defense Report looks across the threat landscape, cybercrime, resilience, and the relationships among technologies, identities, systems, and people. Taken together, those findings give us a broader view of the increasingly interconnected environment security teams are responsible for understanding and protecting. I encourage you to read the full report for a deeper look at the findings, data, and recommendations from Microsoft’s security and threat intelligence teams. Read the 2026 Digital Defense Report for the full findings, data, and recommendations. To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website. Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. Also, follow us on LinkedIn ( Microsoft Security ) and X ( @MSFTSecurity ) for the latest news and updates on cybersecurity. CVP & Deputy CISO, Customer Security Management Office October 1 4 min read Preparing governments for an era of interconnected cyber risk According to this year’s Microsoft Digital Defense Report, government agencies and services were the sector most impacted by cyber threats in 2026, accounting for 27% of observed activity, up from 17% in 2025.

events.title: Debt-saddled Argentina pitches 'golden passport' scheme to woo wealthy foreigners
events.summary: Argentina is putting a price on citizenship as President Javier Milei searches for dollars to help the country meet its debts BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- Argentina on Friday announced plans to offer citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for cash contributions or investments in government bonds, as libertarian President Javier Milei seeks new sources of dollars for the debt-burdened nation. Economy Minister Luis Caputo unveiled the so-called “golden passport” scheme at an investor event in Paris, saying applications are expected to open before the end of the year. Applicants have two options: make a nonrefundable $350,000 contribution to the Argentine Treasury or invest $800,000 in a new government bond that must be held for seven years. Contributions would increase depending on family size, with a family of four expected to pay $500,000, officials said. Securing dollars is critical for Milei as he prepares to seek reelection next year. Argentina’s Treasury faces nearly $25 billion in foreign-currency debt payments coming due in 2027. But having narrowed its financing options by holding off on a return to international bond markets , the government is searching for alternative sources of revenue. A consortium of investment firms advising the government estimated that the paid-citizenship program could raise up to $2.5 billion for Argentina if it receives the expected number of applicants. So-called “golden visa” programs have become increasingly common among cash-strapped countries battling to attract deep-pocketed foreigners, with about 60 nations offering residency privileges in exchange for one-off investments. U.S. President Donald Trump launched his own “gold card” program for the U.S. last year. Citizenship-for-investment programs go further, offering more rights and a passport that opens doors abroad. Only about a dozen countries have active programs, including small Caribbean island states. Argentina, a G-20 nation of 46 million people home to a vast Patagonian wilderness and culturally vibrant capital, is set to become the first South American country to join their ranks. “The Argentine passport is highly valued, accepted in more than 140 countries,” Caputo said, referring to destinations Argentines can visit without obtaining a visa in advance — from China and Russia to Europe’s Schengen area and most of Latin America. For wealthy people from countries that face visa restrictions, whether in Southeast Asia or the Arab world, Argentine citizenship could make it easier to travel and do business internationally, said Kristin Surak, a professor at the London School of Economics and author of “The Golden Passport: Global Mobility for Millionaires." "It’s not only the benefits that you get within Argentina,” she said. “You also get benefits globally in terms of where you can go.” The clientele of such programs has shifted since the COVID-19 pandemic, industry experts say, with more Americans and Europeans — whose passports already offer extensive visa-free travel — seeking a foothold abroad as an escape hatch at a time of mounting geopolitical uncertainty. “The Southern Cone of South America is the ultimate Plan B destination. It’s not on the way to anywhere strategically important. It’s a region that’s always staying out of global armed conflict,” said Christian Nesheim, editor of Investment Migration Insider, a trade journal. “It’s self-sufficient when it comes to food, to energy.” Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' A country with a history of military coups, debt defaults and runaway inflation that long sent its own business elite seeking opportunities abroad might seem an unlikely refuge for investors chasing stability. But Milei is trying to recast Argentina as a destination for foreign wealth, slashing public spending , dismantling regulations and courting investment in the country’s vast oil and mineral resources. Caputo said the idea for the citizenship-for-investment program emerged during Milei’s July 2024 visit to Sun Valley, Idaho, when tech executives expressed interest in obtaining Argentine citizenship. A self-proclaimed “anarcho-capitalist,” Milei has cultivated close ties with libertarian-minded tech billionaires such as Elon Musk , a vocal supporter of Milei's drive to shrink government. Last year, he brandished a chainsaw gifted by the Argentine leader as a symbol of his own campaign to slash U.S. government spending . Another ideological ally is Peter Thiel , a co-founder of software firm Palantir who temporarily moved his family to Buenos Aires in April. Corporate records obtained by The Associated Press show that a company linked to his investment firm, Thiel Capital, owns a $13.5 million mansion in the city’s upscale Barrio Parque neighborhood.

events.title: Meta parts ways with Virtue AI
events.summary: Meta said it’s letting go of employees it hired from AI safety startup Virtue AI four months after they joined the company in June, Meta spokesperson Andy Stone told Semafor, chalking it up to clashing work styles. The departures show Meta is still shaping its strategy around AI and AI safety amid new calls for regulation in Washington. “Unfortunately, the arrangement didn’t work out as planned,” Stone said, adding that Meta Superintelligence Labs remains focused on AI safety, alignment and frontier risk. Virtue, an AI security startup, had previously done work with Anthropic, OpenAI and the Commerce Department’s NIST. Axios reported in June that Virtue AI co-founders Bo Li, Dawn Song, and Sanmi Koyejo were joining Meta along with other employees from the startup. The team didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

events.title: Brazil's Lula-Bolsonaro showdown unfolds in Trump's shadow — with the Amazon at stake
events.summary: Brazil votes Sunday in a presidential election that could reshape its relationship with President Trump , return the Bolsonaro movement to power and alter the future of the Amazon. Why it matters: The showdown between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro has turned into something bigger: a test of Trump's influence in Latin America's largest country, with stakes for the region and the global climate. The latest: Trump said Thursday he's following Brazil's election "very closely" and called it "very important," though he didn't endorse a candidate. Catch up quick: Trump inserted the U.S. into the contest when his administration imposed additional 25% tariffs on some Brazilian goods this summer — prompting Lula to accuse the American leader of "interference" in Brazil's affairs. The dispute has become campaign ammunition for Lula and Bolsonaro, the eldest son of Trump ally and former President Jair Bolsonaro . Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of plotting a military coup to overturn Brazil's 2022 election . He's currently under house arrest due to health issues. Context: The confrontation escalated in 2025 when the Trump administration targeted Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes , who oversaw the prosecution of the elder Bolsonaro. The U.S. revoked his visa and sanctioned him, though the sanctions were later lifted. State of play: Jair Bolsonaro is barred from running, but his son has pledged to continue his father's political legacy. That leaves the heir to a right-wing populist movement facing a left-wing president seeking a fourth, nonconsecutive term. A candidate must win more than 50% of valid votes to avoid a runoff. Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro lead the field, with recent polling showing them essentially even in a potential runoff . The big picture: Nearly 60% of the Amazon rainforest is in Brazil. The forest stores enormous amounts of carbon and helps regulate the climate, giving the next president influence over an ecosystem with consequences far beyond Brazil's borders. Amazon deforestation fell by roughly half since Lula returned to office, though his climate record is complicated by his support for expanded oil development. Flávio Bolsonaro has backed loosening environmental regulations and said in August that he doesn't believe climate change is real. The election could determine whether Brazil continues its renewed forest protections even as it expands fossil-fuel production. Lula's pitch: The 80-year-old president is campaigning on his economic and social policy record : state-led national development, income redistribution and continuing welfare programs. Bolsonaro's pitch: The 45-year-old lawyer, who has represented Rio de Janeiro in Brazil's Senate since 2019, is campaigning on conservative social policies, tax cuts and a tougher approach to crime. He has pointed to Argentina as a model for closer bilateral trade with the U.S. , while libertarian President Javier Milei appeared with him at a São Paulo political event in July to support his candidacy. Flávio Bolsonaro met with Trump at the White House in May and afterward pledged that Brazil would join Trump's " Shield of the Americas " initiative if he wins — a grouping that includes Argentina and El Salvador. He's also praised El Salvador President Nayib Bukele's security crackdown as an inspiration for Brazil and vowed to build "many, many prisons." What's next: Brazil votes Sunday. If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes, the top two finishers will advance to an Oct. 25 runoff.

events.title: AI campaign deepfakes are starting to draw legal threats
events.summary: Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-Wis.) was hit with a cease-and-desist letter this week over an AI deepfake he posted falsely depicting his Democratic opponent voicing positions her campaign says she rejects. Why it matters: Van Orden is the latest in a growing number of candidates and elected officials facing legal complaints and threats over AI deepfakes in campaign ads. Driving the news: Attorneys for Rebecca Cooke, Van Orden's Democratic opponent, sent him a cease-and-desist letter on Wednesday over his "pattern of posting misleading AI-generated videos that falsely attribute statements to Cooke." The letter singled out an August X post by Van Orden showing an AI-generated Cooke saying she wants to "take advantage of as much corruption as possible and give every illegal alien free healthcare" — something she never said. Van Orden's team didn't respond to Axios' request for comment, but he responded to Cooke publicly with an AI-generated video of a duck wearing a Democratic Socialists of America T-shirt, yelling, "cease and desist." The big picture: AI deepfakes have proliferated this election cycle, while Congress has yet to establish a federal standard governing their use. Some campaigns have used hyperrealistic ads. Texas Senate GOP nominee Ken Paxton combined real and inaccurate statements from his opponent, James Talarico . In Louisiana's Republican Senate primary, one candidate was shown busing undocumented immigrants to polling places. Others have used more cartoonish ads that candidates have said are intended as parody. About 31 states regulate political deepfakes, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, including at least 28 that require disclosures for AI-generated content. Zoom in: Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick (R) faced a criminal complaint from his Democratic opponent, state Rep. Vikki Goodwin, in September under Texas' deepfake election law. The law says AI-ads cannot be aired within 30 days of an election if the intent is to influence the outcome. Goodwin argues that the window should mean 30 days before the start of early voting. Patrick's campaign ran AI-generated attack ads falsely depicting Goodwin at a football game wearing a shirt that read "taxes" instead of "Texas." The campaign later removed the ads, and a spokesperson called the video "obvious parody." North Carolina state Sen. Michael Lee (R) was also issued a cease-and-desist letter by his Democratic challenger, Jessica Bichler, in August over his use of AI-generated ads. North Carolina does not have any laws prohibiting the use of AI in campaign ads. Zoom out: Political experts say AI deepfakes erode trust in the political system, making it harder for voters to know what a candidate actually stands for. The ads can be effective even when viewers know they're fake, UC Irvine epistemologist Cailin O'Connor previously told Axios. The ads could also compound broader declines in Americans' trust in the federal government, institutions and news media. The bottom line: These legal challenges are likely just the beginning, as targeted candidates turn to the courts, law enforcement and warning letters to police what federal regulations leave unchecked. events.title: These AI Experts Want to Do High-Stakes Research Out in the Open
events.summary: Some big AI companies seem to think that the best way to keep models from becoming too chaotic or too mischievous is to keep them locked inside of labs. If only a chosen few can access them, the thinking goes, they can do less damage in the real world while researchers try to understand what they’re capable of. Nathan Lambert and Tom Zick, two industry scientists, believe the opposite. The pair founded a nonprofit, Trillium Labs , that will work on various areas of AI research—including potentially problematic areas like recursive self-improvement (RSI) and agents—in a more transparent way. In practice, this will mean publishing the details of experiments so that outside scientists can study and replicate them. Lambert says the way frontier AI labs keep their work secret reduces the community’s ability to scrutinize ideas and contribute new approaches. He believes that letting outside experts see how models are built and tuned could be crucial to mitigating risks. “Over the past few millennia, humanity has had the scientific method in our toolbox as a way to mitigate harms and build better futures,” Lambert tells WIRED. “The current closed trajectory of frontier AI development is taking us a step backwards.” The world’s most powerful models, like those from OpenAI and Anthropic , can only be accessed through an app or an application programming interface (API). Often, this comes at the cost of transparency about how the model is built and how it behaves. Other companies, especially those in China, offer relatively powerful models that can be downloaded and run on a user’s own hardware. The Chinese company Xiaomi, for example, recently published live details of a major training run involving one of its models. And researchers at Stanford are pretraining the AI model Marin in the open. The industry is currently locked in a battle over which strategy is best, mostly because of how powerful frontier models now are. They can automate the discovery of new software vulnerabilities and automatically probe and hack into systems , and recent high-profile hacking sprees have prompted even greater scrutiny. Proponents of a limited-access system say it’s crucial to keep that power in the hands of a trusted few, while those in Lambert and Zick’s camp believe that a shared understanding of the risks means we’re all better off. Lambert previously worked at Ai2, a research lab that has taken an unusually open approach to AI, including publishing details of the data and the training methods used to build models alongside the models themselves. He previously worked at Hugging Face , runs a popular technical blog , and founded the American Truly Open Models , an initiative aimed at encouraging US companies to release more open models. Zick worked at Harvard University and helped Charles Schwab devise policies around “responsible AI.” The two met over Zoom during the COVID-19 pandemic, when both were graduate students at UC Berkeley working on AI. They got the idea for the new nonprofit after seeing how disconnected industry AI research has become from academic work; Lambert says professors and students are often unable to replicate the work going on inside big company labs because they lack the resources required. Zick says Trillium Labs, which launched today, will initially focus on post-training—fine-tuning large models after they’ve been built. Another key area will be RSI, a process for developing new models by having AI contribute research. The prospect that ongoing progress could continue indefinitely, leading to a loss of human control, has alarmed many AI researchers . The issue gained mainstream attention earlier this month when an Anthropic researcher left the company and warned that RSI could pose an existential threat to humankind. The nonprofit will also look at how reinforcement learning, which rewards a model for good results and punishes it for bad outcomes, can improve its capabilities. That approach has made agents far more capable, but also more inclined to do unexpected things. They’ll study how reinforcement learning shapes the character and behavior of AI models, a method that can pose problems when a model becomes overly sycophantic, for example. “To understand something like how reinforcement learning scales in post-training, you need significant compute and a lot of careful experimentation,” Zick says. She says that publishing details of how reinforcement training runs work could yield surprising insights as outside researchers scrutinize the work. The lab has raised an undisclosed sum from Schmidt Sciences, Halcyon Futures, and others. The founders say they aim to raise $40 to $100 million in total and plan to spend $30 million on training over the next 18 months. “I'm a massive fan of much more transparency than we currently have in R&D,” Tim Fist, director of emerging technology policy at the Institute for Progress, a policy thinktank, tells WIRED.

events.title: Amazon to invest $1B into communities amid backlash against data center rollouts
events.summary: Amazon is investing more than $1 billion over the next five years into communities where it operates data centers for education, job training, water preservation projects and other local priorities as it reacts to a growing backlash from politicians an... NEW YORK -- Amazon is investing more than $1 billion over the next five years into communities where it operates data centers for education, job training, water and energy preservation projects and other local priorities as it reacts to a growing backlash from politicians and consumers to the tech industry's rollout of the massive buildings. According to a blog post on Friday by Matt Garman, Amazon’s CEO of its cloud computing arm, Amazon has already spent more than $1 billion in communities with a large data center presence over the past three years. Garman also said that Amazon is no longer using nondisclosure agreements with government agencies it works with on its projects, and it said it hosts open houses in communities where it operates to share information about what it's doing. He also warned against the spread of what he believes is misinformation about data centers' impact on the environment and energy rates — and he cited the dangers of over 100 moratoriums against these centers being considered across the country. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” he wrote. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position. There is urgency to this data center build out because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security.” Garman's pledge comes as data centers, which power artificial intelligence and cloud computing, have become a hot political issue heading into the midterms as tech giants race to invest more money in expanding these infrastructures. Small, under-the-radar data centers have been around for decades. But the explosion of artificial intelligence chatbots has resulted in data centers that are bigger than anything just about any town has ever seen . Some of them dwarf football stadiums and factories and consume more energy than small cities. Amazon said in July that it now expects to spend $220 billion in capital expenditures in 2026, including on data centers and other technology investments. That’s up from its prior estimate of $200 billion. President Donald Trump has embraced the building of more data centers, but there is growing wariness from voters. About 6 in 10 Americans support limiting the number of new data centers that can be built, including most Democrats and Republicans. And a majority of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centers on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built.
