events.title: Germany's chancellor under pressure over failures
events.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz came under growing pressure from allies and rivals alike over electoral and legislative failures, raising the possibility that the leader of Europe’s biggest economy could be ousted. His government yesterday withdrew a key tax proposal, while labor and pensions plans that economists regard as necessary to bolster the country’s languid growth are also under pressure. His party’s retreat comes after a series of embarrassing election showings in which the far-right AfD made huge inroads. Germany has little record of a mid-term change in federal leadership, but at least two European capitals have held internal war games on the implications of Merz’s chancellorship ending, Politico reported, while Handelsblatt described him as a “pseudo-dead man.” — Prashant Rao

events.title: Fears of European debt crisis send bond yields soaring
events.summary: Soaring borrowing costs spurred experts to warn of a gathering fiscal crisis, particularly in Europe. France remains at the epicenter of the storm, after a proposed budget yesterday failed to quell investors’ anxiety over its fast-rising borrowing. But worries are growing elsewhere: UK 30-year yields hit 6% , the first time a G7 member has faced such high interest rates since the 2012 eurozone crisis, while other indebted countries such as Italy and Greece saw bond yields widen sharply compared to those of the European benchmark, Germany. “European bond markets are showing the first signs of broader contagion,” ING economists said, while one portfolio manager told The Wall Street Journal, “markets have the faint smell of a crisis in the making .” — Prashant Rao

( Facebook ) Married couple Michael Zheng and Angela Wang died after a multi-vehicle crash in Ledcourt on Sunday night. A friend says the couple had a bright future ahead in Australia, with plans to have a child. The police investigation into the crash is ongoing. Friends and colleagues have paid tribute to two Chinese nationals who were victims of a crash in Victoria's west that claimed three lives. Michael Zheng, 38, and his wife Angela Wang, 31, died at the scene after their car was involved in a collision with a Mitsubishi Triton and a truck at Ledcourt about 6.45pm on September 27. Tenesha Fieldsend, 14, a passenger in the Mitsubishi, driven by a learner driver, later died at hospital. The couple, who recently celebrated their fifth wedding anniversary, had been living in the town of Horsham, approximately 300 kilometres west of Melbourne. Friends have described them as two "wonderful people" with "so much hope for their future in Australia". Mr Zheng had recently been promoted as the manager of the Horsham Dentist Group, while Ms Wang was a nurse at Grampians Health. JingJing Tang got to know the couple last year when she was helping them look for their missing dog. Ms Tang said they were a lovely young couple. "They had been granted Australian permanent residency last year, and I remember how happy and hopeful they were about building their life here," she said. Angela Wang and Michael Zheng met while living in Africa. ( Facebook ) Ms Tang last spoke to Mr Zheng and Ms Wang a few months ago, when they came to Ms Tang's newly opened takeaway restaurant for a meal. "The shop wasn't busy, so we sat together and talked for quite a long time," she said. "I could never have imagined that would be the last time I would see them. "Looking back now, that ordinary and happy conversation has become a very precious memory for me." During that conversation, Ms Tang said the couple had spoken about their new home being built in Ballarat, and their hopes for the future — including having a baby one day. "It's heartbreaking that their journey ended. I hope they are together in heaven now … continuing the dreams and beautiful life they had planned together." Michael Zheng and Angela Wang enjoyed living in Australia. events.title: Who gets to decide if AI is safe? Africa wants a say
events.summary: African companies race to adopt American and Chinese AI, with little attention paid to safety. Incidents of AI misuse and malfunction are growing across Africa. Companies are piloting American and Chinese AI systems, with little consideration for safety. Frontier models should undergo Africa-centric safety evaluations, experts say. African leaders called last week for a greater role in setting global standards for artificial intelligence. Their statements at the United Nations came amid warnings from Silicon Valley executives about AI models being misused , and sometimes going rogue and taking unauthorized actions. OpenAI’s agents hacked government websites across the world in June. Models from Anthropic , Google , and Meta , too, hacked into other companies’ systems during tests. “Africa … must be equal co-architects in determining the standards, ethics, and architectures of this technological era,” Lewis Garseedah Brown II, permanent representative of Liberia, said at a U.N. Security Council meeting on AI. African companies and governments are racing to deploy AI systems built in the U.S. and China. But many nations lack the ability to independently test whether those systems are safe for their populations, experts told Rest of World. “ There’s essentially no real discussion about AI safety. So, there’s a real vacuum,” said Jonathan Shock, associate professor in math at the University of Cape Town. If countries set up their own safeguards, it could complicate operations for American and Chinese companies in new markets. Fragmented regulations could make global deployments of models more costly and difficult. Incidents of AI misuse and malfunction are surfacing across Africa. Kenya’s predictive machine learning algorithm for setting health insurance contributions has driven up costs for poor households. Scammers in West Africa have used AI-generated content to blackmail victims in extortion schemes . The militant group Boko Haram has also used AI to organize attacks and design weapons after bypassing safeguards. “I think it’s going to take a potentially catastrophic incident for governments to really take [heed],” Shock said, which he dubbed his optimistic view. “The pessimistic view is we don’t stop it in time.” Africa currently lags behind other regions in AI adoption, though its companies are moving quickly. Out of 85 large companies surveyed by PricewaterhouseCoopers this year, more than 80% were running AI pilots. Many lack formal structures to oversee safety, according to the report. “Everyone is just trying to catch up [on AI deployment],” Mélanie Keïta, CEO and founder of Nairobi-based financing company Melanin Kapital, told Rest of World . Like many African companies, Melanin Kapital has weighed the choice between American and Chinese AI models, testing both internally. Both come with their own risks, Keïta said. “We might become a product of other foreign corporations that … own all our data as opposed to really being autonomous and free.” Risk also correlates with how easily a model can be shut down if something goes wrong. ChatGPT and Claude are closed-weight models, centrally controlled by their providers. Chinese models such as DeepSeek and Kimi, along with a few American models, are open-weight and can be downloaded and modified by users. That makes it harder for their developers to shut down remotely, Jane Munga, fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told Rest of World . “The distinction that matters is not Chinese versus American; it is: Who holds the off switch?” she said. Governments across Africa are beginning to use AI in sensitive areas such as healthcare, education, and public services, even though fewer than half of African countries have AI policies or strategies, Shock said. Kenya is the only African nation participating in an international AI safety network that is developing methods to evaluate advanced AI models. Last year, the network tested AI agents for risks such as sensitive data leaks and fraud. But the exercise focused on common global risks rather than ones specific to Africa, Joanna Wiaterek, co-founder of the Centre for AI Security and Access, told Rest of World . It found agent safeguards worked unevenly across languages. “Africa-centric” safety evaluations should judge harm by the size of each country’s economy, Gathoni Ireri, research scholar at the Nairobi-based Ilina Program, an AI safety research center, told Rest of World. An incident that might be considered minor in a Western country could irrevocably harm an African one, she said. Companies currently carry out their own safety tests, but this needs to be replaced by third-party evaluations that assess risks specific to Africa, Ireri said. “I think we also have to have our own ideas about what it means for a system to be safe within our own context,” she said.

events.title: Behind the Curtain: AI's existential legal crisis
events.summary: No industry has ever documented its own foreseeable risks as loudly as AI. Imagine a plaintiff's lawyer reading the public warnings of Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: They told the world it was dangerous. They told the world it was moving too fast. Then they unleashed it and sold it to your kid. No industry has ever taken so much copyrighted work and left behind so much proof. Imagine a plaintiff's lawyer reading OpenAI's own files to a jury: They trained on a pirated library. They renamed it to something blander. Then they deleted it when the headlines got hot. Why it matters: AI's origins, use and future will be picked apart in countless epic court fights, with a historic paper and public statement trail to tap. Every significant invention — be it social media, automobiles, electricity or capitalism itself — gets disrupted and eventually shaped by the courts. AI, with its tentacles into every part of industry and life, will experience this at scale. The big picture: The fights are no longer theoretical. They're underway, in discovery and headed toward juries. Early verdicts and settlements capture the risk for the biggest players. 🤖 Chatbots are being treated as products, not speech. Unlike social media companies, they likely can't hide behind Section 230 , which protects platforms from liability for what users post — not what the platform itself creates. 📖 Copyright is a massive problem. Anthropic already paid the biggest copyright settlement in history, $1.5 billion to authors and book publishers, and now music publishers and news media want a piece. 💻 Agents gone wild. What happens when they do damage — and it was foreseeable and foreseen? ⚖️ Discovery gone wild. AI leaves LOTS of receipts (and, ironically, makes it easier for the lawyers to comb through them, too). Product liability turns on two words: foreseeable and knew. Punitive damages turn on whether you knew the danger and shipped anyway. This is where all these memos and warnings could really backfire. Candor is good for safety but terrible for litigation. The companies that warn most honestly create the most discoverable evidence of foreseeability. Expect general counsels to push hard to tone down the candor. It's the rational legal move. ⚠️ The intrigue: The liabilities won't be limited to AI companies. Any corporate user of powerful AI systems that unleashes rogue agents, even without intending to do harm, would face substantial penalties as well. "It's not if, but when," said Miriam Vogel, a former senior Justice Department official who now leads EqualAI. "An algorithm will do what it's told to do. The more power and capability it has, the more access it has, the more it will do anything in its power to achieve a goal." That will create another layer of litigation as companies fight back. The CTO of a top Wall Street hedge fund who spoke to Axios after the notorious OpenAI/Hugging Face hack said his first call, if his firm's systems are breached, will be to his general counsel. President Trump, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former FTC chair Lina Khan have all argued that AI companies are responsible for making sure their products are safe. If not, a wave of lawsuits awaits. The other side: There's a school of thought that AI companies might escape the worst liability, despite their frankness about things they and their products might have done wrong. One way to see it, and the argument lawyers will undoubtedly make, is that the labs spoke about dangers frequently, and took pains to protect users and mitigate harms. The bottom line: For all the fights in Washington about whether or not Congress will act, the U.S. legal system may be the ultimate, and most powerful, regulator of the AI industry. Bradley Olson, Axios managing editor of AI & tech, contributed reporting. 📈 If you're a CEO or on a CEO's team: Ask to join Jim's new weekly Axios C-Suite newsletter.

events.title: Inside the AI industry's grassroots rebellion, led by elite researchers at frontier companies
events.summary: A small cadre of elite AI researchers is wielding extraordinary influence inside OpenAI and other leading companies, challenging executives, shaping policy and complicating negotiations with Washington. Why it matters: As a safety crisis has unfolded across the industry, it's an open question who is doing more to shape the national AI debate — top researchers or the executives they report to. The researchers, some of whom are among the most highly paid and sought-after scientists in the world, are outspoken online and have repeatedly clashed with company strategy. The big picture: The situation has the makings of a grassroots uprising, where any potential deal the companies may strike — with the Trump administration, one another, or even globally — will also have to pass muster with their top scientists. Behind the scenes: OpenAI, Anthropic and others at the frontier of AI aren't like other companies. Many began years ago as idealistic research labs with scientific cultures that prized openness and collaboration. To function, and to continue to build better and better models, the companies need highly specialized machine learning researchers and scientists to push the frontiers of what's technologically possible. The trouble is, the best of those researchers are in extraordinarily short supply. Last year's talent wars drove compensation packages into the hundreds of millions of dollars for the most elite, giving top researchers enormous leverage over their employers. Perks include favorable vesting schedules for their compensation and largely freewheeling policies that allow them to share triumphs, trash rivals and offer their perspectives about the AI race frequently on X. AI CEOs must prioritize safety and embrace regulation to retain top research talent, an OpenAI investor told Axios. Zoom in: OpenAI president Greg Brockman scrapped plans to donate another $25 million to a pro-AI political group that some researchers had openly criticized. Researchers and employees say they helped push OpenAI from resisting regulation — and candidates who supported it — toward working more closely with lawmakers in several states. The company recently backed a transparency bill in Illinois and, at the 11th hour, an independent auditing bill in California. "We have a lot of debate inside OpenAI, and that's a good thing, but what ultimately drives our policy positions is what we're seeing in our own technology and how quickly its capabilities are advancing," an OpenAI spokesperson said. Yes, but: OpenAI signaled Thursday that there are limits to how much dissent it will tolerate, firing three employees for allegedly mishandling sensitive information. The employees broke the "deep level of trust" needed to keep systems safe, the company said. Friction point: In Washington, the unusual dynamic has frustrated policymakers who see AI companies as inconsistent on regulation — opposing proposals at some points and supporting them at others, sources tell Axios. OpenAI is "no longer seen as or acting as a leader in driving policy," one source close to the administration said, arguing researchers have "neutered" the company. A White House official said OpenAI has been an incredible partner and pointed to the recent accord the company signed with the president. Zoom out: It's not just OpenAI. Researchers also complicated Anthropic's efforts to strike a deal with the Pentagon after a clash between the company and senior administration officials earlier this year. Employees at OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have signed high-profile letters at pivotal moments between companies and the government, including more than 1,000 who backed the viral "Pacing the Frontier" petition. In a remarkable show of internal solidarity, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned and publicly blasted the company's safety practices — only to have several colleagues still inside Anthropic endorse his concerns. Reality check: Executives have also adapted as political backlash to AI has grown and safety incidents have drawn more scrutiny, sources close to the companies say. With some level of regulation seen as inevitable, companies have focused on molding the rules as favorably as possible rather than simply resisting them. The bottom line: In the debate over AI safety and regulation, some researchers have become nearly as influential in setting the terms as OpenAI's Sam Altman or Anthropic's Dario Amodei.

events.title: AI Is Making a Mess of Nurses’ Schedules. They Say It’s a Safety Issue
events.summary: Over the past four months, Amber Retzloff, a critical care nurse in Florida, requested to work 50 specific 12-hour shifts. But over half the time, she says her hospital’s Palantir -powered scheduling software assigned her to different shifts, often putting her on back-to-back-to-back days and leaving her mentally drained. Retzloff doesn’t expect to always get the slots she wants, but by her count the tool does a far worse job honoring her preferences than managers did when they assigned shifts by hand. Retzloff’s experience mirrors that of other nurses across HCA Healthcare, the largest hospital chain in the US. Since 2023, HCA has rolled out an AI scheduling tool it co-developed with Palantir called Timpani at roughly 130 of its 190 locations. Retzloff’s hospital adopted it nearly two years ago. “No one is happy with Timpani,” says Retzloff, echoing what five nurses at other locations reported in interviews with WIRED. “Everyone complains all the time.” Other purported HCA workers have expressed similar gripes about the tool on platforms like Reddit . The nurses who spoke with WIRED allege that Timpani has potentially harmed patients by causing care teams to be understaffed, imbalanced, and exhausted. Operating with minimal oversight, they say the tool routinely schedules too few nurses or not enough experienced veterans during shifts, particularly on Sundays. It also frequently ignores nurses’ stated preferences for spacing out shifts, working nights and weekends, or taking specific days off. As a result, nurses say they are being forced to waste more time trying to trade shifts or appeal their schedules than prior to the arrival of the software. They also believe colleagues are increasingly calling out, using paid or unpaid time to skip assignments, though doing so more than a few times annually puts them at risk of termination. Retzloff, 34, a National Nurses United labor union leader with a decade of bedside experience, recalls recent shifts where all four of her colleagues were junior. Because she was the only senior nurse working, Retzloff says she had to delay care for the sickest patients to guide the novices through milder cases. HCA is “letting AI dictate,” Retzloff says. “We are overriding clinical judgment and the human-to-human piece of health care with an app.” Previously, managers handled scheduling manually and generally consulted nurses well in advance when overriding requests. With Timpani, nurses report needing to make alternative arrangements on shorter notice and an increase in temporary reassignments to different teams. “I can’t remember any issues before,” says a non-union nurse in Texas who asked to remain anonymous out of fear of retaliation from HCA. “Everything came out on time.” Harlow Sumerford, an HCA spokesperson, says that nursing leaders, not Timpani, make final scheduling decisions. Assertions that the tool “is designed to reduce staffing at the expense of patient care” are misrepresentative, he adds. HCA’s goal is “to have the right caregivers, with the right skills and experience, available to meet the needs of our patients while also considering our colleagues’ scheduling preferences,” Sumerford says, noting that the company is continuing to improve Timpani based on nurses’ feedback. On average, Timpani schedules nurses for 1 percent of their requested days off, or what are known as red days, according to HCA. Lee Barker, an HCA nurse in Missouri, says while that number might appear relatively low, getting scheduled on red days was previously unheard of at their facility. But less than a year after management introduced Timpani, Barker says now essentially every nurse has been assigned to work on a day they were supposed to be off. Barker delayed a long-planned doctor’s appointment for a chronic condition after struggling to trade an assigned red day. “It feels like we’re being kicked while we’re already down,” Barker says. Complaints about Timpani have prompted HCA management to make minor updates to the software, but problems still persist, according to nurses across the US. Leaders of National Nurses United, the labor union representing about 10,000 of HCA’s 100,000 nurses, says the company has rejected their requests for information about the technology. Some purported details emerged in July when a former HCA data science manager, Angelique Russell, sued the company for allegedly firing her in retaliation for raising concerns about Timpani. She accused HCA of routinely deleting data the tool uses to create schedules, which prevented auditing how well it worked and she claimed may have violated several healthcare laws. (HCA has yet to formally respond in court, and Russell declined to comment.) Timpani was built on Palantir Foundry , a software platform for storing and analyzing different data from across a company’s operations.

events.title: Why Washington and Tehran keep talking past each other
events.summary: The Trump administration and the Iranian regime both say they prefer a diplomatic solution to the war , but a deal looks more elusive than ever. The root causes of the impasse may be irreconcilable. Why it matters: In the last 18 months, two failed rounds of negotiations have led to two wars. The June MOU collapsed within days and led to renewed escalation. If the current effort to reach a diplomatic breakthrough ends in a deadlock, another outbreak of fighting is likely within weeks. Here's a look at some of the deep-seated dynamics between the two countries — personal, cultural, and political — that have stymied efforts to broker a deal: "Trump has ADD; Iran has OCD" One reason for the failures is that the U.S. and Iran see the timeframe for negotiations very differently. Trump is all about getting a quick deal — he gets impatient and frustrated when things move slowly. The Iranian negotiation style is the complete opposite. They are all about playing for time. "America under Trump is the attention-deficit superpower ... incapable of sustaining a strategy. Iran under the Islamic Republic is the obsessive-compulsive theocracy, fixated on resisting America far more than advancing the welfare of its own people," Karim Sadjadpour, a senior analyst at the Carnegie Endowment, told Axios. "Trump has ADD; Iran has OCD." For example, in April 2025 Trump set a deadline for negotiations at 60 days — an extremely short and unrealistic timetable. The Iranians, on the other hand, saw the negotiations as a longer process and didn't take the deadline seriously enough. They didn't think Trump meant it when he said 60 days. The negotiations in February of this year were even shorter — around three weeks. The chances of getting a deal that quickly were close to zero. A megadeal vs. a narrow truce Trump loves a splashy show of political theater, with him cast as lead actor. He envisions a legacy-making accord that redefines the relationship between the U.S. and Iran and reshapes the Middle East. The Iranians prefer a narrow, transactional deal that's negotiated indirectly — or with the lowest public profile possible. They view any deal as a truce rather than a peace agreement. "Trump and his negotiators pride themselves on being dealmakers. In Iranian political culture, the word for compromiser — 'sazeshkar' — is practically a slur," Sadjadpour said. He added: "Iran's leaders were never willing to meet with Trump directly. Had they been willing to do so, I think the outcome of events could have been very different. Trump wants to resolve the conflict; the Islamic Republic's entire identity is premised on continued confrontation with the U.S." A matter of mistrust The fundamental impediment in the negotiations is mistrust. The Iranians claim Trump cheated them twice when he attacked them in the middle of negotiations. Many inside the Iranian regime think any negotiations with the U.S. are just a ruse to mask preparations for a surprise attack. The U.S. side counters it was Iran that cheated when it violated the June 2026 memorandum of understanding, by attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz days after signing the deal. U.S. officials say that they can't count on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps or other radical elements inside the regime to abide by any deal they negotiate with more pragmatic members of the regime. Domestic pressure The negotiations are a fraught domestic political issue for both sides. Iran's negotiating team and others inside the regime who support a deal have come under constant attacks back home. It's pushed them to take a harder line in talks. Trump and his negotiators are getting pressure from the right not to cut a deal — and mocked by the left for potentially accepting one that either restores the pre-war status quo or resembles President Obama's 2015 nuclear deal. That kind of criticism made Trump pull back from more moderate positions he took several times over the last 18 months, including earlier this week. What to watch: White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President Vance still think diplomacy is worth pursuing. But Trump seems much more skeptical. In an interview with Time magazine published on Thursday, he said what Iran is ready to do "is not good enough" for him. "With Iran, I don't think you could ever have peace," he said, reiterating that he's considering resuming major combat operations after the midterms. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday defended the negotiations with the U.S. "We have never and will not run away from dialogue, although the U.S. targeted our country three times despite having signed the agreement," he said, referring to the June MOU. "The U.S. should get rid of the idea that it would bring us to our knees through terror." But other Iranian officials, especially inside the IRGC, think negotiations are useless and that the only way to end the war is by inflicting more costs on the battlefield. What they're saying: "Iran is adopting a strategy toward the United States defined by escalation and continuous offense," Mohammad Ayatollahi Tabaar, associate professor of international affairs at Texas A&M University's Bush School of Government and Public Service, writes in a new Foreign Affairs article . "[The regime] is clear about what it wants — the removal of all U.S. forces from the region — and it is prepared to remain indefinitely on a wartime footing to get it."

events.title: Developers vie to land plum HK$2 billion residential site in Ho Man Tin
events.summary: The government received 10 tenders for the site on Fat Kwong Street ahead of a deadline on Friday The sole residential site included in the Hong Kong government’s latest land sale programme has attracted interest from a host of major developers, with 10 tenders being submitted before a noon deadline on Friday. Chinachem Group, Wheelock Properties, Kerry Properties and Sun Hung Kai Properties all confirmed to the South China Morning Post that they had submitted individual bids for the site on Fat Kwong Street in Ho Man Tin, Kowloon, while Sino Land issued a joint tender with Great Eagle Group. Representatives from other developers including CK Asset Holdings, K Wah International, China Overseas Land & Investment and Poly Property were also seen submitting bids at a government office, according to media reports. The Land Department said it had received 10 tenders in total. The site has a maximum gross floor area of 19,300 square metres (207,750 square feet) and is expected to accommodate about 250 flats. It was originally included in the government’s 2026-2027 land sale programme.

events.title: "Strange bedfellows": Bernie Sanders, Florida Dems and a benchmark $250k donation
events.summary: MIAMI — Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders is sending the Florida Democratic Party $250,000. It's a relative pittance in the Sunshine State — but the check signals a big political shift. Why it matters: The state party's moderate leaders have resisted the rising tide of democratic socialists elevated by Sanders for years. But political changes and financial need have brought the two together like never before: The Florida Democratic Party is essentially broke after decades of being out of power, and national establishment Democratic organizations have so far refused to help. Florida state Rep Angie Nixon , who joined the Democratic Socialists of America this summer, is the state party's U.S. Senate nominee. Sanders endorsed her and has long wanted to help, an aide said. Zoom in: Despite being vastly outraised and outspent in Florida, Nixon and Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly are stubbornly close in polling to their respective Republican opponents, Sen. Ashley Moody and Rep. Byron Donalds. Until now, national Democrats have been hesitant to spend in Florida due to years of soul-crushing defeats —especially at the hands of President Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis — that made the state and its 10 expensive media markets look like a bad investment. This year, with Republican fortunes sagging nationwide, Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska look more promising for Democrats. That could change soon. Nixon told a liberal podcaster Thursday that the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, held a fundraiser for her. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), whom Nixon called out last week for not helping, also might make money available. "Folks are a little gun-shy because, unfortunately, Vice President [Kamala] Harris lost as a Black woman. And so people are being very hesitant in terms of funding Black women, especially in the South," Nixon told MS NOW's "Clock It with Symone & Eugene." Behind the scenes: Florida Democratic Party chair Nikki Fried has been constantly working national donors for money, allies say, but she never asked Sanders for help because of their ideological differences and resistance within the state party. Socialists — and Sanders' associated views — have long been regarded as political liabilities in a state where so many Hispanic voters hailed from countries associated with leftist violence. But when Sanders signaled he was ready to give to a " victory fund " that joins the state party and Nixon's campaign, Fried didn't stand in the way. "Angie's going to turn out our base," Fried privately told skeptical allies in the party. "Every dollar that helps Angie, helps Jolly and helps the candidates down ballot." Friction point: Establishment Democrats are divided between those who don't want to be associated with Sanders and those who wanted him to give more of his $23 million campaign fund than just $250,000. "That's it? He should send more," said Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, who has been critical of Sanders and doesn't agree with Sanders' and Nixon's criticisms of Israel. "Republicans are going to kill us for taking Bernie socialist money and we're not even getting enough of it," one Democratic candidate groused. "But yeah, strange bedfellows." Said Javier Fernandez, a Democratic mayor of the city of South Miami: "The more we rally around Bernie, the more we hurt our long-term prospects." "It's a Faustian bargain: The party captures the energy and dynamism of the Bernie/DSA that are trying to use the party, but it compromises core values of moderate and progressive Democrats and puts us further out of step with the views of mainstream voters." The big picture: The Democratic Party is evolving as progressives and socialist-aligned candidates and activists energize its base. Nationwide, 65% of Democrats now have a favorable view of socialism, according to a Gallup survey released last week that also found support rising among independents. Nixon is the Democratic engine drawing enthusiastic crowds in Florida. Her rallies double as organizational events to harness volunteers to knock on doors, make phone-bank calls or volunteer. She also has a notable social media presence and a stable of influencers. It's a stark contrast with Jolly's low-key candidacy, which has a small social-media footprint and events. Between the lines: After some initial tension , Nixon's campaign is aligned with the state party, which is providing additional organizational support. Statewide, the state party reports an army of 6,000 volunteers who helped Democrats flip 46 seats in legislative, school-board and local-government races across Florida in two years. Florida Democrats are now keeping pace with the GOP in voter registration gains. Sanders has sent his staff and organizers to Florida to help Nixon with literature, texting and phone-banking. Yes, but: Florida Republicans still have far more registered voters, an edge of more than 1.5 million. And the Florida GOP has a well-oiled turnout machine and a stable of political pros who have consistently helped keep the state reliably red. "We don't lose Florida," one of them said, noting Moody and Donalds are marginally ahead of Nixon and Jolly in most polls. Still, there are jitters in the GOP as gas prices rise along with interest rates and the real estate market cools. "I'm not going to say Angie or Jolly are going to win," said one GOP consultant. "It's hard to see a DSA candidate winning a general [election], but could I see a world where she turns out the base and falls short but Jolly benefits from it and ekes it out? Nobody knows." What they're saying: Nixon's campaign manager, Eunic Ortiz, said the money from Sanders helps, but big money is less salient nowadays. Republicans' "billionaire donors will likely outspend us, but we know we will out-organize them," Ortiz said. "We're going to win with people on the ground, neighbors talking to neighbors, and the kind of energy and excitement money can't buy." "Did we see a world where Bernie led the way in getting national money to Florida? No," said an ally of Fried's. "But national donors are starting to give to Florida. And Bernie was the first nod the nation is paying attention." Axios' Holly Otterbein contributed to this story.

events.title: ‘It’s not about the champagne:’ Why VistaJet thinks the private flights boom can last
events.summary: The Signal Insight Swiss billionaire Thomas Flohr is a World Endurance Championship racing driver who has spent 22 years building VistaJet into a $2.9 billion revenue private aviation business with global reach. He is now weighing a possible market listing that could value his holding company at $10 billion , even as war in the Middle East sends jet fuel prices higher and economists debate how much longer the boom in global luxury spending can continue. Flohr, with a fleet of almost 200 planes and an order for up to 160 new Bombardier jets over the next decade, doesn’t see any turbulence on the horizon. Vista has seen “an explosion of demand at the top end” of the market for its longest-haul flights, he says, with growth from Asia to Africa driving record sales and 28% growth in flying hours sold in the group’s latest quarter. Even in the Middle East, where many planes were grounded immediately after the US-Israeli strikes on Iran, Vista’s founder and chairman says there has been “a significant surge” in demand from local clients. Second-quarter sales in the region, measured in hours, were up more than 68% year over year. Private aviation has undergone “a massive change in perception” since Vista was founded in 2004, Flohr says, shedding its “Hollywood image” as companies prize the ability to move their executives around the world quickly and jets with ranges up to 17 hours bring more locations within reach. In business today, “everything is now,” he says. Flohr’s company has a subscription model and typically charges between $11,000 and $25,000 per hour for its flights, but he says companies have become more willing to entertain such operating expenses than the tens of millions of dollars in capital expenditure required to buy their own jets. A company-owned aircraft might fly 250 hours a year, but Vista’s fleet averages 1,000 hours, allowing it to recoup its fixed costs faster. “If you control and own the airplane, you can offer the client ultimately what he wants, and I think that is the key to our success,” Flohr says. “It always starts with the customer because in the end, we’re not paying our own bills. It’s the client that awards you the revenue.” Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson: How’s business right now? What’s driving the growth? Thomas Flohr: We see a surge in global demand. Obviously, the tech sector is on fire, and they of all the industries have the biggest global coverage demand. One day, a meeting in South Korea; the next day, a meeting in Japan; then there is a meeting in Abu Dhabi; then everybody is back in Silicon Valley, so they’re zooming around the world. Even if you own your own jet or two of them, you can’t really effectively cover the globe unless you have a global fleet, and they’re very conscious of the time efficiencies that they gain by flying point to point. You have told bond investors that you’re considering an IPO, possibly this year. What can you say about those plans? I can’t really say much. We have an obligation to communicate if we’re considering certain alternatives. But considering is one thing, and execution [is another]. We continue to explore our capital market alternatives. It’s prudent in the debt and the equity markets that you always have all alternatives available to you. So you’ve got to be ready for the bond market, and the same is true for the equity markets. If you’re ready, and the right opportunity comes, you can go. That’s what I’m drilling into the heads of my company, that this is always a prudent thing to do, because you never want to be in a situation where you say, “Ah, I have an opportunity. I might need capital. Oh, OK. I need nine months to get there.” Your headquarters is in Dubai. There was a period where airspace was closed in the Gulf after the Iran conflict began, and then questions about whether the region’s growth story would be interrupted. What’s your appraisal now? Yes, the airspace was closed for a little while, as it would be in any conflict. But the level of long-term vision and commitment to that region is incredibly strong. It’s like, for us, nothing changed. Today, when you’re actually spending time in the UAE, you don’t feel anything. It’s business as usual. People need to move, and it’s much more difficult for an airline to restart a global logistics infrastructure than it is for us. So our hours signed up in Q2 were up about [68%] year-over-year. In a way it sounds surprising, but it’s exactly what happened post-COVID. What does your experience during the COVID pandemic tell you about how much of that short-term gain you’ll sustain? In the five-year period from 2019 to 2024, the company grew 3x. I think that’s the answer, really. After about 18 months, the whole thing starts to go back to normal growth levels, but on a much higher level. Think about the psychology: We have yet to find someone who says, “No, I don’t want to fly private.” So, if you have an external event like this, which drives people to private aviation, nobody comes and volunteers and says, “Oh, let me please fly commercial again.” So corporations make the budget available, and it’s part of doing business. It’s not about the champagne or caviar. [That] is just, like, movie stuff. It is all about the time efficiency. The question is to what extent can the C-suite convince the CFO to allow for such a travel budget. But the level of efficiency is undebated. The president of the United States said [in September] that nobody should buy Bombardier jets any more. You’ve got a big order for 160. Is it going to be affected? I did very well for the last 22 years to stay out of politics, and I will stay out of politics for another 22 years. That’s really between two countries. It has nothing to do with me. We have a multi-fleet approach, and we have our contract in place, and the rest is really between the two countries to sort out. You have this racing career as well. Is there a connection? How do you think about those two careers alongside each other? The one connection is the word ‘endurance.’ In racing, you’re not going to win Le Mans if you do 10 good laps [out of a typical 300 to 400]. And if you can consistently perform at 97% or 98%, you get very far in life. And I think that’s the same philosophy, in endurance racing and in business: Stay humble, stay with your feet on the ground, carefully analyze what is in front of you and what is behind you. Don’t rush, but be decisive, and for the long term. What about your appetite for risk? This is not a low-risk pursuit. From the outside, it might look like risk, but I’m rather risk-averse. I’m extremely diligent about preparation. I feel personally more uncomfortable driving on a country road than in a World Endurance Championship. [In a race,] you’re 100% clear. You’re prepared. The safety measures are in place. The support system is right there. The same is true in business. events.title: "We're not asking for charity": Wikimedia CEO calls out AI for unpaid data use
events.summary: Wikipedia is starting to feel the effects of the AI-driven shift in how people find information, with page views falling 8% in the latest year, new Wikimedia Foundation CEO Bernadette Meehan told Axios. Why it matters: Wikipedia is a crucial source of information for AI models, but those same models increasingly allow people to get Wikipedia-derived information without ever visiting the site — potentially threatening the ecosystem that keeps the online encyclopedia running. Driving the news: Wikipedia page views declined 8% in 2025, and while the drop wasn't unexpected, "that doesn't mean that we're sort of starry-eyed about it and not concerned about it," Meehan said. Follow the money: The problem is that even though generative AI systems rely heavily on Wikipedia's vast trove of human-created information, some companies won't pay for it, she said. Wikimedia has a program that charges large-scale commercial users for reliable, high-volume access to its data. Publicly disclosed enterprise customers, whose payments make up 10% of the organization's operating expenses, include Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Perplexity and others. OpenAI and Anthropic, two of the largest makers of generative AI models, aren't among Wikimedia's publicly disclosed enterprise customers. Meehan noted that Wikimedia has other agreements that aren't publicly disclosed and declined to identify those companies. OpenAI and Anthropic both declined to comment. What they're saying: Meehan, a former U.S. ambassador to Chile who took over Wikimedia's top job in January, said the reception from big technology companies has been mixed. Some have embraced the idea that companies benefiting from Wikipedia should help sustain it. Others, she said, have acknowledged what Wikimedia considers excessive use of its data but declined to pay for enterprise access. "We're not asking for charity," Meehan said. Between the lines: There's an unusual economic tension here: Wikipedia makes its content freely available and has no intention of changing that, leaving it with limited leverage over AI companies that don't want to pay. The big picture: Traffic matters to Wikimedia for reasons that go well beyond bragging rights for being one of the most popular destinations on the internet. Roughly 80% of Wikimedia's operating budget comes from small donations, many prompted by banners shown to visitors to its site. Readers also provide the pipeline for future Wikipedia editors. "If less readers are coming, that's less conversion to editors," Meehan said. Ironically, Wikipedia has arguably never been more valuable to the broader information ecosystem. "We're the backbone," Meehan said when asked about Wikipedia's importance to AI knowledge engines. Meanwhile, Meehan is drawing a distinction between AI using Wikipedia and AI creating Wikipedia. AI remains controversial among Wikipedia's volunteer communities, which set their own rules, but it is already being used for tasks such as translation, finding broken links and helping new editors spot problems with their contributions. Meehan sees a clear boundary, though: AI should assist Wikipedia's human editors rather than replace them. "I don't think you will ever see AI writing or generating Wikipedia articles," she said. Asked whether she believes Wikipedia articles five years from now will still be written by humans for humans, Meehan replied: "I do." Zoom out: Meehan also pointed out who and what gets left out if commercially developed AI becomes a principal gateway to knowledge. Wikipedia exists in roughly 300 languages, including many that aren't likely to represent commercially attractive markets for AI companies. She also raises the possibility of a knowledge divide in which the best access to information increasingly requires paying for an AI subscription. The bottom line: Wikipedia spent the first phase of the generative AI boom becoming indispensable to AI. Its next challenge is ensuring that AI doesn't weaken the human and financial ecosystem that made Wikipedia indispensable in the first place.

events.title: A new contest pits competitors against each other in a race to biological youth
events.summary: This week, I officially signed up for an unusual competition. One that rewards competitors for getting younger . I recently turned 40, and I don’t need reminding that both time and my chronological age only tick forward. But this game is focused on competitors’ biological ages—figures that are meant to provide a better way to measure the age-related health of our organs and bodies. Over a six-month period, around 500 of us will try to reverse our biological age as measured in a bunch of different ways. There’s even a leaderboard! The winners will include the person who shows the greatest difference between their chronological and biological age, as well as the person who manages to reverse their biological age the most. The competition is the brainchild of the neuroscientist and physician Christin Glorioso, who is also founder and CEO of NeuroAge Therapeutics. The company offers tools to track brain health and aging and is running a trial to find out if biological brain age can predict the onset of Alzheimer’s disease. Glorioso says she has several goals for the Younger contest . The first, she tells me, is to “explain to the world what aging clocks are.” Regular Checkup readers will be familiar with these tools, but for the uninitiated, they are basically designed to measure biological age. Many measure chemical signatures that form a layer on top of our DNA and seem to change with age. But others might involve looking at proteins or lipids in blood. Some are designed to measure functional health, while others predict when a person will die. There are more than a hundred clocks out there, and they probably each capture a specific aspect of the biological process of aging. These clocks are proving very useful for scientists , who use them to study aging and development in humans and many other species. But using them to estimate the biological age of an individual person is more controversial. They’re just not good enough for that yet. Part of the problem is that we don’t really understand what each clock is capturing. Glorioso hopes that data collected through the Younger contest might help answer that question. She’s hoping to generate “the world’s most comprehensive clock dataset.” Some longevity clinics try to get around the limits of biological age testing by using multiple clocks. That’s this competition’s approach too. As a standard competitor, I’ll be sending a blood spot sample to TruDiagnostic, a company that measures epigenetic chemical groups on DNA and offers to reveal an overall biological age as well as a person’s pace of aging and the biological ages of each of 11 organ systems, including the heart and brain. I’ll get a brain age score from NeuroAge once I complete the cognitive tasks on offer. I’ll also submit some physical measures like grip strength. And I’ll upload a series of selfies to an app developed by a team at Harvard that promises to tell me my face age. That’s exactly what it sounds like—an estimate of how old my face looks. I’m intrigued to see my scores, even though I know I shouldn’t put too much stock in them. The first time I took a test, four years ago, the company I used gave me a biological age that matched my chronological age, which was a little disappointing and, if I’m honest, a bit underwhelming. A year later, the same company told me I had a young heart but a relatively old brain, liver, and hormonal system. My lifestyle hasn’t changed much since then. Will the years have made much difference? (Ultra competitors—who pay $4,499 rather than the $999 cost of regular entry—are also offered a range of other blood tests and clocks, as well as MRI and DEXA scans. I’ve got complimentary press access to the standard package.) Glorioso is also hoping to gather information about the effects of some purported longevity approaches. During the competition, some participants will be offered red-light masks, access to a sauna, or other low-risk offerings that partner companies who are sponsoring the event to varying degrees might want to collect data on. “A lot of these companies just can’t afford to run [clinical] trials,” says Glorioso. She also sees the event as a public health initiative. A couple of years ago, David Sinclair, who studies aging at Harvard Medical School, and his colleagues estimated that if we could slow down aging in the general population and increase life expectancy by one year, it would save the US economy $38 trillion . The event officially kicks off in January, but around 120 people have already signed up, says Glorioso. Ultimately, she expects 500 participants. Each person’s six-month run starts as soon as they take their baseline measurements, whenever that may be. A handful of people have already started. “I think the majority of people are going to want to sign up after the holidays,” says Glorioso. “They’re not going to want to be trying to win an aging contest over Christmas and Hanukkah.” Glorioso took her own baseline measurements back in August. Those initial tests suggested that her biological age was around 10 years below her chronological age. That sounded pretty impressive to me until I looked at the leaderboard and saw that competitor @Fred had a biological age 28.8 years below his chronological age. The leaderboard is pretty sparse at the moment, as only seven people have logged their baseline measurements so far. Six of them have biological ages tracking low, but one 47-year-old has been given a biological age of 68.1. She’s competing publicly, so I can see the breakdown of her scores. The worst is for the speed at which she can stand from sitting in a chair—by that measure, she’s been given a biological age of 100. Hillary Lin, a longevity-focused physician in New York, has just started logging her baseline measurements for the competition. She tells me she’s taken biological age tests in the past and that they’ve tended to give scores below her chronological age, which is currently 37. Last year, the TruDiagnostic test put her pace of aging at 0.75—suggesting she’s only doing nine months’ worth of aging in a typical year. “That’s supposed to be quite good,” she says. If it had been up to her, Lin says, she would have incorporated more blood tests into the competition, to build a fuller picture of a person’s health. And she’s worried that a six-month period might not be long enough to see changes in biological measures of aging. Still, she’s excited, and is already making plans to improve her sleep, diet, and exercise. But she already follows a high-protein, low-carb diet and works out at the gym every day. She also visits a sauna every few days (sauna use has been linked to improved heart health ). Glorioso’s efforts are impressive too. She tells me she’s started drinking a smoothie made from a pond plant that has been linked to health improvements , and that she’s cut added sugar and deep-fried foods from her diet. events.title: US pressures Europe to release diesel reserves as Trump threatens export ban
events.summary: Donald Trump has said he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves as he considers banning US exports of the fuel. The president's comment comes after diesel prices hit record highs on UK forecourts this week, as the Iran war continues to put pressure on the supply of refined fuels. The UK is heavily reliant on imported diesel from the US. But with US voters also facing higher fuel costs ahead of the midterm elections in November, Trump has threatened to restrict diesel exports . The UK has been discussing the US supply threats with the EU which is holding a meeting on Friday on the issue. Banning exports would flood the US market with diesel, and could bring prices down significantly for American drivers. But experts warn such a ban would put further pressure on diesel prices in other countries, unless they can access further supplies. The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels per day, with most of it going to Latin America. European countries including France, the Netherlands and the UK, also import a significant amount from the US following the reduction in Russian and Middle Eastern sources of diesel. Russia's invasion of Ukraine led to sanctions, diverting Russian sales away from Europe. More recently Ukrainian attacks on Russian refining capacity has had a knock-on effect on global supply. The US-led war on Iran has constrained the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel from that region. On Thursday, Trump was asked whether he would call on European countries to release some of their own diesel reserves. "We may do that. They have some diesel," he said. An earlier post from US Treasury Scott Bessent on social media urged Europe to get ready to release some of their own diesel supplies immediately, arguing that US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar. Diesel prices in the UK hit record highs this week and are hovering just under 200p per litre, according to motoring organisation the RAC. Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of the imports coming from the US. The Netherlands and Belgium together provide more than a third of UK diesel imports. UK Energy Minister Martin McCluskey was on a call with European counterparts on Thursday to discuss the potential ban. A source familiar with the discussions told the BBC it was prudent to prepare a co-ordinated response with other countries, including those across EU, but added that there were still European reserves left from a coordinated release of strategic fuel stocks earlier in the year. "We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry," a government spokesperson said. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages, though prices are expected to rise further. What a US diesel export ban could mean for you Published 6 days ago International Energy Agency rules say member states, including the UK, must hold oil stocks equivalent to 90 days of net oil imports. EU rules say member must hold reserves to cover 61 days of domestic consumption. In total the EU holds nearly 109 million tons of emergency crude and fuel stocks, with around a third in diesel and related fuel products. A European Commission spokesperson said that there were "lots of calls, lots of meetings" taking place on the diesel situation, including with "high level contacts" in the US administration. Potentially adding to the pressure on the global diesel market, Chinese refiners have reportedly halted October exports of some fuel products as Beijing prioritises domestic supplies.Prices of petrol and diesel globally have skyrocketed since the outbreak of the US-Israel war in Iran in February. The closure of the vital Strait of Hormuz, which typically transports around a fifth of the world's oil and gas, has pushed up the price of products made from oil. An export ban from Russia, also a major supplier of diesel, has added to the pressure on prices. Trump has argued that keeping any surplus barrels of diesel in the US would lower pump prices domestically, offering immediate relief to drivers, truckers, and businesses ahead of the midterm elections. But David Fyfe, chief economist at Argus Media, said cutting off American supply would be likely to cause international prices to skyrocket. Diesel prices have hit an all-time high in the UK, with the latest RAC figures showing average pump prices at 199.79p per litre, up from 142.38p Diesel is harder to refine than gasoline and, because it is used by the haulage industry and in agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand. The UK has four refineries which produce more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel to meet the country's needs. There were 15.1 million diesel vehicles on UK roads at the end of June, according to the Department for Transport.

events.title: How Greg Jackson runs Octopus Energy with no HR, no bonuses, and no succession plan
events.summary: The Signal Interview In a little more than a decade, Octopus Energy has grown from an outlandish idea into Britain’s largest energy provider. It now powers 12 million homes in eight countries, manages wind and solar farms from Scotland to South Korea, manufactures heat pumps, installs smart meters, leases out 50,000 electric vehicles, and supplies technology to utilities around the world. The tentacles of this “Octoverse” all lead back to Greg Jackson, a founder-CEO who has built his 13,000-person company without bonuses, HR or IT teams, or a succession plan. Beyond the walls of the company’s London headquarters, which is filled with thousands of its plushy pink octopus mascots, Jackson’s empire may look like an unwieldy one. It is not, he insists: “The thing that’s connecting it all is the underlying insight: that the technologies of electrification can deliver tremendous cost savings, but only if you build a new system.” And building that new system requires using every tool at his disposal. “There’s a scene in the movie where the astronauts are stranded and they’re going to die unless the solution is found. And on the ground, Mission Control assembles … everything there is on the space station, like duct tape and bits of piping, and they say, this is all we’ve got to save their lives,” he explains. “In any business, you choose your constraints, and then how you assemble the stuff you have to create the outcome you want.” Octopus’ job is “to take all these ingredients and say, how can we outcompete the old world of energy with better products and services with better value?” Jackson says, before reaching back to the beginning of that old world for another analogy. “When [Thomas] Edison first started building electricity businesses, he didn’t just have to innovate, fund, and build centralized electricity generation, which he did. He also had to invent the grid and distribution model. He also had to invent or sell the products that use electricity, from lightbulbs to music players. And if I look at what we’re doing, it’s almost trivial in comparison.” How to run a 13,000-person company with no HR department The growth of Octopus, which had revenues of £13.7 billion last year and a valuation of $9 billion at its last fundraising, poses a challenge for its irrepressible founder: how to transmit to thousands of employees the energy that has powered him since he dropped out of school at 16 to write video games. Jackson no longer knows each staff member by name, but he still runs his company by the same rhythms with which he started it. Each Monday starts with a gathering of senior executives to review performance data from the previous week. That helps maintain “pace and alignment,” Jackson says. Each week ends with “family dinner,” a Friday afternoon all-hands event at which the company recaps its latest innovations, achievements, and challenges. The Friday sessions began over beers with a small founding team, and Jackson “discovered that it was the best way of reminding you how great your colleagues were, and re-energizing you on the big picture.” Livestreams have since replaced in-person drinks. But the gatherings help Octopus “start the week left-brain, end it right-brain,” Jackson says, and help him explain to staff what they need to do next “and maintain the energy to feel great about it.” The company has no intranet or staff newsletters, he adds, so if people don’t tune in to “family dinner,” they won’t know what’s happening. Less is more in internal communications, he says: “The more information you put out there, the less it gets read. What you want to do is make sure the stuff that goes out there is canonical and consumed.” Octopus also has no central human resources department, devolving people management responsibilities to individual teams unless legal staff need to step in. Still a private company, it gives equity to every employee, but it pays no bonuses outside a few sales roles. Jackson says this is because he’s determined to focus people on the company’s success, rather than their own individual advancement. Similarly, Octopus sets no divisional performance targets, to keep each division from promoting whatever will make them look best at the expense of others, he adds. “The most important thing for us is to build trust among our team, so they wake up every morning thinking, ‘How do I drive the company’s mission?’ Not, ‘How do I get myself promoted?’” Hands-on leadership, from the cockpit to the customers Even as Octopus has grown to span industries as diverse as renewable power generation and software licensing, Jackson says his job has barely changed. The CEO’s role is still to understand customers and industry economics; set the vision for where the company needs to go; and build a team with the expertise and innovative impulses to get it there. For a pilot, the view from the cockpit window of a small Cessna is not that different from that of an Airbus A380, he says: “The difference comes when you look back.” If Octopus became a more complex organization, “then I’d get drawn more into wandering down the aisle of the plane than looking forward out the window,” he reasons. “The bit that really matters for me is being in the cockpit, looking forward, however many people we’ve got behind us.” So Jackson is constantly checking that his headcount is not growing faster than Octopus is adding new customers, as he looks to avoid diseconomies of scale and guards against the spread of bureaucracy. Yet he is equally anxious about ensuring that he is not losing touch with customers as their numbers run into the millions. Octopus was built on a proprietary technology platform called Kraken, which now has an $8.7 billion valuation and will soon spin out as a standalone company with its own listing. Kraken gives Jackson and every member of his staff a “single view” of everything that is happening in the company, from customer service to pricing, energy trading to finance. Despite that tech-driven transparency, Jackson has maintained a habit of regularly meeting customers face-to-face. In the two weeks before our interview, he met roughly 1,000 customers at three different events, he estimates. “I stand on stage and talk to them, and then I get off the stage and have beers with them and understand their real experiences. They tell me not what our reports say, but what their real experience of dealing with our team is.” Everyone who signs up for an Octopus service is given Jackson’s email address. He used to answer each message himself, until Octopus reached 1.2 million customers and he found himself falling asleep at his keyboard at 2 am. Now his chief of staff and a team of five people farm out customers’ complaints and observations to the relevant executives, but he thinks the system still builds a “magic connectivity” with customers. “We’re not crazy hippies,” he says. “If we genuinely love our customers, they reciprocate.” How a CEO replaces themself when there’s

events.title: Third-country decision a ‘devastating result,’ lawyer says
events.summary: Immigrant advocates are grappling with the Supreme Court’s decision to allow the Trump administration to move forward with third-country deportations, which will leave the policy in place for months while they wait for the court to rule on it. Trina Realmuto, lead counsel for the plaintiffs that challenged the policy at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, called it a “devastating result.” She warned migrants could be sent to countries “where they may face persecution, torture, imprisonment, or other grave danger.” The Trump administration has signed deals with various countries to accept deported migrants, many of them in Africa. Burundi was the latest to announce it will accept migrants. The Supreme Court’s unsigned order this week lifted a ruling requiring migrants receive notice of — and a chance to challenge — their deportation to countries where they have no personal ties. The high court will hear oral arguments on the case, but not until December, meaning a decision will come next year. The Department of Homeland Security celebrated this week’s move, with the agency’s general counsel declaring it “a bad day for criminal illegals and open borders activists alike.” The arrangements have drawn mounting scrutiny, most recently after migrants deported to Equatorial Guinea were held at gunpoint and beaten . Congressional Democrats are vowing to investigate the deportations if they take control of the House or Senate — or both — in November’s midterm elections. — Adrian Elimian

events.title: West Virginia's Justice may delay decision on running for governor
events.summary: Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., “may have to” wait until after the midterms to decide on whether to run for his old job as governor — and challenge incumbent Gov. Patrick Morrisey, he told Semafor in an interview this week. The Republican senator said he doesn’t “like jerking people around” and wanted to announce within a couple weeks, but added there’s “too much stuff going on” in the Senate for him to reflect on the choice. “I really wanted to put some time in to really think: Do you really want to do this?” he said. Nonetheless, Justice said he plans to make his decision “really soon.” Most Republican senators think he will challenge Morrisey for his old job; Justice has made no secret that he thinks he’d do a better job than his successor. “I love the people in West Virginia, and I don’t know that we’re going the right way,” he said.

events.title: A potential 2028 Democratic kingmaker has advice for candidates
events.summary: The News New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham has a message for the potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidates who are passing through her state: Focus on the children. Lujan Grisham, a Democrat who’s set to leave office after this year, told Semafor the candidates “absolutely should” be running on universal childcare proposals. Her state has enacted its own universal childcare program, though she acknowledged a national program could be “challenging” without tax increases. “What I would do in that position is make it really clear that you’ll create incentives and grants so that states have real opportunity,” she said. Lujan Grisham said she’d met or spoken with many of the possible presidential aspirants who have visited the state, including Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. Their conversations were “less introductory and more policy,” she said. Know More New Mexico has been added to the early primary states, following the familiar trio of South Carolina, Nevada, and New Hampshire, and it could shake up Democrats’ strategies in the presidential primary. Lujan Grisham said she plans to endorse, depending on how the field shapes up. “It depends on who’s in that primary, doesn’t it? I mean, I would like to be in a position to get to do that,” she said. Lujan Grisham also weighed in on the criticism that the Democratic Governors Association has received for not investing more in the Texas gubernatorial race. “I think the DGA in this climate should be spending everywhere, and they’re raising to do exactly that. I mean, they’ve never done an expanded map like this,” she said. The DGA’s chair, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, a potential 2028 presidential candidate himself, has faced criticism from other Democrats for not putting more resources into the expensive Texas race. But Lujan Grisham said that “picking on the DGA is not the best strategy.”

events.title: The AI industry balances Trump and a changing Washington
events.summary: Ashley’s view The tech industry is facing strange headwinds in Washington after meeting with President Donald Trump and senior administration officials this week and signing a “morally binding” accord on AI. The meeting with Trump was largely successful for all of the companies involved. But now these same firms have to navigate maintaining ties with the president while placating Democrats who could very well control both houses of Congress next year. That’s not to mention what could be a massively consequential midterm election, fueled by AI anxiety among voters , that could test the bounds of their power. “Companies are going to have to make it more specific, on how they’re going to operationalize it,” Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, told Semafor about the new White House accord on “Super Intelligence” signed by the leaders of several top firms and Trump this week, including OpenAI President Greg Brockman. “We’ve certainly approached this believing … it’s also in our self-interest to make sure that people feel that we are actually building things safely and deploying responsibly,” Lehane said, adding that OpenAI’s support for certain state-level AI bills and its hopes for a federal bill will remain the same. “That’s almost either a democratic market force, or the actual market forces themselves. Like, if you’re making cars, you’re going to want to make sure the cars are safe, or people aren’t going to buy your cars, whether there are regulations or not,” he added. Know More Before lawmakers departed Washington to focus on campaigning ahead of the November elections, AI companies were still in active discussions on Capitol Hill. They’re trying to influence forthcoming bills and determine where they can find consensus with lawmakers, a tech industry source and a source who works on AI policy told Semafor. Companies know that the midterms are likely to mean a Democratic-run House and possibly a Democratic-run Senate, and with that will come more momentum to pass AI legislation — and likely more scrutiny of their operations, particularly for firms that have demonstrated ties with the Trump administration. “There’s a world where people are smarter and smarter about these issues, and bills are going to be introduced imminently that are much better than what we’ve seen,” the AI policy source told Semafor. After the election, legislating is an obvious place to go, given the public and many lawmakers in both parties want to see something done, the tech industry source told Semafor. Considering where the Trump administration was a year ago — that is , attempting to ban state-level AI bills — progress toward federal AI policy is slow, but it’s inching forward, the tech industry source said. The FTC also kicked off its own AI inquiry, which may not yield much in the end, but nevertheless represents a signal from the administration that regulators are prepared to use existing laws to go after any companies that they suspect have hurt consumers. Still, the White House’s pro-AI posture is unlikely to fundamentally change, and Trump will remain the most important voice on it until the end of his term. Groups that are pushing for data center expansion and industry-friendly laws have plenty of money and resources, plus their own complicated financial ties to the AI and tech companies themselves. Anthropic may be experiencing the most whiplash since the surreal AI summit: Days after a federal court upheld its designation by the Pentagon as a supply chain risk, CEO Dario Amodei dined with Trump at the White House. The administration has repeatedly painted Anthropic as the face of a pro-AI safety movement that is “woke” and composed of “doomers” — too focused on AI’s harms and trying to gin up fear for ulterior motives. “I think they’re going to try to walk this tightrope for two years,” the person who works on AI policy told Semafor. “They’re in a weird place. [Undersecretary of Defense] Emil Michael hates you, and is tweeting about you every day. Nonetheless, the government seems to find you indispensable to their operations.” Sarah Heck, a policy lead at Anthropic, posted on X following the White House meeting: “You can’t do safety from second place.” She shared a video clip of Amodei applauding the accord while saying AI still has very real risks and how companies address them is still under discussion. On Thursday, Heck added: “To be clear, I’m talking about the US and its allies here: We can’t ensure AI is developed safely unless the US is in the lead.” Notable The idea for what became Trump’s pact with the AI industry came from a conversation between Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and House Speaker Mike Johnson, Semafor scooped .

events.title: OpenAI fires workers for 'mishandling sensitive information'
events.summary: OpenAI has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling information, including work which involved an external organisation analysing AI models. "Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," a spokesperson told the BBC. The ChatGPT-maker did not name the sacked workers, but at least two of them were involved in safety research at the firm. The firings come as the debate over AI safety and the risks the technology may pose to humanity intensified in recent months. "We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," a spokesperson for OpenAI said. Concerns over AI safety have made headlines after some researchers and industry executives called for more guardrails around the technology. OpenAI has come under under intense scrutiny after its models went rogue and hacked several platforms, including Australian government websites . In an incident in July, one of the firm's AI models accessed the internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face. That incident led OpenAI to review the activities of its AI agents, which are designed to execute tasks autonomously based on simple instructions. The firm said this week it has notified more than 100 organisations about incidents involving unauthoritised activity linked to its systems. Being notified "does not mean that any private information was accessed" or that a system was compromised, it said. Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit Published 4 days ago OpenAI says its rogue AI tried to hack other companies Published 29 July OpenAI scraps rollout of new model over safety concerns Published 5 days ago In September, researcher Jacob Coxon, who left Anthropic , called for AI development to slow down so its potential risks could be properly assessed. Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman have also called for measures to address concerns over AI. On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses - including leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - to discuss AI. After the gathering at the White House, Trump posted a document that he called a "morally binding" agreement that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks. Some technology experts criticised the pact, pointing out that it allowed AI companies to regulate themselves. Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight of the technology.
